#7830. The Best Non-Electric Heaters of 2026, Tested and Reviewed

By Tom Scalisi, Stacey L. Nash, Additional research provided by Tony Carrick

Published Nov 4, 2026 9:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

When a storm knocks out power, a non-electric heater is your best defense against plummeting temperatures. If your local utility is sidelined by impassable roads, it’s one of the only reliable ways to keep your family warm until your HVAC system is back up.

Choosing the right unit means evaluating fuel types, heating capacity, and portability. To find the top choices, we assembled and tested a range of well-reviewed models across indoor and outdoor spaces. The Mr. Heater MH9BX Portable Buddy Propane Heater earned our top spot overall thanks to its lightweight design, versatile tank hookups, and dependable performance inside and out. Read on to explore our hands-on test results and see the rest of our picks for the best non-electric heaters.

Bottom line: Non-electric heaters provide essential backup heat during power outages, but safety and proper use are critical. Explore our top picks to find the best option for your needs.

Before shopping for a non-electric heater, it’s important to understand the product’s limitations. A non-electric heater shouldn’t replace a home’s primary HVAC system. Attempting to use a non-electric heater as the main source of heat for a home presents several hazards. Gas heaters can produce high carbon monoxide levels in a home, which can cause illness and even death if not carefully monitored. Non-electric heaters also use an open flame and fuel, creating a potential fire hazard.

For these reasons, non-electric heaters should never be left unattended for long and should never be used in a confined space with sealed doors and windows. It’s also a good idea to have a separate carbon monoxide detector in the same room as the heater. Look for non-electric heaters that will shut off automatically when carbon monoxide levels in a room reach too high a level. If you’re looking for a primary heat source for your home, you’ll want to shop for an HVAC system.

Whether it’s propane, kerosene, natural gas, indoor, or outdoor, our top picks include non-electric heaters to suit a variety of different needs. These heaters were put through the paces in our hands-on testing. They come from some of the best-known names in heaters and range in size from portable 3,800 British thermal units (BTU) models for camping to large 50,000 BTU heaters for industrial use.

Take heat where it’s needed with this portable propane heater from Mr. Heater. The Buddy weighs just 10.6 pounds but packs a punch with a maximum output of 9,000 BTUs, which is enough to heat a 225-square-foot room or the inside of a large tent. With its rugged design and large handle, the Buddy can be transported almost anywhere. It also has a bevy of safety features, including a low oxygen shutoff and a tip-over shutoff. Power and portability make the Buddy an excellent option for a wide variety of heating needs.

Let’s start by saying that the tip-over shutoff works. Testing started inside a somewhat crowded garage, and the heater got tipped over. It shut off immediately and no propane leaked. As far as performance, this heater puts out an impressive amount of heat for its size. We used it in a small office and nearly got cooked out.

The weight, even with the 1-pound propane bottle attached, is light enough to be portable. We used the swivel regulator to attach a hose to a 20-pound tank. Of course, the heater loses some of its portability when it has a 20-pound tank attached.

This heater worked inside or out and got tested in a garage, a living room, on a patio, and in a shop. The only issue was the slight odor from the propane and a light hum from the pilot light. Once the propane started to get low, the heater got noisier, emitting a popping noise in the few minutes before the propane ran out.

What our tester says: “I was blown away by how much heat this little thing puts out—it nearly cooked us out of a small office. Plus, when it accidentally got knocked over in the garage, the safety shutoff kicked in instantly.”—Stacey L. Nash, Product Reviews tester and writer

Get the Mr. Heater MH9BX non-electric heater at Amazon or The Home Depot.

This relatively affordable outdoor gas heater boasts a 9-foot heating radius thanks to its height. However, in hands-on testing, we found the height put that heating radius a bit high for most uses. With some adjustability, this heater puts out 46,000 BTUs. The heat is comfortable, and the attractive design feels upscale in the backyard.

Assembly took about 30 to 45 minutes and included filling the base with water or sand (we chose water). You can use the included tools, but a ratchet wrench of your own will help when tightening down all the screws and covers. The body is made of durable stainless steel that had no problem weathering a blustery rainstorm (or two).

The heater stays maneuverable with two small wheels on the base. At 91.3 inches tall, this model towers above most of the competitors. In this instance, we’re not sure the height really helped; during testing, we found that it was so tall that we couldn’t feel the heat quite as well in colder temperatures. It still radiated that full 9 feet, but heat rises, which meant that those of us on the shorter end of the spectrum couldn’t feel the warmth when farther away from the heater.

Get the Amazon Basics non-electric heater at Amazon.

The small size and weight of this heater are ideal for taking it along on a cool-weather camping trip or an outdoor picnic in brisk autumn air. It can even warm up a chilly garage workshop. The Little Buddy measures just 12 inches high and 9.75 inches in diameter and weighs just 5.85 pounds, which is small enough to fit into most backpacks. With its ability to pump out 3,800 BTUs of heat per hour, this little heater can warm up to 95 square feet of space. It runs off of a standard 1-pound propane canister, which lasts between 5 and 6 hours. Safety features include a low-oxygen supply shutoff and an accidental tip-over shutoff.

This little heater is incredibly handy, lightweight, and quiet; we barely noticed it was there. Hunters could use it in a blind without announcing their presence. Assembly and setup were simple, too. All it took to get going was connecting the propane and pressing the igniter button. We happened to have the 20-year-old predecessor to this little guy. While the current Little Buddy doesn’t put out quite as much heat, it’s much safer and quieter. It’s a good thing it has the tip-over shutoff because the 8-inch base is easy to knock over. The downside is a single heat setting and the fact that it can only be used with 1-pound propane bottles.

Get the Mr. Heater MH4B non-electric heater at Amazon, Tractor Supply Co., or The Home Depot.

Pumping out 50,000 BTUs of heat through its cannon-shaped design, this kerosene heater from Dyna-Glo is helpful when it comes to warming up spaces that a home’s HVAC system doesn’t service, like garages and large sheds that function as workshops. A powerful blower allows it to heat up to 1,200 square feet of unheated space, and its ample 5-gallon tank can provide heat for up to 14 hours. A convenient fuel gauge lets the user know how many hours of fuel are remaining. There’s a large handle that lends to easy transport of this heater, which weighs about 27 pounds. Safety features include overheat shut-off protection and a flameout sensor.

This heater is no joke. We tested it in an 800-square-foot uninsulated shop in 50 degree Fahrenheit weather. We already have a wood stove in the shop but wanted to see how the Dyna-Glo compared. This heater single-handedly made more heat than the wood stove. Not only that, but the powerful fan pumped the heat through the space much more efficiently. The owner’s manual specifies that this heater can be used with seven fuel sources, including diesel. Kerosene is the recommended choice because it burns cleaner, but it’s nice to know you have options.

There were a couple of downsides, however. First, we tested the very base model, which has only one heat setting. The second con—this heater is loud. You can’t have a nice quiet conversation while it’s going. Finally, the fan requires electricity, so it’s not useful for power outages.

Get the Dyna-Glo non-electric heater at Amazon.

For raw heating power, it’s tough to beat this natural gas heater. With 30,000 BTUs, this convection heater can make a 1,000-square-foot space feel toasty. In addition to being powerful, it’s versatile and can be mounted to the wall or sit on the floor. Features include a thermostat that enables easy temperature control and an automatic low-oxygen shut-off valve.

Shoppers will also be attracted to its design. With its narrow profile, fireplace looks, and visible flames, this is a heater that can be displayed in almost any living area. For those without a natural gas hookup, the Mr. Heater 30,000 BTU heater is also available in a propane version.

Get the Mr. Heater natural gas heater at Amazon or Tractor Supply Co.

Dura Heat’s TT-360 propane heater is a great choice for anyone who keeps a 20-pound bottle of propane or two around the home (like under a grill). It features a bracket that attaches directly to the collar of these bottles, holding the burner safely above the control valve. The heater measures 20 inches from the bottom of the tank to the top of the heater, which is compact enough to move around easily, unlike larger models that might look nice but are less portable.

This propane heater produces 30,000; 35,000; or 40,000 BTUs of heat, depending on the setting. It has a 360-degree design, which makes it great for patios and other spaces as well as garages (as long as the garage is ventilated). It has a tip-over switch to keep it safe, but that’s the extent of its safety provisions.

There are two versions of this heater: one with a built-in lighter and the other without (that’s the version we got). It was honestly a nightmare to light with matches. We went through 10 matches before switching to a barbecue lighter (which still required patience). But once lit, it produced lots of heat, even in an outdoor space. When it came to installation, we were skeptical because it’s just one set screw that bolts it to the tank’s collar. Yet, it was surprisingly secure, and it can swap from tank to tank in just a few seconds. Beyond the fact that it was so ridiculously difficult to light with matches, we really liked the Dura Heat TT-360.

Get the Dura Heat non-electric heater at Amazon, Wayfair, or Walmart.

Thanks to this quartz glass tube heater from Hiland, a backyard living space doesn’t have to go into hibernation come wintertime. Rated at 40,000 BTUs, this outdoor heater generates plenty of warmth to ward off the coldest weather. With its stainless steel finish, quartz glass, and visible flames, this Hiland tower heater will add warmth as well as style to a patio. A control knob allows users to adjust the flame size while an auto-tilt shut-off switch provides safety. Thanks to a sturdy set of wheels as its base, this heater can also be moved around a yard or a patio space.

In addition to being an attractive backyard heater, this model looks much heavier than it is. We found it surprisingly easy to move around and even carry. The first time the flame shot up the glass tube, we gasped. The white metal “cage” that surrounds the heater reminded us of a hamster cage at first, but once it’s lit up, it definitely looks like nothing of the sort. It’s beautiful and fun. Although this model doesn’t put out as much heat as other outdoor heaters, it sure looks a lot cooler doing it. The Hiland builds more ambience while putting out a decent amount of heat in the surrounding 3 or 4 feet.

Our one issue was assembly. The directions estimated 1 hour for assembly. However, it took us almost 2 hours from start to finish. We even used power tools instead of the manual tools that came with the heater. A good portion of that time was spent peeling a protective film off of the stainless steel panels. Make sure you have more than one person around when putting this heater together.

Get the AZ Patio Heaters non-electric heater at The Home Depot.

The Sengoku heater is an excellent indoor/outdoor heater. It comes with a tube and pump device to help fill the kerosene tank. Once full, it’s a matter of turning it on, and that’s it. This heater puts out a serious amount of heat. We used it in an open garage on a cold day and had to start taking off layers to keep from overheating. The Sengoku is so quiet that we forgot that it was running.

A big downside to this model is that it gets very hot when in use. It’s not the type of heater for homes with children or pets. And you have to make sure there’s good ventilation when used inside, per the instructions.

Get the Sengoku non-electric heater at Amazon or Ace Hardware.

The non-electric heaters were all tested outdoors, and models approved for indoor use were tested indoors as well. We evaluated each one based on an established set of parameters, including assembly and setup, heating radius, portability, and performance.

Before purchasing a non-electric heater, it’s important to think about what size and type of heater best fits your needs. Manufacturers rate heaters for indoor or outdoor use. Weight is also an issue, especially if you plan on moving the heater from location to location. Also consider tank size, as this will dictate how often it will need to be refueled and also determines the heater’s power, which affects how much space the heater can warm.

Determine whether the plan is to use the heater indoors, outdoors, or both. Outdoor-only heaters create intense bursts of heat that won’t dissipate into the surrounding air quickly. As such, they are significantly more powerful than indoor heaters.

To prevent the buildup of dangerous carbon monoxide, indoor models should not be used in confined spaces, such as a small room. It’s also a good idea to have a carbon monoxide detector in the same room as the unit.

Many portable non-electric heaters can be used indoors and outdoors. Make sure to check the heater’s ratings before making a purchase.

Decide what is needed from an electric heater. For example, do you require a heater for a dedicated space or a unit that can move from place to place? Knowing how a heater might be used can help determine whether to look for a portable or stationary unit.

Portable heaters weigh as little as 5 pounds up to 20 pounds and are available as radiant, convection, or forced-air varieties. Many portable heaters feature impact-resistant construction and large handles for easy transport. Some even come with carrying cases.

Larger non-electric heaters, such as the powerful tower heaters used on backyard patios and in outdoor eating areas at restaurants, weigh upward of 70 pounds, not including the 20-pound tanks that power them. While these are not portable, most have wheels to allow for repositioning. Other permanent heaters include kits that enable mounting on a wall or to the floor.

Tank size determines just how long a heater will work before it’s time to replace the fuel. Kerosene heaters have tanks that hold liquid kerosene. A kerosene heater with a 1-gallon tank will provide about 14 hours of use before it needs more fuel.

Propane works differently. Because propane gas is a compressed liquid, it comes in tanks that attach to the heater via a valve and a hose. Larger heaters use a 20-pound tank, which provides about 10 hours of use. Portable propane heaters use 16-ounce canisters, which last about 3 hours.

Whereas most kerosene tanks include fuel gauges, most propane tanks do not, making it difficult to know just how much remains in the tank.

It’s best to take the Goldilocks approach when selecting a gas heater since a heater with insufficient power will leave a room too cold, while a heater that is too powerful will make it too hot. The best non-electric heater needs to be just right.

Energy is measured in BTUs. More BTUs mean more heat output. Most manufacturers also rate their indoor heaters by square footage. For example, an indoor heater with a maximum BTU of 9,000 can heat up to 225 square feet. While 7,000 BTUs might be adequate to warm a 300-square-foot room, an outdoor heater may need more than 40,000 BTUs to keep an open-air space warm. Indoor and portable heaters typically have an output of around 5,000 BTUs.

Although it’s tempting to get the most powerful heater you can afford, you might regret it. A heater with a high minimum BTU output will quickly overheat a smaller space, making it challenging to regulate the room temperature. Unless a sauna is the goal, make sure to pay attention to square-footage ratings when deciding which heater will provide that just-right temperature.

Non-electric heaters fall into three categories: propane, kerosene, and natural gas. Some heaters are dual fuel, which means they can run off either propane or natural gas. While all these types can do the job when it comes to providing heat, they each operate differently. Understanding which works best for your specific needs is key to making the right decision when purchasing a non-electric space heater.

All non-electric heaters produce radiant or convection heat. Radiant heaters generate infrared heat using metal tubes that radiate heat, which warms objects in the room. With radiant heat, the closer you are to the heater, the warmer you get.

A convection heater pulls in the air around it, warms it, and then distributes the warmed air with a blower. While radiant heaters will quickly warm people close to the heater, convection heaters do a better job of distributing heat around a room.

If you’re a football fan, then you‘ve likely seen propane and kerosene forced-air heaters warming the sidelines of games played in subfreezing temperatures. Forced-air heaters have a distinctive cannon shape and function by blowing heat in one direction. They are mighty but noisy, which makes them attractive for industrial settings such as barns, warehouses, and construction sites, but they’re impractical for home use.

Propane heaters come in various forms, ranging from tower-shaped outdoor heaters to smaller portable models. Propane heaters use refillable tanks and canisters ranging in size from a 16-ounce canister to a 20-pound tank.

Propane heaters that use small canisters are lightweight. When used properly, they can be safe for indoor or outdoor use and are easy to move from room to room. Some are even small enough to take on a camping trip. Small propane heaters are capable of producing up to 18,000 BTUs of heat output. Larger outdoor-only models are tower shaped, making them ideal for patios and decks. These large heaters can pump out up to 40,000 BTUs of heat.

Propane heaters have a low oxygen shutoff and a tip-over shutoff as standard safety features.

Kerosene burns efficiently and heats very quickly, making kerosene heaters an ideal option for supplemental home heating. Like propane, kerosene heaters fall into two categories: radiant and convection. Convective kerosene heaters have a tower shape with a broad base that contains the fuel and a cylinder that comprises the heater’s combustion chamber. Their circular shape allows them to warm air in all directions. Radiant heaters are rectangular and have a reflector or electric blower that directs the heat it produces in one direction.

Kerosene heaters use liquid kerosene, which is available at most home improvement stores. Unlike propane, which uses a spark for ignition, kerosene requires a wick, which soaks up and burns the fuel. Wicks typically last for about a year.

More than half the homes in the United States use natural gas as their primary heat source, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. If you’re in that half, then a natural gas non-electric heater might be for you.

Natural gas heaters function similarly to propane heaters, but instead of needing a tank, they tie directly into the home’s gas line. If the gas line is not already installed, this may require professional installation. A natural gas setup eliminates trips to refill a propane tank, but it sacrifices portability; if you opt to use natural gas, the heater must be installed close to a fixed gas connection. With this in mind, most natural gas heaters are larger, more permanent appliances.

Do keep in mind that you cannot hook up a propane heater to a natural gas line. Only install heaters designed for use with natural gas to a natural gas line.

No matter what type of fuel you choose and whether you decide on a portable permanent indoor or outdoor model, a non-electric heater is a useful appliance to have in most households. Non-electric heaters can supplement a home’s HVAC system, providing heat for those underserved cold spots. They can also extend the usability of an outdoor living space, allowing you to enjoy that deck or patio year-round.

Most importantly, non-electric heaters function as a valuable emergency heat source, keeping a family warm while they wait for the power to return after a home’s HVAC system is put out of commission by a power outage.

The benefits of owning a non-electric heater include the following:

Because non-electric heaters involve fuel and flames, it’s essential to follow certain safety guidelines and consider only models with standard safety features. A non-electric heater should have tipping and low-oxygen sensors that shut off the heater when triggered. Safe heaters will have a shield that prevents contact with an open flame, such as a glass window or a metal grate.

Even with these safety features, it’s also essential to follow some common-sense practices when using a non-electric heater. Make sure to place the heater in a low-traffic area to prevent people and pets from bumping the unit. Set up non-electric heaters on even ground to avoid fuel spills or flame exposure. Also, allow for a buffer of at least 3 feet between the heater and flammable materials.

The safety tips for non-electric heaters include the following:

Now that you’ve learned about what to look for while shopping for a non-electric heater, there may still be some lingering questions about specifics. Read on for answers to some of the most frequently asked questions.

The best way to heat a home during a power outage is to have a gas alternative. This can consist of a ventless gas fireplace that runs off of natural gas or propane, or a gas-powered heater. Since these units require no electrical connection to operate, they are an ideal backup during a winter storm power outage.

Since electric heaters use a minimum of 900 watts and as much as 1,500 watts, even a large 12-volt battery doesn’t have enough juice to power a heater, making a gas heater the best alternative to electric heat.

While there isn’t a single heater that is the safest non-electric heater, those with certain safety features are safer than those without. Look for gas heaters that have auto shut-off features that automatically turn off the unit if it tips over or begins to overheat or senses low oxygen levels in the surrounding air.

#7829. ABA tracks new challenges affecting Public Service Loan Forgiveness borrowers

The ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. (Image from Shutterstock)

For lawyers and other student loan borrowers working in public service jobs, the path to having their remaining federal student loan balances discharged under Public Service Loan Forgiveness program after 120 months of qualifying payments is becoming increasingly difficult to navigate.

Under the PSLF program, created by Congress in 2007 with the support of the ABA, borrowers who have made 120 timely payments on their federal direct loans while employed full time in qualifying public service jobs are eligible to receive forgiveness of whatever portion of their loan remains after completing the payments.

But the ABA is closely monitoring new problems affecting borrowers working toward loan forgiveness. Issues include processing delays, payment record errors, growing application backlogs, and changes in Department of Education policies and procedures—some implemented with little or no public notice. Significant staffing cuts at the department, including a 40% reduction in Federal Student Aid office staff, have added to concerns about whether problems can be resolved promptly.

For reasons that are not yet clear, many borrowers have not received credit for qualifying loan repayments they’ve made since June, which means those payments cannot yet be counted toward their 120-repayment requirement. The Department of Education has not offered information or explanation on the missing information.

Separately, the Department of Education confirmed in August that it has reduced the number of some borrowers’ qualifying payments, potentially delaying when their remaining loan balances will be forgiven. After initially describing the falling payment counts as a “data issue,” the department subsequently said the changes were intentional, correcting coding errors during the Biden administration that resulted in inaccurate payment counts for some borrowers.

For example, some of the PSLF credit reversals may have been for payments made in a repayment plan that didn’t qualify for PSLF, although without an explanation from the Education Department about this process, some borrowers believe their payment counts were removed erroneously.

Without a formal announcement, the department also in July quietly eliminated the Biden-era 15-day grace period on whether PSLF-eligible payments counted as timely. As of July 1, a payment must be made “on or before the due date” to count as a qualifying payment under PSLF.

Also, a “clarification” by the department about the PSLF Buyback program is causing confusion and concern among borrowers.

The PSLF Buyback program allows public service employees to get credit toward the required 120 payments for months their loans were, e.g., in deferment or forbearance and thus not eligible for PSLF. Borrowers can apply to “buy back” those months, however, by paying what they would have paid had they been in repayment during those months.

But under updated Department of Education guidance, borrowers will not be able to buy back credit for payments made while under either of two new repayment plans—the Repayment Assistance Plan or the Tiered Standard Repayment Plan. These two new repayment plans were created in legislation signed into law by President Donald Trump in 2025.

Further causing concern is the significant application backlog for the PSLF Buyback program. As of April, the application backlog was between 70,000 to 90,000, but no new data has been released since that time. Even if the backlog has been reduced, some borrowers have waited two years or more to get credit for retroactive payments. The delay requires them to remain in their jobs and repay their loans for longer than required, thus functionally ending the buyback program.

On Oct. 21, the Department of Justice dropped its appeal of two court rulings that stayed the Department of Education’s controversial proposed rules to PSLF, which would have narrowed PSLF eligibility by excluding employees of organizations engaged in activities the department considered as having a “substantially illegal purpose.”

In August, the department had appealed the separate decisions by federal judges in Massachusetts and Washington, D.C., that had vacated the rules.

The ABA vigorously opposed the department’s proposals. In letters to Secretary of Education Linda McMahon, ABA Presidents Bill Bay and Michelle Behnke cited a lack of statutory and other legal authority. The ABA House of Delegates reinforced that opposition through adoption of Resolution 505 at its February 2026 midyear meeting, which opposes efforts to politicize this politically neutral program.

“Any perception that benefits are awarded based on political affiliation or ideology undermines the legitimacy of programs such as PSLF, discourages participation, and decreases the requisite public confidence they require to be successful,” the report accompanying the resolution states.

The ABA recognizes the crucial role PSLF plays in encouraging individuals to pursue careers that provide much-needed public services, including public defense services and civil legal aid representation to underrepresented communities such as senior citizens and veterans.

Since the program’s creation, the ABA has consistently responded to attacks and efforts to repeal or cut the program, including direct lobbying efforts through multiple Congresses and administrations; major grassroots campaigns including as a priority at past ABA Day fly-in events in Washington, D.C.; and working alongside its allies in the PSLF Coalition, a collaboration of more than 100 nonprofit and public service organizations.

In all, the ABA has adopted three policies supporting the program, including one in 2002 calling for the program’s creation. The most recent, Resolution 505, urges removal of the requirement that applicants be in qualifying employment at the time of applying for discharge of their student loans—a current program requirement that holds borrowers in limbo, unable to change jobs until the paperwork is filed. Once the required service and payment obligations are met, the resolution states, “there should be no further obligation than to apply for the benefits owed.”

As new issues with the program continue to emerge, the ABA will continue to work with allies to identify issues affecting borrowers and press for solutions. To learn more as significant developments occur, follow us at @ABAGrassroots on LinkedIn.

#7828. The Best Holiday Decorations Across the U.S., and How to Steal the Look

These homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

Outdoor holiday decorating is an art. And while we love a tasteful string of white Christmas lights or a few pumpkins placed by the front door, why not really go for it when the holiday season rolls around? Over-the-top outdoor holiday decorations make the whole neighborhood get in the festive spirit! To help inspire you, we found some of the best maximalist holiday homes from coast to coast.

From extra spooky Halloween displays to dazzling Christmas spectacles, these homes are full of ideas you can borrow for your own yard.

A post shared by jessica archibald (@jessicarchibald)

Halloween 2026 has come and gone, but it’s never too early to start thinking about next year! Known simply as The Pumpkin House, @jessicarchibald lines her roof, porch, and yard with hundreds of jack-o’-lanterns every Halloween season. The piles of pumpkins make a big impact both during the day and at night.

Steal This Idea: All you need is pumpkins! Attach faux pumpkins to long boards to make them easier to display on the roof.

The Kraken House (@krakenhousenola) captured here by @amournola, uses blow-up decor to explore the haunted seas. The blow-up tentacles hint at a sea monster hiding beyond the windows, but the dramatic lighting is what really makes this house shine.

Steal This Idea: Skip the kid-friendly Bluey holiday inflatable this year, and attach these terrifying tentacles instead. Then turn up the drama with solar up-lights in green and purple.

Can you believe this amazing black cat is a DIY project? To transform this front porch into a Halloween stage, @allset_bygabrielle hand-carved the cat figure out of wood and painted every detail.

Steal This Idea: In addition to the vintage-inspired cat, the spooky forest framing the door was made with a mix of dead branches and faux botanicals; providing texture and a subtle sparkle.

This front entry in New York City (photographed by @victoria.nycvisit) uses dark drapery, black roses, and a wide variety of unique pumpkins and squashes to create a gothic masterpiece. Trick-or-treaters beware!

Steal This Idea: It’s amazing what a few swathes of black and burgundy fabric can do. Drape the fabric around your front door to make an eerie entrance. Then use pumpkins and vases full of dark flowers to complete the look.

This viral townhouse @stoopandthecity, is dressed to the nines for every holiday. This autumn harvest display features patterned pumpkins and cascades of fall foliage. It’s perfect for Thanksgiving or for those that prefer to skip the ghosts and goblins.

Steal This Idea: Choose faux and glass pumpkins in a cohesive color scheme, and don’t hold back on the fall foliage. Use faux stems to make the display last all season long.

A post shared by Marissa Fiala | Houston, TX (@houstonhotspots)

When it comes to Christmas lights, you can’t find much better than the extravagant homes in the River Oaks neighborhood of Houston, Texas. Each home goes all out with sparkling lights on its exterior, wrapped around every tree.

Steal This Idea: The secret to this colorful tree, captured by @houstonhotspots, is wrapping the lights tightly around the trunk and every single branch. The technique takes time but makes a big impact. Use LED lights to cut back on electricity use.

This famous house on Castro Street in San Francisco does not hold back! (Photo by @415urbanadventures.) Every exterior surface is covered in decor. The symmetrical layout keeps it looking classy instead of gaudy. And of course, the star of the show is Santa hanging in the middle, ready to deliver gifts.

Steal This Idea: The key element of this display is the garland covered in shiny Christmas ornaments. When you think you’ve gathered enough baubles, you’ll probably need even more!

The historic mill in Clifton, Ohio, is known for its over-the-top Christmas light display, featuring over four million lights! While you might not have a historic mill to decorate, the lighting techniques can be used on your own home to dazzle the entire neighborhood.

Steal This Idea: The most memorable element of this display is the iconic red lights cascading down the hillside. Try laying strings lights in rows along your entire yard to get a similar look.

A post shared by Joe Yost | Yost Team -Compass Pittsburgh (@joeyostteam)

Make your house look like one giant Christmas present by adding a larger-than-life red bow. This Pittsburgh mansion is famous for its red Christmas bow that looks beautifully whimsical in the daytime and lights up at night.

Steal This Idea: You don’t need a mansion to recreate this look. Get your own giant red bow and hang it above your front door. Here’s one available on Etsy!

A post shared by Pink Dreams Collection (@pinkdreamscollection)

One way to set your house apart for Christmas is to use a non-traditional color scheme —like pink! This darling cottage from @pinkdreamcollection is a frosted pink confection complete with pink trees and pink nutcracker figurines.

Steal This Idea: Pink or pastel Christmas decor will make your home look playful and unique. Use different shades of pink to add dimension.

A post shared by The Hazard’s Gingerbread House (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse)

This spectacular residential light display by Walter Hazard (@hazardsgingerbreadhouse) makes his home look like a technicolor gingerbread house. The secret is the wire-fencing frames he uses to create methodical light patterns. Visitors come from all over the area to witness the gorgeous lights in action.

Steal This Idea: We might not all have the same light-manipulation talent as Walter, but you can get the same grid-like coverage with LED curtain lights like these.

#7827. The Logic of Voting for a Lesser Evil - and Other Writings on the Ethics of Voting

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

Compendium of links to some of my writings on the morality of voting.

Tomorrow is election day. And - to put it mildly many of the options before voters are far from wonderful.  In all too many races, the candidates with a realistic chance of winning are all bad. This situation, like other recent elections, raises difficult questions about such issues as whether people have a duty to vote, whether it is permissible to vote for a badly flawed candidate if the alternative is even worse, and how to balance competing issues in making voting decisions.

I've written about these kinds of issues in some detail, previously, and this post links and and summarizes some of those writings. This is not a post about which candidate you should vote for in any given race. I've already written a post about why - in most cases - the Democrats are the lesser evil in races for federal offices this year (state and local elections are often a different matter). I've also written about why libertarians (like me) should seek political alliances with "abundance liberals" and why the previous "fusionist" alliance with conservatives probably cannot and should not be revived in the near future.

This post doesn't argue for any particular voting choice, but rather compiles pieces about  how we should make such decisions in general - and whether we should make them at all. Much of the post is adapted from a similar one I put up in 2024. Unless otherwise noted, these pieces were all published right here at the VC blog:

1. "The Logic of Voting for a Lesser Evil"

This post was inspired by the 2016 election, but almost all of it remains relevant today. In it, I explain why it is both permissible and desirable to vote for the lesser evil in an election where all of the viable options are bad. I address a variety of counterarguments, including claims that voting for a lesser evil makes you morally complicit in that candidate's wrongdoing, arguments that it's better to cast a "protest vote" for a candidate that has no chance of winning, arguments based on the very low probability that your vote will be decisive, and more. Here's a brief excerpt:

Imagine an election where the only options are Queen Cersei from Game of Thrones, and Sauron, the Dark Lord from Tolkien's Lord of the Rings. If Cersei wins, she will kill many innocent people, and oppress others. But she will leave much of the population more or less alone (as long as they don't openly oppose her or threaten her family in any way). If Sauron wins, he will kill far more innocent people, and make the survivors his slaves.

You can instead cast a protest vote for a vastly better alternative, such as Gandalf….. But, by assumption, these are purely symbolic options, because they have zero chance of prevailing. If the protest voter would otherwise have backed Cersei, the net effect of his decision to protest is to increase the likelihood of the worst possible outcome: the triumph of Sauron.

Under those circumstances, it seems clear that a person who ensures a Cersei victory has done a good deed. He or she will have saved large numbers of people from slavery or death, even though the Cersei regime would be a deeply unjust one.

The Cersei-Sauron hypothetical was obviously inspired by the contest between Trump and Hillary Clinton, and is an exaggerated version of that tradeoff. But I think it works for many other elections, as well - including many of the choices  voters face this year.

Notice how my logic is different from that of those who say you can only vote for a candidate if he or she meets some minimal threshold of character or good policy. On my approach, it is morally justifiable to vote for almost any candidate - even a cruel despot like Cersei - so long as the only feasible alternatives are even worse.

Canadian columnist John Robson responded to my piece in the National Post, and I, in turn, posted a rejoinder.

2. "Justifying a Moral Duty to Vote is a Lot Harder than You Might Think."

Many people, including some political theorists, believe we have a moral duty to vote. I disagree. Indeed, I think - in many cases - it's better if you don't vote, especially if ignorance and bias make it likely you will make a bad decision. Casting a ballot motivated by ignorance and bias is often worse than not voting at all.

3."Is there a Moral Duty to Vote in an Election Where the Stakes are Unusually High?"

Even if there is no general duty to vote, perhaps we are morally required to do so in situations where the stakes of an election are unusually high. In this post, I explain why I disagree - at least with respect to most voters. There is, however, a limited kernel of truth in this argument. An excerpt:

There is a kernel of truth to the claim that you have a duty to vote if the stakes are high enough. But the resulting moral duty applies far less often than advocates of the argument tend to assume. And the same reasoning actually implies many people have a moral duty not to vote.

Let's start with the kernel of truth. Imagine there's an election for a powerful political office that pits Gandalf (the benevolent wizard in J.R.R. Tolkien's Lord of the Rings) against Sauron, the despotic dark lord from the same story. If Sauron prevails, millions of people will die or be enslaved, while Gandalf would rule justly if he manages to win. And all you have to do to ensure Gandalf's victory is check his name on a ballot. If you do so, Gandalf wins; if not, Sauron does.

In this scenario, it seems like you have a moral duty to vote for Gandalf, at least barring some kind of extraordinary exigent circumstance. In a real election, of course, the odds that your vote will make a difference are far smaller than in this stylized example….

However, a large enough difference between the two candidates could potentially justify a duty to vote for the "right" candidate, even if the odds of casting a decisive ballot are very low….

But notice that the duty in question is not an obligation to participate in the process for its own sake. It's a duty to help good triumph over evil in a situation where you can do so at little or no cost. If you have a moral duty to vote for Gandalf in these types of scenarios, it follows that you also have a moral duty not to vote for Sauron. Indeed, the person who votes for Sauron is more worthy of condemnation than the one who merely abstains. The former is actively helping evil win, while the latter "merely" chooses not to help stop it.

While Gandalf supporters may have a duty to vote, Sauron supporters actually have a duty to abstain from doing so. Ideally, they should stop supporting Sauron entirely. But they at least should not take any actions that increase the likelihood of his victory.

All of the above analysis assumes that the voter knows which candidate is superior and to what degree. But, in reality, we have widespread political ignorance, and most voters often don't even know very basic facts about how government and politics work. Most are also highly biased in their evaluation of the information they do know….

Unless and until a voter becomes well-informed about the issues and at least reasonably objective in his or her evaluation of political information, she has good reason to question her judgment about which candidate is superior, much less by how much. Thus, she cannot conclude she has a duty to vote to help the "right" side win. She may instead have a presumptive duty to abstain from voting until she meets at least some minimal threshold of political knowledge….

Later in this piece, I note some possible exceptions to situations to the presumptive duty to abstain; there are unusual situations where ignorant voting really is better than no voting, and even unusual situations where ignorance leads to better decisions than knowledge (I expand on the latter possibility in greater detail in Chapter 2 of my book Democracy and Political Ignorance). I also address some other caveats and counterarguments.

Some steps you can take to be a better voter, building on a helpful article in Scientific American. I think a wide range of people can do these things. You don't have to be an academic or policy expert to undertake the task. But I am skeptical that more than a small fraction of the electorate will ever be willing to put in the time and effort.

In this post, I make a tentative argument for letting children vote, so long as they show they have attained a level of political knowledge as high as that of the average adult voter -which is not that high a standard! I expanded on the idea here. I do note the crucial caveat that it may not be feasible to do this, because it's possible government can't be trusted to come up with an objective knowledge test for the children (though we do in fact impose such a test on immigrants seeking to become US citizens). Letting knowledgeable children vote is one of my least popular ideas (which is saying no little, given how many other unpopular views I hold!). But I remain unrepentant about it. My 11-year-old daughter is one of the relatively few fans of this policy.

My proposal should be differentiated from the idea of letting parents cast votes on behalf of their children, endorsed by Republican VP candidate J.D. Vance, among others.

6. "Top-Down and Bottom-Up Solutions to the Problem of Political Ignorance," in Hana Samaržija and Quassim Cassam, eds. The Epistemology of Democracy (Routledge, 2023).

Many of the most serious flaws of voting arise from the fact that most voters tend to be ignorant about government public policy, and highly biased in their evaluation of the political information they do know. In this article, I go over a range of possible strategies for mitigating this problem. Here's the abstract:

There is broad, though not universal, agreement that widespread voter ignorance and irrational evaluation of evidence are serious threats to democracy. But there is deep disagreement over strategies for mitigating the danger. "Top-down" approaches, such as epistocracy and lodging more authority in the hands of experts, seek to mitigate ignorance by concentrating more political power in the hands of the more knowledgeable segments of the population. By contrast, "bottom-up" approaches seek to either raise the political competence of the general public or empower ordinary people in ways that give them better incentives to make good decisions than conventional ballot-box voting does. Examples of bottom-up strategies include increasing voter knowledge through education, various "sortition" proposals, and also shifting more decisions to institutions where citizens can "vote with their feet."

This chapter surveys and critiques a range of both top-down and bottom-up strategies. I conclude that top-down strategies have systematic flaws that severely limit their potential. While they should not be categorically rejected, we should be wary of adopting them on a large scale. Bottom-up strategies have significant limitations of their own. But expanding foot voting opportunities holds more promise than any other currently available option. The idea of paying voters to increase their knowledge also deserves serious consideration.

I expand upon the foot-voting approach to mitigating political ignorance in more detail in my book Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom. I also recently summarized and extended my ideas on this score in "Strengthen Democracy by Empowering People to Vote with their Feet," an article for the NYU Democracy Project, reprinted as a book chapter in Democracy's Challenges: I00 Ideas, (Robert Bauer, Samuel Issacharoff, Richard Pildes, and Rosa Po, eds., NYU Press, 2026).

How to decide which issues to prioritize over others. Not solely about voting. But highly relevant to voting decisions.

8. "If You Don't Vote, You Still Have Every Right to Complain."

Feeling down after considering the above? This piece might make you slightly happier; even if you don't vote, you are justified in criticizing the policies of the winners! I would add that the same logic shows that, if you vote for the winner on the grounds that she is a lesser evil, you are still justified in complaining about her policies. Vote for Cersei over Sauron, when necessary. But then condemn the evil she does. Just make sure not to be at the wrong place at the wrong time when she decides to purge her critics.

NEXT: Full Court Denies DOJ Petition In California Election Case In About 7 Hours, No Reply Needed

Ilya Somin is Visiting Professor of Law at the University of Virginia, Professor of Law at George Mason University, Simon Chair in Constitutional Studies at the Cato Institute, and author of Free to Move: Foot Voting, Migration, and Political Freedom, Democracy and Political Ignorance: Why Smaller Government is Smarter, and The Grasping Hand: Kelo v. City of New London and the Limits of Eminent Domain.

#7826. Court finds law protecting judges, officers’ personal information unconstitutional

U.S. District Judge Esther Salas of the District of New Jersey delivers remarks at a news conference in Newark, New Jersey, on Dec. 19, 2022. (Photo By Kyle Mazza/Sipa USA/Sipa via AP Images)

A West Virginia law shielding the online publication of personal information belonging to judges and law enforcement officers was ruled unconstitutional by a federal appeals court Tuesday.

The Oct. 27 ruling by the 4th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals at Richmond, Virginia, is the first instance of a federal appellate court overriding a state law protecting the home addresses and unpublished phone numbers of judges and officers since states began safeguarding personal information after a gunman shot and killed 20-year-old Daniel Anderl, the son of U.S. District Judge Esther Salas of the District of New Jersey, inside their New Jersey home in 2020.

Class action lawsuits filed by Michael Jackson, a retired law enforcement officer, charged Thomson Reuters, Whitepages Inc., PeopleConnect and LexisNexis with violating the state’s Daniel’s Law through online people search services, according to coverage by Reuters.

#7824. Families and Students Need Guidance on AI

Delaware families and policymakers are wrestling with the same issue troubling Americans nationwide: how to handle artificial intelligence.

In 2024, lawmakers in the Blue Hen State created a committee to study AI. Good thing, because parents and teachers badly need guidance on this issue.

Yet AI technology has advanced rapidly over the past two years, so the committee should prioritize drafting recommendations for K-12 schools.

To date, state officials have set only “voluntary” guardrails around AI use in elementary and secondary schools, according to the Delaware-based Caesar Rodney Institute. In May, legislators considered a proposal to create a pilot program that would allow 12 schools to use AI technology.

>>> What’s Really Behind the Call to Regulate AI

Still, the final report on the activities would not be due until 2029, and this year’s freshman class will be seniors by then. These students will be gone before lawmakers act on the report’s findings. Instead, lawmakers should focus on helping students in school today.

Besides, given the pace of change in AI technology, this proposal is too little, too late.

Fortunately, legislative models already exist that lawmakers can apply to allow the use of AI in schools, protect student data and prohibit nonacademic AI activities in classrooms.

Heritage Foundation research explains that lawmakers need not explicitly ban or allow the use of AI in schools. For school officials who allow AI in classrooms, however, educators should adopt training programs for teachers and students. These programs should help teachers and students draft prompts and questions for generative AI bots; create media using AI, such as audio, video and pictures; edit student writing; detect biases in AI results; evaluate different AI bots to decide which are the most effective; and protect student privacy.

Local school boards should adopt policies stating that students may use AI for schoolwork only when specifically allowed by teachers.

The U.S. Department of Education is urging state and local authorities to develop solutions. “Research and experience have demonstrated that technology is a valuable instructional tool when it supports strong pedagogy and effective teaching practices,” writes Kirsten Baesler, assistant secretary for elementary and secondary education. “The U.S. Department of Education believes these decisions [about education technology] are best made by states and local communities.”

Policymakers should move quickly. Even if self-reported student usage numbers are slightly inflated, the share of students using AI remains remarkable.

Education officials in large school systems such as New York City and Los Angeles are attempting to prohibit the use of AI for this school year. With so many students already using bots, however, a ban on AI will be difficult to enforce.

>>> Meta Abandons Its AI-Generating Tool, but Public-Safety Guardrails Are Needed

Instead of prohibiting AI, policymakers should draw on existing research to select appropriate educational applications of the technology. For example, lawmakers should block the use of companion bots that simulate personal interactions and develop relationships with users.

Instead, educators can give students access to generative bots that use data to summarize complex information. Teachers can benefit from AI programs that help organize lesson plans. When teachers assign students to use AI, students should report how they used the technology.

Parents should have the choice to opt out of these assignments and have students complete the work using other methods.

State policymakers must focus on boosting student outcomes as technology evolves. Federal officials agree. Ms. Baesler writes: “The question should not be whether teachers and students use technology. The question should be whether the technology we ask teachers and students to use improves learning and students’ academic outcomes.”

As Delaware’s AI committee drafts recommendations, officials should focus on student success. Those on both sides of the political aisle—and on either side of AI debates—can agree on this.

Then, parents and teachers can share best practices and offer solutions to help students across all 50 states.

#7823. Chemerinsky: Supreme Court once again examines conflicts over the free exercise of religion

On Tuesday, the U.S. Supreme Court will hear oral arguments in a major case about free exercise of religion, St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy. Over the last decade, the justices have greatly expanded First Amendment protections for religion. This case could either go much further in that direction or show a court that is willing to allow the government to stop discrimination even when it infringes on religious beliefs.

The case involves a Colorado law launched in 2023 that provides for universal preschool education. Under the program, the state will pay for preschool at any public, secular private or religious school. To receive funds, the school must agree that it will not discriminate against children based on their parents’ race, ethnicity, religion, sexual orientation, gender identity, disability, income or lack of housing.

St. Mary Catholic Parish in Littleton, Colorado, and another Catholic preschool in the Archdiocese of Denver declined to sign the agreement, saying that it conflicts with church teachings on marriage, sex and gender. Their objection is to having to agree to take children whose parents are gay, lesbian or transgender. They argue that excluding the religious schools from the universal program denies them a public benefit due to their religious beliefs.

The federal district court and the Denver-based 10th U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected their challenge and upheld the Colorado law. Both courts relied on the Supreme Court’s decision in Employment Division v. Smith (1990), which held that the free exercise clause of the First Amendment cannot be used to require exceptions from general laws. That case involved Native Americans who sought an exemption from an Oregon law prohibiting the consumption of peyote on the grounds that its use was a part of their religious rituals. Justice Antonin Scalia wrote the opinion for the court ruling against the Native Americans. The court said that so long as the law was neutral, not motivated by a desire to infringe religion, and so long as it applied to everyone, it could not be challenged as denying free exercise of religion.

The federal district court and the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law prohibiting discrimination by preschools, concluding that it was a neutral law of general applicability. These courts also held that there was no discrimination against religious schools in their ability to receive public funds. In a series of cases—Trinity Lutheran v. Comer (2017), Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020), and Carson v. Makin (2022)—the court held that it violates free exercise of religion for the government to deny funds to religious schools that it provides to private secular schools. The Colorado law was upheld because it does not discriminate against religious schools; it provides funds to faith-based preschools on the same terms as all other preschools.

The plaintiffs sought certiorari, and the Supreme Court granted review on two questions. (1) Whether proving a lack of general applicability under Employment Division v. Smith requires showing unfettered discretion or categorical exemptions for identical secular conduct; (2) whether Carson v. Makin displaces the rule of Employment Division v. Smith only when the government explicitly excludes religious people and institutions.

The last major Supreme Court decision concerning the application of Employment Division v. Smith was Fulton v. City of Philadelphia (2021). The city of Philadelphia contracts with private social service agencies to help place children in foster homes. Every contract is explicit in prohibiting the agency from discriminating on the basis of race, sex, religion and sexual orientation.

Catholic Social Services long had participated in this aspect of the program but in recent years has declined to do so because of the contractual requirement that it not discriminate based on sexual orientation. CSS says that its religious beliefs prevent it from providing inspections or placing children with same sex-couples.

The agency challenged the nondiscrimination requirement as violating its First Amendment rights. The district court and the Philadelphia-based 3rd U.S. Circuit Court of Appeals rejected these arguments. Both courts relied on Employment Division v. Smith.

The Supreme Court unanimously reversed the lower courts and ruled in favor of Catholic Social Services. Chief Justice John Roberts wrote the opinion for the court. He said that under Employment Division v. Smith a “law is not generally applicable if it ‘invite[s]’ the government to consider the particular reasons for a person’s conduct by providing a ‘mechanism for individualized exemptions.’” The Philadelphia ordinance gave city officials the authority to grant exceptions to the nondiscrimination requirement. The court said that it was irrelevant that none ever had been granted and that there was no evidence of discrimination against religious entities. The existence of discretion was enough for it to not be a neutral law of general applicability. Therefore, it had to meet strict scrutiny. The court concluded that the city failed to meet strict scrutiny and that its policy was therefore unconstitutional.

Justice Samuel Alito concurred in the judgment and was joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Neil Gorsuch. In a 77-page opinion, Justice Alito expressly called for the court to overrule Smith. Justice Alito argued at length against the Smith approach and stated: “We should reconsider Smith without further delay. The correct interpretation of the free exercise clause is a question of great importance, and Smith’s interpretation is hard to defend. It can’t be squared with the ordinary meaning of the text of the free exercise clause or with the prevalent understanding of the scope of the free-exercise right at the time of the First Amendment’s adoption.”

Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote a concurring opinion that was joined in full by Justice Brett Kavanaugh. She expressed agreement with many of the criticisms of Smith advanced by Justice Alito. But she said that there are hard questions as to what test should replace the one from Smith. She said that the court did not need to address that in this case because the city of Philadelphia policy was unconstitutional “regardless whether Smith stays or goes.”

The Supreme Court did not grant certiorari in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy on the question of whether to overrule Employment Division v. Smith, but that issue very much underlies the issues before the court.

Petitioner St. Mary’s Catholic Parish clearly is urging the court to jettison Smith. The first argument in its brief is that the “court rarely applies Smith.” It says: “Out of the 18 free exercise cases this court has resolved since Smith in 1990, this court has relied on Smith only twice to rule against the religious objector,” and one of these was Smith itself.

There also is the underlying question of whether a religious belief should be a basis for an exemption from antidiscrimination laws. In Newman v. Piggie Park Enterprises Inc. (1968), the court summarily rejected a claim that a person’s religious beliefs were a basis for their discriminating in violation of civil rights statutes. If the court overrules Smith, or says that strict scrutiny should be used under Smith, the question will need to be addressed: Should free exercise of religion provide a right to harm others by discriminating against them?

For decades, the Supreme Court decided cases about when government aid to religious schools violated the establishment clause of the First Amendment. But over the last decade, the court has held that the denial of funding to religious schools when it is provided to private secular schools violates the free exercise clause of the First Amendment. For example, in its most recent ruling, Carson v. Makin (2022), the court held that it violated free exercise of religion for the state to pay for secular private schools but not religious schools for children in rural areas where there are not public schools.

The district court and the 10th Circuit upheld the Colorado law on the ground that it provided aid to all preschools—public, secular private, and faith-based—on exactly the same terms. But St. Mary’s Catholic Parish argues that Colorado is denying it funding because of its exercising its religious beliefs and excluding children whose parents are gay, lesbian or transgender.

In the prior cases about funding, the state laws expressly excluded religious schools. The Colorado law does not do that. Is it enough for a free exercise violation that its effect is to deny funding to schools that have a religious basis for their discrimination based on sexual orientation or gender identity?

In recent years, the conservative majority on the Supreme Court has greatly lessened the protections of the establishment clause of the First Amendment while simultaneously significantly increasing the safeguards under the free exercise clause. It has shown support for those who want to violate anti-discrimination laws on account of their religious beliefs. St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy will be important in indicating whether the court will go even further in these directions.

Erwin Chemerinsky is dean of the University of California at Berkeley School of Law. He is an expert in constitutional law. He’s also the author of many books, including his most recent ones: Campus Speech and Academic Freedom: A Guide for Difficult Times and The Supreme Court October Term 2024: Taking Sides.

This column reflects the opinions of the author and not necessarily the views of the ABA Journal—or the American Bar Association.

#7821. America 250 at 230 mph

I know nothing about automobile racing, and I confess it at the outset, honesty being the virtue my mother prized above all others save punctuality.

Yet racing has a way of finding a person. When I was a boy in the 1980s and 1990s, my father, on the occasional Sunday afternoon, kept the television tuned to NASCAR. The names drifted through our living room like the smell of pot roast: Richard Petty, Dale Earnhardt, Darrell Waltrip, Jeff Gordon.

Once, the athletic director at our Baptist church loaded the youth group into a van and drove us to Atlanta Motor Speedway. There, amid gasoline and thunder, a cluster of drivers signed my cap. Which drivers, I could not tell you; the cap sleeps on the top shelf of my closet. But I remember running into Bobby Cox and Terry Pendleton, of our beloved Braves, and they signed it, too.

I write now from an Indianapolis hotel room, having spent the week with The Mont Pelerin Society. Friedrich Hayek and a few dozen others founded the Society in 1947, gathering beside a Swiss mountain amid the rubble of a world war to keep alive the idea of a free people prospering through free markets. Last year, readers may recall, we were in Morocco. This year, in honor of the nation’s 250th birthday, we came to Indianapolis, home of Liberty Fund, our host and an institution I love.

>>> The Hidden Jewel at Jacksonville State

Mont Pelerin meetings are known for their excursions. I once climbed a volcano in Guatemala. This week we went to the Speedway.

It’s an immense place. On race day, some 350,000 souls fill its grandstands and infield while jets tear open the sky. On an ordinary autumn afternoon, with the stands empty and the wind moving through them, it feels like an unroofed cathedral. One stands in it smaller and grateful.

I was told I would be offered a lap with a professional driver. At the entrance waited a stack of liability waivers thick as a family Bible, and my hand trembled as I signed. Then, as if Providence had a hand in the seating chart, I saw Sam Karnick of the Heartland Institute, who missed the conference entirely but arrived from Chicago just in time for this excursion.

I will say only that Sam has stood beside me in matters both personal and professional, which in my life were never quite separate. Sam was riding, too. We would go together.

But first, let me tell you about the museum.

The Speedway opened in 1909. Two years later, Ray Harroun won the inaugural Indianapolis 500 in the Marmon Wasp, a long yellow needle of a car equipped with what may have been the first rearview mirror fitted to an automobile. In the museum stood its replica, along with machines that marked the successive revolutions of racing: the 1914 Delage, the 1928 Miller Special, Bobby Unser’s 1968 Rislone Eagle, the 1972 Sunoco McLaren associated with Roger Penske’s first Indianapolis 500 victory, and the 1982 STP Wildcat in which Gordon Johncock beat Rick Mears by a mere sixteen-hundredths of a second.

Each car tells a story of ingenuity, rivalry, and the restless dissatisfaction that facilitates progress. After World War II, the track lay neglected, its bricks surrendering to weeds, until Terre Haute businessman Tony Hulman bought it in 1945 and restored it. Racing moved from the front-engine roadsters to rear-engine cars, from one mechanical innovation to another, each generation testing the limits left by its predecessor. The record was never allowed to stand for long; someone always thought he could go faster.

Consider the distance traveled in little more than a century. The automobile was still a novelty when the Speedway opened. Now, machines hurtle around its oval at speeds exceeding 230 miles an hour. No central planner conceived this progression, no committee assembled all the knowledge required to produce it. Mechanics, engineers, inventors, drivers and investors each contributed something, often without knowing what the next man would do with it. Some made fortunes; some lost them. The accumulated result exceeded what any one of them could have imagined.

Hayek had a name for the order that emerges from such dispersed knowledge and individual effort: the extended order. The Speedway offered a particularly American illustration: 100 years of rivalry and experiment, ambition and failure, producing an achievement no single mind could have designed.

And so, to the car. Sam and I folded ourselves in and drew the belts tight, and I resolved not to utter a sound, lest some small whimper distract the man whose profession it was to keep us alive. The engine woke. We swept down the straight and up the banking toward the wall, the concrete flashing near enough to touch, the world narrowing to a gray blur and a roar.

I was afraid. I was also, I confess, happy, with that doubled feeling Edmund Burke described when he set the beautiful, which pleases, beside the sublime, which terrifies and exalts at once. Indianapolis Speedway is both. The beauty of a thing well made, and the sublimity of a thing just short of control.

Then the lap was over; silence rushed back. Sam looked at me. He laughed; I laughed.

>>> The Great Migration Remaking Higher Ed

Outside the car, the concrete beneath our feet seemed reassuringly solid. My knees were unsteady, and my heart had not yet settled into its usual rhythm. I thought of Harroun with his rearview mirror, Hulman with his ruined track, and the generations of mechanics and entrepreneurs who had risked money, reputation, and sometimes life itself to see whether a new idea might work.

Their stories differ, but they share a certain disposition: a willingness to act without possessing all the answers, to risk failure without a guarantee of success, and to discover through experiment what no amount of speculation could establish in advance.

That disposition has helped make America what it is. The free society does not promise that every venture will succeed or that every wager will pay. It permits people to try, to compete, to learn from failure, and to build on what others have discovered. Its achievements belong not merely to the celebrated winners but also to the countless people whose experiments, including unsuccessful ones, made the next experiment possible.

Sam and I did little more than occupy two seats for what seemed like a few seconds. We weren’t drivers, engineers or entrepreneurs. We’d simply agreed to the ride, signed the waivers, and climbed aboard. But as we walked away from the track, still chuckling, I thought something was fitting about coming to Indianapolis with a society devoted to liberty and leaving with a fresh appreciation for what liberty makes possible.

The car went around in a circle. The country, over the course of two and a half centuries, has traveled considerably farther.

#7820. Today’s Inflation Is Really an Energy Shock

Americans are frustrated with today’s high cost of living, especially fuel prices. Although incomes rose faster than prices last year, it’s been the opposite since February. The only good news is that this inflation will subside when overseas conflicts are resolved, but there is likely more pain to come for consumers until then.

The significant reacceleration of inflation that began in March is due to disruptions in global energy markets. The wars with Iran and in the Ukraine have not only shut off a considerable amount of the world’s crude oil supply, but refined products too, like gasoline, diesel, jet fuel, and home heating oil.

Nations worldwide have coped with this reduction in supply by draining energy reserves, like the Strategic Petroleum Reserve in the U.S., and running refineries at maximum capacity—even delaying critical maintenance. These extraordinary measures blunted but didn’t eliminate the energy shock.

In recent months, Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure have reduced Russia’s diesel export capacity by about 90%, effectively taking one of the world’s largest diesel producers out of the market. That additional supply shock has caused diesel prices in particular to skyrocket.

>>> If It’s Good Enough for Wartime, It’s Good Enough for Peacetime 

It’s clear that such energy shocks will affect energy prices, but people often underestimate how much energy affects the price of everything we do and everything we buy. Thus, the energy shock is slowly transforming into an “everything shock,” and it’s showing up in the data.

When someone grabs an item off a store shelf, whether it’s a gallon of milk or a box of screws, that item arrived there on a truck fueled by diesel—and often a train fueled by diesel too. Higher transportation costs put upward pressure on prices everywhere.

Many products are also energy-intensive to produce, like aluminum, where about one-third of its cost of production is electricity. Increasing that input cost makes thousands of items, from soda cans to airplanes, more expensive.

Moreover, energy is a direct input for countless products, from fertilizer to cosmetics to plastics—all synthesized from oil and natural gas. More expensive fertilizer drives up food prices, and plastics are in just about everything today. As elevated energy prices migrate through supply chains, prices everywhere are starting to rise, even if only mildly.

This is a stark contrast to supply-chain data back in January and February, before the Iran war, which indicated prices for many consumer staples would be falling by this time, not rising. That’s still true for some items like certain pharmaceuticals and dairy products, but higher energy prices have simply overpowered any deflationary pressure on most consumer prices this year.

>>> The Red-Blue Energy Divide: How Overregulation Inflates Prices 

Import price data also confirm that today’s inflation is really an energy shock. America has weathered the oil shortage better than most countries because it’s the world’s largest energy producer, pumping a record amount of oil today. Oil prices elsewhere have been higher, which in turn has increased non-energy prices on products and services faster.

Fuel import prices in September rose 4.8% from August and a whopping 34.5% from a year prior. But non-fuel import prices are also rising fast, up 6% over the last 12 months, the fastest annual increase in almost four and a half years. Conversely, non-fuel prices in the U.S. rose at just one-tenth that pace over the same period.

Despite America’s relatively insulated position, the high energy prices since February—especially the high diesel prices more recently—are already spilling into every corner of the economy. Months of elevated inflation are already baked into the cake, so even if the wars in Iran and the Ukraine end immediately, the effects will continue for a while.

Despite that negative short-term outlook, there is some reason for optimism. Since the inflation this year stems from temporary conflicts overseas and not something wrong with the American economy’s fundamentals, energy prices should start coming down once those conflicts end and oil markets normalize.

Until then, however, people will continue to complain about the economy, with negative responses in survey data like consumer sentiment, consumer expectations, and consumer confidence. That’ll remain true even as—or perhaps especially as—the energy shock looks less and less like an energy shock.
