#7801. Accusing University Lecturer Who Called Police of "Blatant Racial Profiling" Leads to $37,500 Defamation Verdict

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

You can see the verdict form, from Thursday, here. The jury had asked whether they could suggest additional remedies besides the money:

But the court referred the jury to Instruction No. 10, which focused solely on monetary damages.

The backstory, from the opinion this April Judge Rebecca Pennell (E.D. Wash.) in Riera v. Central Wash. Univ., which let the case go forward:

Mr. Riera was employed in a fixed term, non-tenure track faculty at Central Washington University (CWU)…. On the morning of April 1, [2024,] Mr. Riera called the CWU police to report an older, "apparently homeless," woman wandering around Samuelson Hall. He said he wanted to make a report "before things get … out of control." An officer reported to Samuelson Hall and confirmed the identity of the woman as a CWU professor. No further action was taken by campus police or Mr. Riera.

The CWU professor shared her experience with two colleagues. The colleagues immediately filed bias complaints with CWU, alleging the target of Mr. Riera's call—a Black woman—had been the victim of racial profiling.

This led to a great deal of institutional response, including a discussion at a faculty senate meeting. Defendant Erdman, "a lecturer at CWU and member of the faculty senate, emailed unofficial minutes [of the meeting] to non-tenured faculty," and her notes included this:

Without naming names or describing the incident, [CWU President] Wohlpart expressed his outrage at a recent unconscionable incident on campus.

From my own knowledge, I think I can tell you the basics: It was an incident of blatant racial profiling. Campus police were called because a person of color was sitting quietly in the lobby of a CWU building for a brief interval. The person turned out to be a highly distinguished faculty member—but was compelled to produce and show ID before being left in peace.

(I must remark that this is outrageous on multiple levels. All CWU buildings are public; they belong to the State of Washington and its people. Anyone may sit in the lobby of any of our buildings. There was no reason at all to call the police—except, I guess, that this was a person of color.)

Wohlpart called the incident "unacceptable" and said that Central is working to see to it that such a thing doesn't happen again on our campus….

Riera sued Erdman, among others, and the court allowed his defamation claim to go forward in part:

[M]ost of [Erdman's] statements cannot be characterized as false. The only exception is Defendant Erdman's statement that what happened on April 1 "was an incident of blatant racial profiling." A jury could conclude this statement falsely asserts that the person who called police on April 1 engaged in intentional racial profiling. And, given widely-shared public records revealed Mr. Riera as the caller, a jury could also conclude Defendant Erdman's statement was about Mr. Riera.

Defendants argue that regardless of truth or falsity, Defendant Erdman's statement cannot be considered defamatory because it falls under the common interest privilege. "The common interest privilege applies with the declarant and the recipient have a common interest in the subject matter of the communication." The privilege applies to "persons involved in the same organization, partnerships, associations, or enterprises who are communicating on matters of common interest." Examples include officers of a nonprofit association or partners to a partnership. The privilege arises "when parties need to speak freely and openly about subjects of common organizational or pecuniary interest." …

If the privilege exists, it can be lost in two circumstances (1) if the speaker is not acting in the ordinary course of their work or (2) the speaker's statement was made with actual malice; i.e., reckless disregard for the truth. Whether the privilege has been lost under either scenario is a question of fact.

Here, the parties appear to agree that members of CWU's faculty senate are members of the same organization who share a common interest. The dispute lies in whether an exception applies.

The Court concludes there are issues of fact regarding whether Defendant Erdman's statements fell outside the scope of the privilege. Going to the first exception, Defendant Erdman had no official responsibility for taking notes at faculty meetings and she was not required to share her notes with other members of the senate faculty. A jury could therefore conclude that her statements were outside the ordinary course of her work as a member of a senate.

With respect to the second exception, Defendant Erdman was not a witness to the April 1 incident and no investigation had yet taken place. A jury could therefore conclude Defendant Erdman was reckless in asserting that the call to CWU police was an act of blatant racial profiling…. [T]he allegations against Defendant Erdman raise questions of fact that must be resolved by a jury.

Note that the court granted summary judgment as to plaintiff's defamation claim against President Wohlpart; as to plaintiff's defamation claim against CWU, the court stated that "Mr. Riera appears to have abandoned this claim and the summary judgment briefing does not describe how CWU as an institution may be liable for defamation." The one remaining defendant at trial was Erdman.

UPDATE 11/3/26 4:45 pm: I had originally written that the claims against the University were abandoned, but apparently plaintiff's counsel is disputing that, and intends to appeal the court's dismissal of the claims against CWU and Wohlpart. I've revised the post to say that the court stated the claim was abandoned.

NEXT: City's Using Meta Moderation Assist Feature for Facebook Comments Doesn't Violate First Amendment

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7800. No, Mamdani, Socialism Does Not Increase Affordability

Of the many inane comments that socialists have made this year, the one that democracy is “the building block of socialism” might be the most absurd.

Who made the comment? You guessed it: New York City’s boy genius, Mayor Zohran Mamdani.

In a recent episode of “This Past Weekend,” Mr. Mamdani discussed socialism’s ability to ensure affordability with comedian Theo Von. The interview was replete with Marxian nonsense, but Mr. Mamdani also discussed many Americans’ economic frustrations: homeownership feels out of reach; rent is expensive; childcare is unaffordable; and grocery prices are substantially higher.

Young people increasingly feel that the American dream is “slipping away.”

Recognizing affordability problems, however, is not the same as identifying the causes. Mr. Mamdani avers that the free market system cannot solve these problems and that socialism is the silver bullet.

Consider his assertion about democracy. When Mr. Von brought up the concept, Mr. Mamdani interrupted him and claimed, “That’s the building block of socialism.”

>>> Mamdani’s City Grocery Plan Could Leave Taxpayers Paying for Every Banana

Karl Marx and Friedrich Engels would like to have a word.

To them, it was clear that implementing socialism—a word that they used interchangeably with communism—would require the opposite of democracy: tyranny.

In their 1848 “The Communist Manifesto,” the owner’s manual for Marxism, Marx and Engels rightly predicted that people would fight back when the government seized their property—something Mr. Mamdani should bear in mind as he upsets more and more New Yorkers with property-grabbing schemes.

“The proletariat will use its political supremacy to wrest, by degrees, all capital from the bourgeoisie, to centralize all instruments of production in the hands of the State,” Marx and Engels wrote. “Of course, in the beginning, this cannot be effected except by means of despotic inroads on the rights of property, and on the conditions of bourgeois production.”

So, no, Mr. Mamdani. Socialism’s pillars are totalitarian, based on forced nationalization and coercive state control.

Now, let us deal with the fanciful claim that socialism is the best way to order society: “Socialism to me means that you have whatever you need to live a dignified life, and it’s the government’s job to deliver on that.”

It sounds compassionate, but what happens when the government assumes responsibility for determining, financing and delivering the necessities of a “dignified life”?

Here, we begin to understand why Mr. Mamdani mixes socialism with democracy. To him, democracy is not just about electing leaders; it is also about letting people choose things that they cannot afford, courtesy of taxpayers.

In line with his big-government agenda, he explained socialism as “the extension of democracy from the ballot box to the rest of your life … your workplace, your home.”

Yet socialists devalue real democracy when they define it as the “right” for people to own what they have not earned. They also devalue the protection of inalienable rights when they insist that 51% of the electorate can suppress individual liberties such as property rights—something America’s Founders called “mobocracy.”

A free society empowers majorities, but it also protects individual rights. More government intervention will neither expand liberty nor make New York City more affordable.

The Big Apple is indeed the most expensive city in the United States and the third most expensive in the world. Mr. Mamdani said that is because “greed is baked into a lot of this economy.” He portrays capitalist profit incentives as a motive for firms to exploit workers, reduce the quality of goods and break the law.

Still, profit and wealth are not social defects to be discouraged; quite the contrary. In competitive markets, signals indicate that entrepreneurs have found ways to provide goods and services that consumers value. These incentives encourage businesses to innovate, produce more, reduce costs and discover better ways to meet people’s needs.

This must be a foreign concept to Mr. Mamdani, who believes that it is the government’s duty to provide the public with everything, from rent to groceries. He ignores commonsense solutions that have worked the world over, such as tax cuts and deregulation—and deportations, for that matter, which would reduce costs for households and businesses alike.

>>> Mamdani Is about to Make Housing Even More Expensive

Instead, Mr. Mamdani turns to central planning, even though government bureaucrats created many of the affordability problems he now insists they will solve.

Take housing. Mr. Mamdani argues that housing costs are central to New York’s economic problems, and many economists agree. Yet the city’s affordability crisis results from decades of restrictive zoning, burdensome permit requirements, development constraints, rent regulation and political barriers that limit housing construction.

The pattern is familiar: Government intervention distorts the market, consumers suffer the consequences, then socialists point to those consequences as evidence of market failure requiring still more state intervention.

Throughout his interview with Mr. Von, Mr. Mamdani framed his socialist ideology as empathetic, not the state-controlled subjugation that it is. Yet remember, the more “necessities” the government promises to provide, the more power bureaucrats require to deliver them.

When the government assumes control over housing, childcare, grocery access, transportation and healthcare, citizens become less self-reliant and more dependent on political institutions.

Americans are right to be concerned about affordability, but the challenge facing them today is how to improve markets with more freedom and opportunity, not socialism.

#7799. Crime Is Down: Why Leadership Matters

For years, Americans were told by the left that rising crime was either exaggerated, the result of poverty, caused by COVID, or simply the unavoidable cost of modern life. None of those assertions is true.

Victims, police officers, prosecutors, and families living in high-crime neighborhoods knew better. They understood that crime is not an abstraction. It is a stolen vehicle, a broken window, a family traumatized by violence, or a neighborhood slowly surrendered to fear.

That is why the preliminary results of the just-released 2025 National Crime Victimization Survey (NCVS) deserve serious attention. The numbers point in one direction: crime fell substantially across nearly every major category measured by the survey.

The results are preliminary, and responsible observers will await final estimates and additional analysis. But the trend is unmistakable—and it coincides with a national agenda that has placed public safety, border security, law enforcement, and support for victims at the center of federal policy.

According to the preliminary estimates from the Bureau of Justice Statistics, the rate of serious violent victimization—violent crime excluding simple assault—fell 25%, from 9.9 victimizations per 1,000 people age 12 or older in 2024 to 7.4 per 1,000 in 2025. Aggravated assault declined even more sharply, dropping 31% from 4.5 to 3.1 per 1,000.

>>> Americans Lost Over $20 Billion to One Type of Crime. Here’s How We Can Fight It

The property-crime figures are equally striking. Property victimization declined 19%, from 138.0 per 1,000 households to 111.2 per 1,000. Burglary or trespassing fell 25%. Motor vehicle theft declined 30%, representing approximately 349,000 fewer stolen vehicles. Other household theft declined 19%, while burglary and trespassing represented roughly 460,000 fewer victimizations.

These are not minor statistical adjustments. They represent fewer people harmed, fewer families disrupted, and fewer communities forced to absorb the economic and emotional costs of crime.

The NCVS is particularly important because it captures criminal victimization whether or not the victim reported the offense to police. Each year, the Bureau of Justice Statistics gathers information from a nationally representative sample of approximately 240,000 people age 12 or older in about 150,000 households.

It therefore complements the FBI’s Uniform Crime Reporting data, which are based primarily on information supplied by law enforcement agencies.

The two measures tell a consistent story. The FBI’s 2025 data showed the largest year-to-year decline in violent crime since the agency began tracking national crime trends in 1936. Murder and non-negligent manslaughter declined by an estimated 18.1%.

The NCVS now provides an important second measure, reflecting the experiences of victims themselves.

What explains the decline? No serious analyst should pretend that a single policy produces every change in national crime. Crime rates are influenced by many factors, including local policing strategies, prosecution decisions, economic conditions, demographics, and community involvement. Preliminary survey results also cannot establish a definitive cause-and-effect relationship.

But policy choices matter. A president who makes securing the border a priority, removes violent illegal aliens who are subject to deportation, directs the Justice Department to cooperate with the nation’s approximately 18,000 police departments, 3,400 sheriffs’ offices, and 2,300 elected district attorneys, funds law enforcement, and supports victims is sending a clear message: the government’s first responsibility is to protect the innocent.

>>> Another Win for the Task Force To Eliminate Fraud

That message matters. Criminals should expect enforcement, not indulgence. Police officers should know that federal officials recognize the risks they face. Prosecutors should have the resources and cooperation necessary to hold dangerous offenders accountable. Victims should not be treated as an afterthought in a system more concerned with the comfort of defendants than the security of communities.

“This report is proof that President Trump’s ’Make America Safe Again’ agenda is working,” Associate Attorney General Stanley Woodward said, the No. 3 official in the Justice Department.

The statement captures the broader significance of the data, even if conclusions should await final estimates: public safety improves when government treats it as a core mission rather than a campaign slogan.

The lesson is straightforward. Effective enforcement, cooperation among federal, state, and local authorities, secure borders, adequately funded police departments, and meaningful support for victims are not outdated ideas. They are practical necessities.

Americans should celebrate these preliminary gains while remaining vigilant. The goal is not merely to report that crime has fallen. The goal is to ensure that it stays down—and that every community, regardless of size or location, receives the protection its residents deserve.

#7796. Religious Liberty, Terrorist Ideology, and the Limits of School Choice

Last year, Texas enacted one of the country's most expansive school-choice policies. The Texas Education Freedom Accounts program now serves more than 100,000 students, enabling families to choose the learning environments that align with their values and best meet their children’s learning needs.

School choice at this scale is worth celebrating. School-choice policies reflect the Constitution’s commitment to religious liberty and America’s longstanding recognition that parents, not the state, are the primary educators of their children.

A century ago, the Supreme Court struck down a Ku Klux Klan-backed Oregon law that would have banned private schooling, ruling in Pierce v. Society of Sisters that “the child is not the mere creature of the state.” Parents, the Court recognized, have the right and primary authority “to direct the upbringing and education” of their children.

Half a century later, in Yoder v. Wisconsin, the Court reaffirmed the “fundamental interest of parents to guide the religious future and education of their children.” The Court declared that only “interests of the highest order” can override these fundamental freedoms.

The Espinoza v. Montana Department of Revenue (2020) and Carson v. Makin (2022) decisions built on that foundation, holding that states cannot exclude otherwise qualified private schools from generally available scholarship programs merely because they are religious. The Court ruled that such discrimination is “odious to the Constitution.”

But Texas policymakers are now facing a question that school-choice advocates cannot avoid: What if parents choose schools funded by foreign adversaries that indoctrinate students to hate people who are not like them, and whose founders and staff have documented ties to terrorist organizations?

>>> School Choice Is About Religious Liberty, Not Just Better Test Scores

What is the limit of school choice?

Earlier this year, Texas Gov. Greg Abbott drew a line when he declared: “There’s no school choice for schools with ties to organizations that have connections to terrorism.” Several months earlier, Abbott had designated the Muslim Brotherhood and the Council on American-Islamic Relations (CAIR) as foreign terrorist organizations. (CAIR is challenging that designation.)

After those designations, acting comptroller Kelly Hancock wrote to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton asking whether schools with ties to those organizations or the Chinese government could be excluded from the TEFA program. Paxton’s reply was unambiguous: “Let me be crystal clear: Texans’ tax dollars should never fund Islamic terrorists or America’s enemies.” Hancock then announced no schools with such ties would receive Texas tax dollars through TEFA.

That principle—that public funds should not flow to schools with ties to terrorist organizations or hostile foreign powers—is sound. All freedoms have limits. Liberty is not license. A state has a compelling interest in ensuring that taxpayer dollars do not subsidize the indoctrination of children to hate America or to support terrorism.

But even the soundest principle can be implemented in an unsound, or even unconstitutional manner.

In March 2026, Houston-area attorney and father Mehdi Cherkaoui filed a federal lawsuit against Paxton, Hancock, and Texas Education Commissioner Mike Morath, alleging that state officials had “systematically targeted Islamic schools for exclusion based on their religious identity.” His complaint observed that as of early 2026, hundreds of private schools across Texas—including numerous Christian schools—had been approved for TEFA, while not a single accredited Islamic school had been admitted. Cherkaoui sought to use TEFA funds to cover his children’s tuition at the Houston Quran Academy, but the school was not approved under the program. Three Islamic schools and additional parents joined a second suit shortly thereafter.

State officials denied the discrimination charge, explaining to the court that the comptroller’s office “had issues with processing and reviewing schools accredited by the nonprofit Cognia, regardless of whether they have Islamic affiliations.”

U.S. District Judge Alfred H. Bennett was not satisfied with that explanation. On March 17, hours before the original application deadline, he issued a temporary restraining order. At the emergency hearing, Bennett called the complete absence of approved Islamic schools “troubling,” remarking: “If you were to roll dice in a game of chance… you would not come up with those numbers. The appearance of this reeks.” He extended the student application deadline to March 31 and ordered state officials to receive and process applications from Islamic schools through the normal TEFA process. Within days, four Islamic schools were admitted: Brighter Horizons Academy in Garland, Bayaan Academy, Excellence Academy near Plano, and the Houston Quran Academy.

If it is true that the Muslim schools were not approved solely due to their religious affiliation, that would be a clear violation of their First Amendment rights. The Constitution’s guarantee of religious liberty undoubtedly prohibits such blanket discrimination.

However, the story is not so clear-cut. Two of the four schools now receiving TEFA funds—Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy—are at the center of serious, documented concerns regarding their institutional histories and affiliations.

The school’s foreign funding adds another dimension. The Foundation for Defense of Democracies reported that Brighter Horizons received approximately $995,000 from the Islamic Development Bank for construction and expansion. Iran, a U.S.-designated state sponsor of terrorism, holds a significant capital share in the Islamic Development Bank and has representation on its governing board. >>> Stop Writing Blank Checks to Campuses That Protect Hate

These are not isolated cases. Middle East Forum data counts almost 800 Islamic educational initiatives across the United States, of which a clear majority are under Islamist control. Ninety of these institutions are in Texas, and several dozen may benefit from the new school subsidy program. Much of this infrastructure is tied to foreign money and foreign movements.

These are investigative findings, not criminal convictions against the schools themselves. But they are serious enough that state officials were right to ask questions. The comptroller’s supposed initial approach—a blanket exclusion of all Islamic schools—collides with the Constitution’s guarantee of free exercise of religion. Judge Bennett was right to find that troubling. But a blanket approval driven by litigation is also troubling.

The solution to an overbroad exclusion is not a rubber stamp, but due diligence. States must comply with the Constitution while protecting against terrorism. That requires examining each applicant school on its own record. Some Islamic schools clearly should qualify for the TEFA program. Whether Brighter Horizons and the Houston Quran Academy belong there is a harder question, and one the state should be able to answer through genuine investigation rather than blanket exclusion or court-compelled approval.

States should provide families access to robust school-choice options while protecting religious liberty. State officials should also take their duty seriously to avoid funding schools with genuine ties to terrorism. Those goals are not mutually exclusive. They require only that officials be precise, consistent, and willing to do their homework.

#7792. A Ken Paxton Moment

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

As Texas AG, Paxton's done a lot of controversial and in-my-opinion unwise things, but this is the one that sticks in my craw

I have stayed away from discussing any of the many important electoral contests that will be (hopefully) decided today.  But given that he is at the center of one of the most hotly-contested Senate seats, I can't help being reminded of his conduct during the campaign to overturn the 2020 election results, and what may have been the lowest of many low points in Ken Paxton's career to date.

In December 2020, when he was Attorney General of Texas, Paxton was the attorney of record in a lawsuit against the states of Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, seeking to overturn the 2020 election results in those states.  He petitioned the Supreme Court to exercise its original jurisdiction to hear the case, and to do so on an expedited basis. [See my blog posting at the time here; Paxton's papers filed at SCOTUS are posted here].

Expert analysis using a commonly accepted statistical test raises serious questions as to the integrity of this election. The probability of former Vice President Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States—Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin—independently given President Trump's early lead in those States as of 3 a.m. on November 4, 2020, is less than one in a quadrillion, or 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000. For former Vice President Biden to win these four States collectively, the odds decrease to less than one in a quadrillion to the fourth power (i.e., 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000^4).

The same less than one in a quadrillion statistical improbability [applies to] Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in the four Defendant States. . . . Again, the statistical improbability of Mr. Biden winning the popular vote in these four States collectively is 1 in 1,000,000,000,000,000.

Put simply, there is substantial reason to doubt the voting results in the Defendant States.

Indeed there is!  Prima facie proof of fraud in the counting of ballots, I'd say. But only, of course, it it's correct, or at least close to correct. But it's not correct.  It is, as anyone with a knowledge of elementary statistics would have recognized immediately, simply and laughably wrong. The technical term is, I believe, "utter bullshit." I explain why here.  The probability that Joe Biden would end up with a majority in any of those is not one in a quadrillion - let alone one in a quadrillion to the 4th power (!), which is approximately equal to the probability that the sun will rise in the West tomorrow, and will have developed the capacity for human speech - nor anything close to one in a quadrillion.

Hey, we all make mistakes, right? What is most disgraceful about this episode is not that Paxton screwed up in his brief to the Court; it is that he never acknowledges his error, either publicly or, more importantly perhaps, to the Court. His assertion that the probability that Biden actually carried these States was equal to the probability that you would pick the single blue marble from a collection of 1,000,000,000,000,000 marbles, is a falsehood, and it is one that is at the core of his argument, in a case that was of grave importance to the future of the country. If Paxton didn't catch that falsehood before he filed his papers with the Court, he's merely a lousy lawyer, which I suppose is nothing to get too worked up about, given that there always will be plenty of lousy lawyers out there. But if he doesn't acknowledge that he has misled the Court after those misstatements are revealed - if he doesn't tell the Court that it has to ignore the part of his argument that relied on this incorrect understanding of statistics - then he's in a much more sinister category.

That this is the candidate whom the Texas Republican party chose as its candidate for U.S. Senate speaks volumes about the current state of the Rule of Law in this Administration. I'm sure that Mr. Paxton is looking forward, assuming the results go his way, to forging a close working relationship with Attorney General Todd Blanche, who is similarly scrupulous in his adherence to fundamental Rule of Law principles (as in the Slush Fund fraud-on-the-court perpetrated by Blanche and the DOJ].

David Post is currently an Adjunct Scholar at the Cato Institute, and was previously a professor at Beasley School of Law at Temple University.

Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic announced Wednesday the release of Claude for Legal artifacts, with plans to provide users with 12 practice group-specific plug-ins and connectors to over 60 other legal platforms. (Image from Shutterstock)

Artificial intelligence developer Anthropic announced Wednesday the release of Claude for Legal artifacts, with plans to provide users with 12 practice group-specific plug-ins and connectors to over 60 other legal platforms.

Claude for Legal’s expansion encompasses reusable digital products, or artifacts, featuring tools, dashboards and workflows. The release of about 18 artifacts for commercial legal work will be tailored for intake, tabular review, regulatory tracking, jurisdiction surveys and citation confirmation. Users will have the option of customizing the artifacts and designing their own, according to coverage by Law.com.

Anthropic’s artifacts release continues a trend in Big Tech that includes Microsoft, Legora and OpenAI, which also launched legal-specific tools. Anthropic is also unveiling artifacts designed by partner organizations Goodwin Procter, Foley & Lardner, Harvey and PricewaterhouseCoopers. In addition, the company will launch a program for law schools and justice-oriented organizations that provides them with Claude seat licenses and application programming interface.

“We heard from legal users that they wanted something that was a little bit easier to use and adapt, rather than this blank screen that the Claude chat experience is,” said Robert Mahari, the head of Claude for Legal. “You can now take this, and it’s pretty close to ready to use.”

#7788. Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

after noting that many of plaintiff's filings contained seeming AI hallucinations, despite assertions in plaintiff's filings that all the citations were valid.

From Judge Aileen Cannon (S.D. Fla.) in Paulk v. Larva Labs, LLC, decided in June but just posted on Westlaw:

This case presents a dispute over Defendant's alleged fraudulent interference with Plaintiff's Non-Fungible Tokens ("NFTs"). Plaintiff's Complaint, initially filed in Florida state court on January 20, 2026, alleges that in June 2017, Plaintiff used a publicly available software tool to generate 141 NFTs on the Ethereum blockchain. Each of these NFTs represents ownership of a unique CryptoPunk that was part of the first version of CryptoPunks ("V1"), a pioneering generative art project consisting of 24x24 pixel portraits. To create the NFTs, Plaintiff paid only nominal "gas fees" (i.e., fees paid to third parties who validate transactions on the Ethereum blockchain), and the NFTs "have remained in [a] dormant wallet" controlled to this day by Plaintiff.

Plaintiff alleges that, on June 23, 2017, Defendant "deployed" a second version of CryptoPunks ("V2"), "claiming V1 contained a 'bug.'" The Complaint then asserts that Defendant "suppressed V1 marketplace activity while promoting V2 as the sole authoritative collection, rendering Plaintiff's assets commercially impaired". Based on these allegations, the Complaint asserts causes of action for fraudulent concealment (Count I), unjust enrichment (Count II), declaratory relief (Count III), and injunctive relief (Count IV), seeking unspecified monetary damages and an injunction.

The court discussed various procedural issues, and then added:

As a separate matter, the Court is concerned more generally about the plethora of legal filings seemingly prepared by artificial intelligence and submitted by Plaintiff that make frivolous and unsupported arguments to the Court [see, e.g., ECF Nos. 15, 16, 17, 18, 19, 26, 26-1, 31, 32, 33]. As an example, Plaintiff makes the obviously incorrect submission that the citizenship of Defendant's counsel can be considered in determining complete diversity.

And many of Plaintiff's filings contain disclaimers to the Court, expressly certifying "that every legal authority, statutory provision, rule of procedure, and historical case citation referenced within [the filings] has been independently read, analyzed, verified, and cross-referenced against official federal and state legal repositories." In each of these filings, "Plaintiff guarantees that every cited case stands as valid, binding law within the United States Supreme Court and the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals, possesses an active and unchecked standing, and accurately represents the procedural postures asserted." And he expressly warrants that he has not included any "fictitious or unverified citations," and that he has "manually double-checked" each case to ensure that it "support[s] Plaintiff's cause perfectly, ensuring that no unverified or 'hallucinated' data is presented to the Court."

No doubt Plaintiff's artificial intelligence legal counsel told him to say all this. And the AI certainly had the right idea—litigants should not make misrepresentations to the Court. Unfortunately, Plaintiff did not practice what his artificial counsel preached. Instead, he cites to "Snapper v. Redan, 523 U.S. 83 (1998)"—a case which does not exist—for the proposition that "when a company's chief legal representative has been sent formal notification at a publicly advertised professional office location, the entity cannot assert an administrative breakdown within its secondary commercial mail hubs as an equitable basis to vacate an otherwise valid default". Notwithstanding the made-up citation, the case Plaintiff means to cite, Snapper, Inc. v. Redan (11th Cir. 1999), is an Eleventh Circuit case that says nothing of the sort. Instead, Snapper established that federal appellate courts have jurisdiction to review remand orders based on the enforcement of contractual forum selection clauses. It does not mention vacatur, or default, or even mail—and it certainly does not stand for the extremely narrow proposition for which Plaintiff cites it.

In light of all this, Plaintiff has violated his duty of candor to the Court and has committed a Rule 11 violation…. [T]he Court [therefore] imposes filing sanctions as follows:

Plaintiff failed to respond to the motion to dismiss, and in a later opinion the court granted that motion.

Eugene Volokh is the Thomas M. Siebel Senior Fellow at the Hoover Institution at Stanford, and the Gary T. Schwartz Distinguished Professor of Law Emeritus and Distinguished Research Professor at UCLA School of Law. Naturally, his posts here (like the opinions of the other bloggers) are his own, and not endorsed by any institution. He is also the co-host of the Free Speech Unmuted podcast.

#7786. Another Trump term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

President Donald Trump and his policies were a consistent and high-profile theme during the Supreme Court’s last term. The justices weighed in on several of Trump’s signature initiatives, from sweeping global tariffs and his efforts to limit the availability of birthright citizenship to his attempts to fire members of the Federal Trade Commission and Federal Reserve’s Board of Governors – as well as various important immigration cases. And that’s all before you get to the court’s interim docket, where Trump chalked up a number of significant victories.

As it currently stands, the Supreme Court’s 2026-27 term is much less Trump-centric than its predecessor, featuring two challenges to Trump’s immigration policies and a dispute over access to information about Trump’s U.S. Department of Government Efficiency, also known as DOGE. But that could change soon: between Nov. 6 and mid-January, the justices are likely to consider a number of petitions for review filed by the Trump administration or Trump himself. Given the Office of the Solicitor General, which represents the federal government before the Supreme Court, has a high success rate – usually somewhere around 60% – for petitions that it files with the justices, Trump could once again end up dominating the term.

Immigration is already a hot topic on the court’s docket, but two immigration disputes could raise the prominence of the issue even more. When the justices meet for their Nov. 6 conference, one of the cases that they will consider is Mullin v. Refugee and Immigrant Center for Education and Legal Services, a challenge to a Trump administration policy of quickly removing immigrants who cross the border illegally without giving them the chance to seek asylum.

Two federal courts in Washington, D.C., agreed with the challengers – a group of immigrants and three immigrants’ rights groups – that the policy violates federal immigration law. That prompted U.S. Solicitor General D. John Sauer to come to the Supreme Court in August, where he argued that the decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit “threatens to dismantle” what Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin “describes as an ‘indispensable’ tool for controlling the border.”

Last month, the Trump administration asked the justices to weigh in on another dispute arising from its immigration agenda – this time involving the government’s efforts to detain and deport several students and academics because of their support for Palestine. The government’s petition came in the case of one of those detainees, Badar Khan Suri, an Indian national who came to the United States for a postdoctoral fellowship at Georgetown University. The Trump administration has told the justices that they should also consider granting the petition for review filed recently by Mahmoud Khalil, an Algerian national who was born in a Palestinian refugee camp in Syria and became a lawful permanent resident of the United States in 2024. The government contended that both men should be deported based on determinations by Secretary of State Marco Rubio that their conduct – alleged support for the Islamic militant group Hamas, in Suri’s case, and participation in “antisemitic protests and disruptive activities” for Khalil – compromised U.S. foreign policy.

Attorneys for Suri and Khalil went to federal court in New Jersey and Virginia, asking judges there to review the legality of their detentions on the ground that (among other things) they had been detained in retaliation for their speech. As their cases come to the court, the question that the justices have been asked to decide is whether federal trial courts even have the power to consider such challenges, or whether (as the Trump administration argues) those claims are instead barred by federal immigration law, which generally requires all challenges “arising from” deportation proceedings or the decision to begin such proceedings to go first to a federal appeals court, because they are also related to whether one can be deported. The federal courts of appeals have reached conflicting conclusions on the issue, which increases the likelihood that the justices will agree to weigh in.

Suri’s response to the government’s petition for review and the government’s response to Khalil’s petition are both due on Nov. 20. The justices will likely consider both petitions at a private conference sometime early next year.

In June, the Supreme Court granted the federal government’s petition for review in Genalo v. Black, agreeing to address whether there is a point at which a noncitizen has been detained so long that he or she has a constitutional right to a bond hearing and, if so, what standard the government must meet for him or her to remain in detention. That case was scheduled for oral argument in October, but it was dismissed in September because it was moot – that is, no longer a live controversy.

The Trump administration returned to the court later that month, asking the justices to grant a petition for review involving the same questions, which Sauer called “exceptionally important.” The case was filed by a citizen of the Dominican Republic, identified in court filings only as D.C., who has spent most of his adult life in the United States and has three daughters with a U.S. citizen. D.C. was detained on the same day that he finished serving a prison sentence, and the government sought to deport him.

In March 2026, when he had been in immigration custody for almost six-and-a-half months, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer agreed with D.C. that he was entitled to “an individualized bond hearing, with constitutionally adequate procedural safeguards.” The Trump administration is now appealing that decision to the Supreme Court without waiting for a federal appeals court to rule on the case. Sauer told the justices that “granting immediate review would allow the Court to consider” the questions it had already agreed to decide in Black during the 2026-27 term.

D.C.’s response is currently due on Dec. 8; if that deadline remains in place, the court would likely consider the government’s petition sometime in early to mid-January.

In Trump v. Thakur, the justices will consider a petition for review stemming from the 2025 decision to end research grants from the Environmental Protection Agency, National Science Foundation, and National Endowment for the Humanities for researchers at the University of California. The researchers went to federal court, where they argued that the termination of those grants violated (among other things) their rights to free speech and fair treatment, as well as the federal law governing administrative agencies.

A federal district court issued a preliminary order requiring the government to reinstate the grants. The government went to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit, which upheld that decision with regard to the claims on the basis that the administration had ended the grants because of the recipients’ “perceived expression of DEI, DEIA, or environmental justice viewpoints.”

The court of appeals rejected the government’s contention that it could terminate funding for programs that, in its view, are not in the public interest. “This overlooks that there is a critical distinction between creating or ceasing a particular program (or subsidy, or forum), on one hand, and discriminating against disfavored speaker viewpoints within a program (or subsidy, or forum), on the other,” the 9th Circuit wrote.

The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court in August, asking the justices to weigh in. Sauer told the court that “if left to stand, the Ninth Circuit’s decision will establish precedent forcing taxpayers to waste countless dollars on private projects promoting ideologies that their public stewards reject.”

Last week Sauer asked the Supreme Court to distribute the government’s petition, as well as the researchers’ brief opposing review, on Oct. 28, without waiting the 14 days normally prescribed by the court’s rules. This would allow the justices to consider the case at their Nov. 13 conference.

In United States v. Jackson, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to rule on the legality of Trump’s appointment of an acting U.S. attorney in Nevada. Sauer told the justices that the appointment of Sigal Chattah (as well as others around the country) was not only lawful, but “a critical tool that the Executive Branch has used without meaningful objection for 25 years.”

Under the Federal Vacancies Reform Act, the federal law that governs how the executive branch can temporarily staff vacant positions that require presidential appointment and confirmation by the Senate, interim officers can serve for 120 days. Under that law, then-Attorney General Pamela Bondi appointed Chattah as the interim U.S. Attorney for the District of Nevada, effective April 1, 2025, after Jason Frierson, who was nominated by then-President Joe Biden, stepped down.

With only a few days remaining before her interim appointment was set to expire, Chattah resigned, and Bondi designated her as the first assistant U.S. attorney. In that post, Bondi said, Chattah would have the power under the FVRA “to serve as Acting United States Attorney upon a vacancy in that office.” Bondi also gave Chattah the powers of a U.S. attorney for legal proceedings in Nevada.

Three men who had been indicted on felony charges in Nevada after Chattah’s designation as the first assistant U.S. attorney sought to have, at a minimum, Chattah disqualified from appearing in the case as the “Acting U.S. Attorney.” The lower courts agreed that Chattah was not eligible to serve as the acting U.S. attorney, and that she could not play any role in the prosecution of the defendants’ cases.

In a 34-page opinion, Judge Eric Miller of the 9th Circuit wrote that the “text and structure” of the FVRA are “unambiguous: The statute does not permit the executive to fill an existing vacancy by designating a new first assistant.” Instead, he reasoned, the FVRA “provides that a first assistant automatically succeeds to a vacant office” only if the first assistant was first assistant when the principal office became vacant. The automatic-succession rule, he concluded, “does not apply to a first assistant” – like Chattah – “who never served under a validly appointed official.” Moreover, Miller continued, the attorney general cannot achieve the same result “by delegating all of the functions and duties of the U.S. Attorney to someone else.”

In a second petition, United States v. Office of the New York State Attorney General, the Trump administration has appealed a ruling against it by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 2nd Circuit in a dispute over the appointment of John Sarcone as the Acting U.S. Attorney for the Northern District of New York. When Sarcone obtained grand jury subpoenas for information from the New York attorney general’s office relating to its investigations of the National Rifle Association and Trump, the office sought to quash the subpoenas on the ground that Sarcone had not been validly appointed.

A federal district court granted that request, and the 2nd Circuit upheld that decision. Sauer came to the Supreme Court in September, where he told the justices that Jackson was a better case in which to consider the validity of Trump’s appointments because the grand jury that issued the subpoenas in the New York case had been discharged and, as a result, the subpoenas were no longer enforceable. He urged the court to hold the New York case until it acts on Jackson.

The defendants challenging Chattah’s appointment have until Nov. 5 to file their brief opposing review; the response of the N.Y. attorney general’s office is currently due on Nov. 2.

There are several other notable petitions pending.

In May 2025, the Supreme Court cleared the way for the Trump administration’s request to temporarily enforce a ban on transgender servicemembers. In a different case just over one year later, a divided panel of the D.C. Circuit upheld part of an order by a federal judge in Washington, D.C., barring the Trump administration from expelling several challengers to the policy from the military. (At the same time, that panel lifted the part of the order that would have required the military to admit transgender people who want to join the armed forces.)

In its petition for review in United States v. Talbott, filed in August, the federal government asked the Supreme Court to review and eventually reverse the D.C. Circuit’s decision. Sauer called it “gravely erroneous” and argued that its “reasoning cannot be squared with this Court’s precedents or deference to the military.”

The response from the challengers is currently due on Nov. 2.

In Department of Health and Human Services v. Texas Medical Association, the Trump administration has asked the Supreme Court to weigh in on whether and when a federal court can throw out an agency’s action or rule in its entirety – a concept known as “universal vacatur.”

The question comes to the court in a case that began as a pair of challenges (that were later combined) to rules issued to implement parts of a 2022 law that was intended to protect patients from surprise healthcare bills. A federal district court in Texas ruled for the challengers – the Texas Medical Association, a hospital, and four air ambulance companies – but a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit reversed that decision in part.

The case then went to the full 5th Circuit, which threw out some of the challenged provisions. The Trump administration came to the Supreme Court this month, asking the justices to take up the dispute. It pointed to the Supreme Court’s 2025 decision in Trump v. CASA, holding that federal courts do not have the authority to enter so-called universal or nationwide injunctions, which prohibit the government from enforcing a policy anywhere in the country. The same logic underlying that case – the idea that courts “can grant ‘complete relief’ to parties before the court but cannot, as a rule, reach beyond them” – should apply to such regulations, Sauer contended.

The challengers’ response is currently due on Nov. 13, although that deadline may be extended.

Petitions filed by Trump’s personal lawyers

Although the federal government filed all of the petitions discussed above, Trump is also seeking Supreme Court review in three petitions filed by his personal lawyers. The most recent petition is also the one that the justices could consider first: Trump v. Clinton, the president’s bid to revive his lawsuit against Hillary Clinton (and several others, including the Democratic National Committee) alleging “a coordinated scheme … to undermine his candidacy and Presidency through fabricated accusations of Russian collusion.”

U.S. District Judge Donald Middlebrooks dismissed the lawsuit, finding (among other things) that Trump had brought his claims too late, and that many of the statements alleged to have been made by the various defendants were “plainly protected by the First Amendment.” Middlebrooks also sanctioned Trump and his attorney, Alina Habba, ordering them to pay nearly $1 million.

On appeal, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 11th Circuit largely upheld Middlebrooks’ decision and affirmed the sanctions orders. The full 11th Circuit rejected Trump’s request for reconsideration, prompting Trump – represented by Richard Klugh – to come to the Supreme Court on Oct. 9. He asked the justices to weigh in on two questions: whether the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended because of his unique role and responsibilities as president, and whether a court can fine the president and his lawyers for making the “substantial, unresolved argument” that the time to file Trump’s claims should have been extended.

Through her longtime attorney, David Kendall, Clinton waived her right to file a response to Trump’s petition. The case has been distributed to the justices for consideration at their Nov. 6 conference. The court is extremely unlikely to grant review without first calling for Clinton to file a brief opposing review.

In Trump v. CNN, the president is seeking to reinstate his defamation case against cable news giant CNN. Trump contends that when CNN used the phrase “the Big Lie” to describe his insistence that he had actually won the 2020 election, which had been stolen from him, it was attempting to link him with Adolf Hitler and Nazi propaganda – which, Trump said, was defamation.

A federal judge in Fort Lauderdale, Florida, dismissed Trump’s case. In an eight-page, unsigned opinion, the 11th Circuit upheld that ruling.

In his petition for review, which was filed in August, Trump contended that “CNN falsely and maliciously portrayed” him “as a knowing liar who fabricated objections to the 2020 election, lacked supporting evidence, and deliberately deceived the American people.”

And in July, Trump filed the second of two petitions arising from lawsuits brought by E. Jean Carroll, who had alleged that in 1996 Trump had sexually abused her in a dressing room at a New York department store. The lawsuit leading to the second petition claimed that in June 2019, Trump had defamed her by calling her a liar – saying, among other things, that Carroll “was trying to sell a new book” and that her accusations were “totally false.” A jury awarded Carroll $83.3 million in January 2024.

The 2nd Circuit upheld the award in 2025, finding “ample evidence that Trump was recklessly indifferent to Carroll’s health and safety” and that “Carroll was subjected to ongoing and prolific harassment as a result of these statements, including a multitude of death threats and other threats of physical injury.” The full court of appeals in April declined to rehear the case.

Represented by a private lawyer, Robert Giuffra, Trump argued in his petition for review that in the wake of the Supreme Court’s 2024 decision in Trump v. United States, in which it held that presidents generally have broad immunity for their acts while in office, the $83.3 million award cannot be allowed to stand. “The threat of even a single damages judgment based on official acts will render all Presidents ‘unable to boldly and fearlessly carry out [their] duties for fear that [they] may be next,’” Giuffra wrote.

The federal government filed its own petition backing Trump, in which it (like Trump) urged the Supreme Court to also decide whether the court of appeals should have granted then-Attorney General Bondi’s request to recertify that Trump made his statements as part of his role as president and therefore the federal government, rather than Trump, should be the defendant in Carroll’s case.

Carroll’s response to both petitions is currently due on Oct. 30.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

Recommended Citation: Amy Howe, Another Trump term?, SCOTUSblog (Oct. 27, 2026, 9:30 AM), https://www.scotusblog.com/2026/10/another-trump-term/

#7784. Choosin' Texas I Can Tell

Mostly law professors | Sometimes contrarian | Often libertarian | Always independent

A few moments ago, the networks called the Texas Senate and Governor races for the Democratic candidates. Those outcomes will get a lot of attention. But of significant interest will be the downballot judicial races in Texas.

This year, four of the nine seats on the Texas Supreme Court were on the ballot. Unless something unexpected happens, all four will lose: Chief Justice Jimmy Blacklock, Justice James P. Sullivan, Justice Kyle Hawkins, and Justice Brett Busby. These are all brilliant judges. Two of them clerked on the United States Supreme Court. Chief Justice Blacklock has been a strong leader, following in the footsteps of Chief Justice Nathan Hecht. But the qualifications do not matter. Everything was on the party line. The Texas Supreme Court will now have five Republican members and four Democratic members. One might expect a number of 5-4 cases for controversial cases. Then again, the Chief Justice is now the administrator of the state court system, which entails some important responsibilities.

The Texas Court of Criminal Appeals (the court of last resort for criminal cases) had three seats on the ballot. Again, unless something happens, all three will lose. There will still be a six-member conservative majority. I don't see too much changing on that Court.

Recently, the Fifteenth Court of Appeals was created as a statewide constitutional court. Virtually all suits against the government are routed to that court. (Think of something like the D.C. Circuit.) All three members of that court were on the ballot. Unless something happens, all three will lose. The Court will now have 100% Democratic members. I would expect a lot mandamus suits to the Texas Supreme Court.

I haven't had time to go through the returns from the local courts, but it appears that most of the incumbent republican judges will lose office. This will be an even bigger bloodbath than 2018, when the Beto wave wiped out nearly all of the Republican judges in Houston, Austin, Dallas, and other large cities. So much judicial experience for non-controversial judges will go down the tube.

The Governor of Texas is fairly weak, as compared to other states, but he does have the power to appoint new members of the Texas Supreme Court and other courts when vacancies arise. Recently, the Texas legislature created a new Texas Business Court. This court was designed to compete with Delaware. Many of the current Texas business courts are not likely to be reappointed. This election will significantly affect businesses that chose to make Texas their headquarters. Speaking of which…

The Texas Attorney General Race will also likely go to the Democratic candidate. I would suspect that all of the conservative strategic litigation cases brought by Attorney General Paxton will be dismissed. Indeed, it is conceivable that the new Texas Attorney General would not defend the Texas Ten Commandments Law if cert is granted. (The BIO will be filed soon.) The Texas Attorney General will also not bring original jurisdiction actions before the Supreme Court of Texas. Going forward, all of the strategic forums in Texas will be severely underutilized. The only court where the Texas Attorney General might file cases will be in Austin. I should note that one seat on the Western District of Texas remained vacant for two years, and will likely remain vacant. But beyond the strategic litigation, the Texas Attorney General will now be able to investigate all of the corporations that moved to Texas. There are a lot of them.

What about judicial nominees? Despite my best efforts, Judge Southwick will get the last laugh. Todd Butler will almost certainly be confirmed. But the Fifth Circuit will likely be a lot quieter, given the lack of Texas Attorney General cases. I also hope this means that Judge Rudofsky will get a vote, as that Eighth Circuit seat would remain vacant for the foreseeable future. Indeed, the Eighth Circuit may be the only viable forum for a Republican AG to bring cases starting in 2026.

Going forward, Senators Cruz and Talarico will have to agree on blue slips for District Court nominees. Still, I suspect zero nominees will get a vote over the next two years unless there is some deal struck with the Senate Democrats.

What about Justices Alito and Thomas? They did what Justice Breyer could not--resist the pressure. I hope they live long and prosper.

Ultimately, I'm reminded of something I tell my students--we are never more than two years away from a midterm election. Despite threats about fascism and totalitarianism, the people are able to effect change.

NEXT: Court Orders Plaintiff to File Handwritten Opposition,

Josh Blackman is a constitutional law professor at the South Texas College of Law Houston and the President of the Harlan Institute. Follow him @JoshMBlackman.

#7782. Law firms face increasing AI-fueled cyberattacks, new report says

Researchers are warning that cyberattacks using agentic artificial intelligence on law firms and other groups in the legal profession are on the rise. (Image from Shutterstock)

Researchers are warning that cyberattacks using agentic artificial intelligence on law firms and other groups in the legal profession are on the rise.

These attacks have doubled since 2023, according to cybersecurity company CrowdStrike’s 2026 Legal Threat Landscape Report, which was released Wednesday.

The report shows that between August 2025 and August 2026, cyber adversaries named 455 legal entities as hacking targets, an increase of 39% from the prior year.

While CrowdStrike did not name specific firms or other legal groups as the victims of attacks, Reuters has reported that Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan, Wilmer Cutler Pickering Hale and Dorr and Seyfarth Shaw are among those that have experienced cyber breaches in recent months.

“What we’re seeing across the broader threat landscape, more and more threat actors are using agentic technology ⁠to democratize hacking,” said Adam Meyers, CrowdStrike’s senior vice president for counter adversary operations. “It’s going to get a lot worse before it gets better.”

#7781. The Trump administration’s attempt to prevent noncitizen voting and the role of the Supreme Court

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court may soon see another clash between the original public meaning of the Constitution and President Donald Trump’s wishes. The birthright citizenship case, Trump v. Barbara, is one previous example of this. The next instance, which looms on the horizon, involves the issue of noncitizen voting.

The Trump administration has been aggressively undertaking efforts to get states to take steps aimed at preventing noncitizens from voting. The latest such effort is a lawsuit that Trump’s DOJ has filed against California seeking to force the state’s election officials to segregate mailed ballots cast by anyone on a list of 20,000 registered voters whom the Trump administration believes to be noncitizens. As of this writing, the suit is pending in the federal district court, after the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit denied DOJ’s emergency appeal for failing to give the district court an adequate chance to issue a ruling, but the merits of the case are likely to make their way to the Supreme Court very soon.

As authority for its suit against California, Trump’s DOJ is relying upon the federal statute that makes voting by noncitizens in federal elections a crime: 18 U.S.C. § 611. There are two fundamental problems, however, with DOJ’s reliance on this statute. First, the original public meaning of the Constitution does not give Congress the authority to make voting by noncitizens a crime; rather, the Constitution leaves it to the states to decide whether or not noncitizens may vote, and this is true even for federal elections.

Second, even assuming that 18 U.S.C. § 611 is a valid exercise of congressional power under the Constitution, it does not authorize DOJ to seek an injunction that would interfere with a state’s rules and procedures for conducting the “manner” of the current congressional elections. Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution provides that state law will govern the “manner” of administering congressional elections unless and until Congress enacts alternative procedures for their administration; 18 U.S.C. § 611 is a criminal law and does not regulate the “manner” of administering elections and thus offers no basis for DOJ or a federal court to supersede the state’s administration of the election.

As to the first problem, the Constitution creates a clear division of authority between determining who can vote in congressional elections and regulating how the voting process occurs. As to the how, as noted, Article I, Section 4 of the Constitution empowers Congress to override state regulations if Congress so wishes. But as to the who, the Constitution lodges the power to determine the qualifications for voting in congressional elections to the states, with Congress having no authority to change those qualifications.

To be sure, a series of important constitutional amendments constrains the degree to which states can set those qualifications. The 15th Amendment prohibits racial discrimination in doing so. The 19th Amendment similarly prohibits sex discrimination with respect to voting rights. The 24th Amendment prohibits a state from making payment of a poll tax a qualification for voting in a federal election. And the 26th Amendment prohibits states from denying an equal opportunity to vote based on age to any citizen at least 18 years old.

But none of these amendments prevent states from setting other qualifications or extending the right to vote. States, for example, could grant 16-year-old citizens the right to vote in congressional elections, and Congress cannot override a state’s decision to do this. The Constitution is explicit on this point. Article I, Section 2, clause 1 provides for the House of Representatives that “the Electors in each State shall have the Qualifications requisite for Electors of the most numerous Branch of the State Legislature.” The 17th Amendment contains the same provision for elections to the U.S. Senate. Thus, if a state were to grant 16-year-old citizens the right to vote for the lower house of the state legislature, the Constitution requires that 16-year-old citizens in that state must have the right to vote for that state’s Representatives and Senators in Congress. No Act of Congress could take away this right to vote in congressional elections granted to 16-year-olds by the state.

The same point applies to voting by noncitizens. Currently, no state chooses to let noncitizens vote for the lower house of the state’s legislature. But if a state decided to let resident aliens vote in these elections, then resident aliens would also be eligible to vote in the state’s congressional elections.

The Supreme Court previously has made clear this distinction between who and how. In 2013’s Arizona v. Inter Tribal Council of Arizona, Inc., which involved the National Voter Registration Act, Justice Antonin Scalia wrote in the opinion for the court (with its own emphasis on the two key words): “Arizona is correct that the Elections Clause empowers Congress to regulate how federal elections are held, but not who may vote in them.” Scalia elaborated: “Prescribing voting qualifications, therefore, ‘forms no part of the power to be conferred upon the national government’ by the Elections Clause, which is ‘expressly restricted to the regulation of the times, the places, and the manner of elections’” (quoting Alexander Hamilton in The Federalist No. 60). Scalia then explained why: “This allocation of authority sprang from the Framers’ aversion to concentrated power. A Congress empowered to regulate the qualifications of its own electorate, Madison warned, could ‘by degrees subvert the Constitution.’”

The prohibition on noncitizen voting in 18 U.S.C. § 611 contravenes this constitutional division of authority. This congressional statute makes it “unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for … Member of the Senate [or] Member of the House of Representatives,” and it does so regardless of whether the state in question permits noncitizens to vote in these elections. The statute lets states allow noncitizens to vote for state or local offices, but a state must do so “in such a manner that an alien has the opportunity to vote for such other purpose, but not an opportunity to vote for a candidate for any one or more of such Federal offices.” Thus, according to this federal statute, a state has no choice in the matter of whether or not a noncitizen can vote in a congressional election. This makes 18 U.S.C. § 611 unconstitutional.

I am not the first to reach this conclusion. A federal district court in Florida did so recently. More significantly, that district court had asked Paul Clement, the distinguished former U.S. solicitor general in President George W. Bush’s administration, to write an amicus brief on the issue. After undertaking a thorough analysis of the matter, Clement concluded “the better view is that because §611 was intended to criminalize alien suffrage in federal elections, regardless of state law, it sets a voter qualification—which only the states may do.”

To be clear, Congress can make noncitizen voting a crime if (but only if) that criminality is contingent on noncitizen voting also being unlawful in the applicable state. In that context, the congressional statute could be understood as merely regulating procedures for implementing congressional elections, and not determining who is permitted to vote in them. One might then try to argue that 18 U.S.C. § 611 can be sustained as this kind of statute as long as the relevant state currently criminalizes noncitizen voting. The difficulty with this argument, as Clement explained, is that § 611 is not written that way; instead, it emphatically makes noncitizen voting in congressional elections a federal crime regardless of what the state wants.

In any event, let’s assume that 18 U.S.C § 611 could be construed to be constitutional in the way just described. That still doesn’t give Trump’s DOJ the authority to seek an injunction in federal court to force California to change its procedures for administering the current congressional election. Congress would have needed to enact a different law, exercising its authority under the Constitution’s Article I, Section 4 to “alter” the “manner” by which California has chosen to regulate the voting process.

There was a time in American history when Congress enacted a statute to provide federal oversight of a state’s procedures for conducting congressional elections. In the wake of the Civil War, the first Enforcement Act of 1871 empowered two federal “supervisors” in each of the state’s voting precincts, who were appointed from “different political parties” by the federal circuit court for their state, to monitor the voting process for congressional elections. This statute gave these supervisors authority similar to what Trump’s DOJ is currently seeking. The supervisors, for example, could “challenge any vote offered by any person whose legal qualifications the supervisors, or either of them, shall doubt.” To be sure, these supervisors were not part of the Department of Justice, which Congress had created the previous year. Rather, the requirement that these two supervisors be from “different political parties” and appointed by the judiciary was designed to keep them insulated from a cabinet department under the control of a partisan president.

In any event, in 1894 Congress repealed all the provisions of the 1871 Act that had created these supervisors for congressional elections. Nothing like them existed until the Voting Rights Act of 1965, when Congress enacted new provisions for monitoring elections and enforcing the prohibition against racial discrimination in voting. These new provisions did give some significant enforcement powers to the DOJ and federal courts, but they were focused on guaranteeing the equal opportunity to vote regardless of race. These new provisions did not give DOJ or the federal courts any authority to interfere with the counting of ballots in a congressional election in order to prevent ballots cast by noncitizens from being counted.

Indeed, throughout the 20th century, the prevailing understanding was that federal courts lacked the power to intervene in a state’s procedures for counting votes in a congressional election, even if a suit was brought by a candidate with a direct stake in the matter. The most famous example of this is the 1948 Senate race that Lyndon Johnson won by 87 votes. His opponent, former Texas governor Coke Stevenson, sued in federal court to block the counting of votes believed to be fraudulent in the infamous Ballot Box 13. In an exercise of the Supreme Court’s emergency docket, however, Justice Hugo Black ordered that the federal court refrain from interfering with the state’s counting process. After an unusual four-hour oral argument held in Black’s chambers, which he permitted members of the press to attend, he announced his ruling orally. The New York Times reported that he stated that “before a court interfered with an election there must be a statute clearly authorizing this.” The Times also quoted Black as saying, “I think it is impossible to interpret present statutes that Federal courts may go into a state and suspend its process of electing a Senator.” (For more details on the fight over Ballot Box 13, see chapter 8 of my 2024 book “Ballot Battles: The History of Disputed Elections in the United States.”)

There is one caveat. In Bush v. Gore, the court modified Black’s understanding of the federal judiciary’s power insofar as that unusual (and controversial) case permitted a candidate to assert an equal protection claim as grounds for constraining a state’s election procedures. But Bush v. Gore did not involve a suit by the federal DOJ. Indeed, President Bill Clinton insisted that his administration refrain from any involvement in the litigation between the two candidates in the 2000 presidential election. The idea that the federal DOJ could have brought suit in federal court to control the counting process in that election – contrary to Florida’s own procedures – would have astonished even those who supported the idea that the candidates themselves could invoke the authority of the federal courts to enforce Florida’s compliance with constitutional requirements respecting the electoral process.

The bottom line is this: In a congressional election, the state administers the electoral process according to its own laws, subject to the prerogative granted to each congressional chamber by Article I, Section 5 to be the “Judge of the Election … of its own Members.” If Congress wants to add DOJ-initiated federal court proceedings to the overall process of counting, canvassing, and certifying the votes in a congressional election – which would still be subject to being overridden by the ultimate authority of each chamber to adjudicate any disputes over the outcome pursuant to Article I, Section 5 – Congress can do by exercising its Article I, Section 4 authority. But unless and until Congress does that, DOJ has no role to play.

Trump and his DOJ clearly wish the situation were different. But it is the job of the Supreme Court to uphold the law as it is. That job may require the court to reject the effort by Trump’s DOJ to interfere with California’s procedures for conducting this year’s midterm elections.

Edward B. (Ned) Foley holds the Ebersold Chair in Constitutional Law at The Ohio State University, where he also directs its Election Law program.
