He said that within a 30-day window of sending the emails about Breyer, Pokorny also sent emails targeting âCIA officers, Kanye West, traitors, Catholics, Democrats, rock stars, DJs, clerks, managers, janitors, the Pope, Ukrainian Nazis, the U.S. armed forces, the mayor of Chicago, and letâs not forget the freemasons.â

After opening statements, presiding U.S. District Judge Jon Tigar, a Barack Obama appointee, instructed the jury that the government doesn’t have to prove that the Pokorny intended to carry out the threat for it to supersede the protections of First Amendment free-speech rights.

Dorsey, a supervisor for judicial security officers in the Northern District of California federal courts, said he considered the emails âescalatingâ by the language and specificity and started a âfull threat caseâ investigation on Sept. 2, to find out who sent the emails and ensure Breyerâs safety.

#7669. Ignition, Inc.: MSP Mac Help Desk Guru (work from home)

Ignition is one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and the only fractional IT firm that specializes in the venture-backed technology ecosystem.

Fully Remote · Work from home · Full-time (Eastern or Pacific time zones) · Apple-first

ignitionit.com is a seasoned, Apple-first MSP — in business for almost 30 years — and we're hiring a Help Desk Technician to be the friendly, capable first voice our clients reach when something isn't working. This position is a remote, work-from-home, full-time role.

We've written this as a junior-to-mid-level job description because that's where most great people start on our team. But if you're more seasoned — comfortable in identity, MDM, or security work — don't scroll past. We'd be delighted to find someone who can step in higher up the ladder, and we'll happily talk about a more senior scope and comp if that's you.

Unlike many IT shops, we believe that the technology is the tactic. The actual job is making people feel taken care of. One of our core values is “49% tech support, 51% human support.”

You'll succeed by configuring devices, resetting access, untangling email, and chasing down the gremlin that's been haunting someone's conference room. But you'll know you succeeded when a client exhales and says, “Thank goodness you're on it!” That Warm Fuzzy Feeling™ is the actual product. The green lights on the dashboard are just how we get there.

Onboard a new hire at a fast-growing startup: provision their Mac, set up their Google Workspace or Microsoft 365 accounts, enroll the device in MDM, and make sure day one feels effortless.

Offboard a departing employee cleanly — recover the laptop, revoke access, and close the loop so nothing's left dangling. All boxes checked, ticket notated and closed, client followed up with.

Field a "my email stopped working" ticket that turns out to be a DNS thing, a phishing-filter thing, or a "they changed their password on their phone three weeks ago" thing.

Help a family office or RIA get a touchy Zoom Room or conference-room AV setup behaving before a meeting — over the phone.

Triage the queue so phones get answered fast, emails don't rot, and nobody feels forgotten — even when the honest answer is, “We're on it, but here's the realistic timeline."

⠀ You'll be the front line: helping with what you can, researching what you can't, and pinging the rest of the team when you're genuinely stuck. That last part is a skill, not a weakness — knowing when to ask is half the job.

We're one of the oldest Apple Technical Partners on the planet, and one of the only certified Apple Premier Partners — that’s kinda like getting knighted by the ghost of Steve Jobs. We started where you’d expect to find Macs (creative agencies, non-profits, education) but our primary clients today are cutting-edge, venture-backed AI SaaS startups, VC and private equity firms, registered investment advisors — many of them operating under stringent compliance expectations (SOC 2, SEC). That means we hold ourselves to a higher standard than the scrappy shop we started as. Polished, reliable, security-minded work is the baseline now — but always with a smile!

What hasn't changed: relationships are still our most valuable currency — with clients, with vendors, and with each other. We're a tight, supportive team. We teach each other what we know, cover for each other when life throws a punch, and care a little too much about doing things the right way. We're still a bit weird, and our clients seem to like us that way.

We move fast, priorities shift, it’s not always documented (whatever it is), our tool set and list of supported platforms is sprawling, and some days the to-do list is longer than you'd like. If you can stay warm under pressure, create order out of chaos, learn new stuff fast because you love it, and speak up when you need help, you'll thrive here.

If you need a rigid, fully-documented, never-changes environment where nobody trusts you with admin access, where you will be micro-managed so you never have to wonder whether or not you’re doing the right thing, this isn't it. You’ll have a ton of independence on our team, and freedom to use your best judgment to get the ball over the finish line, but that also means we expect you to be naturally responsible, honest, and highly accountable — to yourself, your teammates, and the clients. As they say, the price of freedom is eternal vigilance.

The tech you'll work with (and grow into)

Apple at the core — macOS, iOS, Apple Business Manager, and MDM (Jamf / Iru / Intune / Workspace ONE / and more)

Yes, PCs too — about one-third of our users are driving Windows

Google Workspace and Microsoft 365 admin consoles

Identity and access — SSO, MFA, and security keys (Okta, Entra ID, Yubikey, and friends)

Lots of other security tools — our stack is constantly evolving and may vary from client to client

The everyday productivity stack — Slack, Zoom, conference-room AV, networking basics (Meraki), and endpoint tooling

⠀ You don't need to know all of this. You need to be the kind of person who wants to. As you grow, there's a clear path into infrastructure administration, project architecture and implementation, and — for the right person — security and compliance work (phishing simulations, endpoint detection, SOC 2 / CIS / SEC readiness, due diligence questionnaire support, etc.). That's where our most senior people live, and it's wide open.

The hard requirements — we won't move forward unless you:

Can work standard business hours in Eastern or Pacific time zones (we currently need both)

Have a quiet home workspace and reliable broadband

Have proven Apple aptitude — you actually use and like the Apple ecosystem

Have at least 5 years of IT support experience on the job.

⠀ Everything else — and this is the longer list, on purpose. We figure technical skills are teachable; character takes a lot longer. So we're looking for someone who:

Genuinely cares — about clients, teammates, and doing right by people

Loves to learn, and proves it in how they spend their time

Reads, and writes clearly — clear writing is clear thinking, and you'll do a lot of it

Stays calm and kind with a frustrated person on the other end of the line

Can tell the difference between good customer service and fantastic customer service, and refuses to settle for the former

Notices when something's being done inefficiently and fixes it (you may boast about it later, that’s fine)

Proofreads their own work (yes, we noticed whether you proofread your application)

Has a sense of humor, and doesn't take themselves too seriously

Our company founder/CEO is headquartered in the Bay Area. We work with innovative, ambitious companies developing AI products. Our team members hold a range of opinions about whether AI is “good or bad” for humans, but at the end of the day, we embrace the plain fact that it is here, we must embrace it to evolve, and our clients increasingly depend on us to help them embrace it, too, to help them evolve and stay competitive.

Our CEO's opinion: AI will not replace human labor any time soon; rather, AI is a new opportunity to either (a) get things done faster, or (b) get a much higher quality of output than before. If you’re an AI tinkerer, great! We want to hear how you’re using it and see your latest vibe project. If you’re allergic to AI or have no interest in learning new habits to work effectively with it, this is not the place for you.

Base salary: Applicants outside the USA will be compensated according to your local employment market. For applicants closer to the junior side who are located in the USA, $50,000–$65,000/yr, depending on experience level and your local geographical price index. With experience, comp goes up from there. Genuinely experienced, more senior candidates can be slotted higher — let's talk.

Type & location: Full-time, work from home, fully remote. Eastern or Pacific time zones.

Benefits: Medical / dental / vision for the employee, 401(k) with employer contribution, 2 weeks of PTO annually to start, and a stipend for your home internet.

The first step is really easy and only takes 10 minutes — no resume, no cover letter, no essays. Here's how:

Take this online Culture Index assessment (about 10 minutes): We use it to screen for people whose natural wiring fits how our team works.

If your profile lines up with what we're looking for, we'll reach out and ask you to complete a 60-minute TestGorilla assessment for critical thinking skills, send us your resume, and maybe a couple of other items.

From there, we conduct between 2-4 video interviews. One of these might be a live technical assessment.

If the Culture Index step feels like a strange way to start a job application — that's kind of the point. Remember the phrase Think Different?

Ignition is an equal opportunity employer. We welcome and will consider all qualified applicants. Good luck in your search — and may the Force be with you!

#7668. Law firm apologizes to truckers for ‘serial killer’ ad

A Texas law firm is apologizing for an ad in Maxim magazine that created such an outcry among truckers that truck stops pulled the publication from their shelves.

The full-page ad for San Antonio law firm Villarreal & Begum showed a picture of a truck cab beneath the words “serial killer.” Both the law firm and Maxim are apologizing for the ad after Pilot Flying J and TravelCenters of America pulled the magazine from their shelves. Publications with stories include HDT Trucking Info, TheTrucker.com, CSPNet.com, KIROTV.com and LandLinemag.com.

The copy read: “3,561 people died on America’s highways last year. Another 2.36 million were injured. You need a law firm you can Trust. You need Experience. You need Strength. You need Villarreal & Begum. We’re proven leaders in prosecuting cases involving death and catastrophic injury.”

In its statement, the law firm says it never intended “to disparage the hardworking Americans that drive tractor-trailers for a living. Our intent was to reach out to those individuals who have been involved in catastrophic accidents as a result of irresponsible drivers. The ad was inartfully created, and we could see how it may have caused our message to be misconstrued. We recognize the service that truck drivers provide to this nation and acknowledge that most truck drivers are safe and responsible drivers.”

Maxim also issued a statement saying the ad “does not reflect the beliefs or opinions of the people at this magazine, which recently has begun operating under new ownership.” The ad has been pulled from Maxim’s digital copy and replaced with facts about the trucking industry.

#7667. Sony smart TV privacy suit survives as judge rejects arbitration bid

A federal judge rejected Sonyâs attempt to force consumers into arbitration over claims that its smart TVs secretly collected viewing data and shared it with advertisers.

SAN DIEGO (CN) â A federal judge denied a bid by Sony Electronics to send a class action to private arbitration over claims its smart TVs secretly tracked viewing habits and shared that information with advertisers, while also allowing the suit to proceed in court.

The plaintiffs claim Sony embedded automatic content recognition technology into its smart TVs and used it to collect viewing data without their consent. The technology captures fragments of audio and video content, turns them into a digital fingerprint and shares them with third parties for targeted advertising. The technology also creates viewing profiles that can be shared across connected devices, such as phones.

The plaintiffs claim Sony failed to meaningfully disclose this technology in its devices.

Sony, which has used the technology since at least 2017, argued the plaintiffs are bound by a provision under the smart TVsâ limited warranty that requires disputes to go to arbitration and prevents them from suing in court. The provision required them to opt out within 30 days of purchase.

But Senior U.S. District Judge Marilyn Huff found the company effectively hid this in a separate document.

âHere, nothing outside or on the box alerted plaintiffs to additional terms and conditions, the arbitration provision itself was in a document titled âlimited warranty,â and nothing near the top of the limited warranty or elsewhere alerted consumers that the document contained bilateral terms and conditions that may be accepted by using the smart TV,â the George H.W. Bush appointee wrote Monday. âThe language relating to arbitration was bolded and separated by a heading, but other sections also had bold headings, and the provision was in the same small print as the rest of the dense one-pager. On these facts, a reasonable person receiving Sonyâs Limited Warranty had no fair notice that he should read the document for binding terms and conditions before using his Sony Smart TV, or that an arbitration provision contained therein would extend beyond the scope of the warranty.â

Citing a related case, Norcia v. Samsung Telecommunications, Huff ruled reasonable consumers would not know the limited warranty also included the arbitration provision.

Sony Electronics moved to dismiss all claims as untimely, arguing the statute of limitations bars the plaintiffs’ claims. However, Huff declined to dismiss at this stage, writing this argument was best suited for a motion for summary judgment.

The plaintiffs also accuse Sony Electronics of publicly disclosing private facts. They say Sony distributed their data downstream to companies such as Samba TV, a content-tracking software company, and Google, which then distributed it into a broader advertising ecosystem.

Huff declined Sony’s motion to dismiss both claims.

âGiven the broad dissemination alleged, the court concludes that plaintiffs adequately plead disclosure,â Huff ruled.

Sony’s arguments were, again, better suited during the summary judgment stage, she wrote.

However, Huff dismissed the plaintiffsâ remaining 12 claims with leave to amend.

âThe complaint lacks detail as to how an ordinary person could use this information to identify Plaintiffs,â she wrote. âIndeed, the complaint and plaintiffsâ opposition to Sonyâs motion to dismiss reference unique capabilities of Samba and Google, not the ordinary person.â

Huff also agreed with Sonyâs request to dismiss claims for injunctive relief.

âAs pled, the complaint fails to show why, despite now knowing of Sonyâs embedded automatic content recognition system, plaintiffs still face a credible threat of harm,â she continued. âPlaintiffs do not allege a desire to re-purchase Sony smart TVs. Indeed, they repeatedly claim the opposite by stating that if they had known what they do now, they never would have purchased the smart TVs or would have paid substantially less for them.â

A spokesperson for either party did not respond to requests for comment.

The Japanese electronics and entertainment company has developed televisions since the 1960s. Sony Electronics is based in San Diego County, where the class action was filed.

#7666. South Dakota voter wins order allowing ‘Natives Vote’ T-shirt at polling site

Yankton Sioux tribe member Lonnie Provost sued Monday, claiming a First Amendment violation after he was turned away from a South Dakota polling place for wearing the shirt.

(CN) â A member of the Yankton Sioux tribe cast his ballot Tuesday at a polling place in Wagner, South Dakota, wearing the apparel of his choice. But he needed a a federal judge’s order to do so.

In a complaint filed in federal court Monday, Lonnie Provost said Charles Mix County election officials turned him away from his polling place during 2024 general election because he wanted to cast a ballot wearing a “Natives Vote” T-shirt.

Jason Gant, the auditor, has said those tees violate state laws against electioneering, which prevents anyone from displaying campaign materials within 100 feet of a polling place, according to Provost in his complaint.

Since that day, Provost’s attorneys repeatedly told state and county officials the policy violated his and others’ constitutional rights. Those officials did not see it his way.

On Monday, Provost sued and requested a temporary restraining order allowing him to vote the next day wearing the shirt. U.S. District Judge Karen E. Schreier granted the motion Tuesday morning following a hearing at the federal courthouse in Sioux Falls.

“Plaintiff has demonstrated a likelihood of success on his First Amendment claim,” wrote Schreier, a Bill Clinton appointee, in her order. “His shirt conveys a nonpartisan Native voter participation message without advocating for or against a candidate, political party, or ballot measure. On the present record, defendantsâ treatment of that message as prohibited campaign material lacks an objectively reasonable basis consistent with the First Amendment.”

Schreier required Gant to instruct election workers at every Charles Mix County polling place that any voter wearing the “Natives Vote” shirt or similar apparel be allowed to vote.

Following Schreier’s order, Provost successfully cast his ballot wearing the “Natives Vote” shirt.

âNo voter should have to choose between expressing pride in Native electoral participation and casting a ballot,â said Samantha Blencke, senior staff attorney for the Native American Rights Fund, which co-represented Provost.

âThe actions by Charles Mix County send precisely the wrong message,â added Thad Titze, an associate at Robins Kaplan firm in Sioux Falls, which is co-representing Provost. âOur democracy depends on an active citizenry, one that takes the responsibility for casting a ballot seriously. We need more people following Lonnieâs enthusiasm, not less.â

An emailed message to an attorney representing Gant and the county was not immediately returned Tuesday afternoon.

Provost seeks a declaratory judgement and permanent relief.

Blencke said in an interview with Courthouse News that the Native American Rights Fund had been working with Provost since the 2024 incident. They initially reached out to the South Dakota Secretary of State’s Office with no success.

After Gant remained unmovable following a message sent Wednesday, Provost’s attorneys realized they would have to sue in federal court.

The order remains effective until voting is completed at all Charles Mix County polling places Tuesday.

Michael Clubfoot is accused of holding a woman at gunpoint over a missing truck in 2024, but he likely won't get his trial until at least 2027.

ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. (CN) â Despite telling the courtroom that the case was the oldest on her docket, a New Mexico federal judge granted a request to delay trial over a violent kidnapping and assault of a woman on Zuni reservation land.

Originally scheduled for Dec. 14, Michael Clubfoot’s trial won’t happen this year, after U.S. District Judge Kea Riggs, a Donald Trump appointee, granted a 90-day continuance.

Susan Burgess-Farrell of Burgess and Porter Law, Clubfoot’s defense, initially requested a 60-day continuance, citing pretrial preparation and plea negotiations.

Burgess-Farrell did not appear in court Tuesday. Barry Porter, of the same firm, told Riggs that Burgess-Farrell was in Texas with a family emergency. He suspected this played into the requested length of time, he said.

Beyond Burgess-Farrellâs own schedule, Porter told the court that the case was âcomplex.â Burgess-Farrell likely needed the time to review new DNA evidence, look over Clubfoot’s co-defendantsâ testimonies and continue plea negotiations, he said.

âThis case is pretty close to resolution with a plea agreement,â Porter said. The government offered Clubfoot a plea deal on Oct. 7.

Clubfoot, 45, faces six counts, including kidnapping in Indian Country, assault with a dangerous weapon and firearm charges, stemming from a May 2024 kidnapping and severe beating of a woman alongside two co-defendants.

Assistant U.S. Attorney Eva Fontanez did not argue against the motion.

Clubfoot’s co-defendants, Carlyn Calavaza, 41, andAlexis Mahooty, 40, accepted plea agreements in 2025 to their charges of kidnapping in Indian Country and aiding and abetting.

Clubfoot, Calavaza and Mahooty are accused of kidnapping Jane Doe on May 18, 2024. Doe reportedly arrived at Clubfootâs residence that day, where Clubfoot told her to âget inâ and proceeded to question her on the location of Calavazaâs truck.

According to prosecutors, Clubfoot âwailedâ on and threatened Doe, assaulting her while awaiting Calavazaâs arrival. During the assault, Clubfoot reportedly pointed a handgun at Doeâs face and hit her on the head with it several times.

âClubfoot kept the gun in his hand throughout the rest of the incident,â prosecutors write in the complaint.

Mahooty, who later arrived at Clubfootâs residence, was also accused of assaulting Doe. Calavaza questioned Doe about the truck, which she said she knew nothing about. Calavaza then reportedly tied her up, after which Doe lost consciousness and later awoke to taillights.

âThe group told her if she wants to keep her friends and family safe then she wonât say who had attacked her and she should keep her mouth shut,â prosecutors write.

The following morning, a rancher found Doe in his barn. He took Doe to the hospital and reported the incident to the Zuni Police Department, prosecutors say.

Investigators located Doeâs necklace, a receipt matching Doeâs card number and a BB gun with blood stains on May 19.

Clubfoot was arrested on outstanding warrants on May 20, and Calavaza and Mahooty were arrested on charges of conspiracy to conceal a fugitive the same day.

Calavaza and Mahooty are awaiting sentencing on their pleas. Calavazaâs date is set for Jan. 25, 2027. The court vacated Mahootyâs date from June and has not yet reset it. They both face up to life in prison for their charges.

Clubfoot was arraigned on Dec. 20, 2024, and has remained in federal custody since.

#7663. Court won’t intervene in California ballot dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

It’s Election Day in the United States. At SCOTUSblog, we’ll be watching not only for race results, but also for new voting-related legal battles. In recent weeks, the Supreme Court has addressed several emergency applications linked to the midterms, and the justices received – and decided – another one on Monday on alleged noncitizen voting in California.

On Monday, the Trump administration returned to the Supreme Court’s interim docket, asking the justices to intervene in its efforts to keep California from counting ballots cast by what it contends are noncitizen voters. Just hours later, the court denied the request. There were no noted dissents. For more on the dispute, see the On Site section below.

Also on Monday, the justices heard argument in two cases: Maxwell v. Dinis, on a federal inmate’s ability to use a habeas statute, 28 U.S.C. § 2241, to contest the Federal Bureau of Prisons’ refusal to accelerate his transfer to a halfway house or home confinement; and Younge v. Fulton Judicial Circuit District Attorney’s Office, Georgia, on whether an affirmative defense may be asserted as a basis for summary judgment if not presented earlier in a pleading.

On Monday afternoon, the court released its calendar for the January argument session, which will begin on Monday, Jan. 11. Learn about the session in the On Site section.

Today, the justices will hear argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a religious discrimination challenge brought by Catholic preschools in Colorado over the state’s requirement that all schools participating in its universal preschool program must admit everyone – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents.

Tomorrow, the justices will hear argument in Guerrero v. Johnson, on the limited circumstances in which a state prisoner can return to federal court for a second round of post-conviction review.

On Oct. 21, the Trump administration asked the justices to allow it to resume construction of its border wall in the Big Bend region of southwestern Texas. The request is now fully briefed, and the court’s decision could come at any time.

Kelsey Dallas is SCOTUSblog's managing editor and the primary author of the SCOTUStoday newsletter.

#7662. Environmentalists successfully block California’s first carbon capture project

TerraVault was one oil and gas company's plan to inject and store up to 2 million tons of carbon dioxide underground every year.

(CN) âÂ A Superior Court judge ruled Tuesday that Kern County’s approval of California’s first carbon capture and storage project violated the state’s bedrock environmental law, the California Environmental Quality Act.

The ruling is a win for local environmental justice and conservation groups, including the Sierra Club and the Center for Biological Diversity, who argued the county had left “multiple environmental, public health and safety issues” unaddressed when it approved the landmark project.

âFor years, Kern County residents have raised serious concerns about increased pollution and the safety of millions of tons of CO2 stored beneath their community," Ileana Navarro of the Central California Environmental Justice Network said in a written statement. “We are so grateful that the court recognized what Kern County failed to see and gave community concerns the serious consideration they deserve.”

Located at the Elk Hills Oil Field in the San Joaquin Valley and built by the California Resources Corporation, the state’s largest oil and gas company, TerraVault began capturing carbon dioxide from oil wells and injecting it underground in May. Once completed, the two vaults, made from depleted oil reservoirs, are expected to capture more than 2 million tons of carbon dioxide every year âÂ the equivalent of what more than 400,000 cars would emit annually.

In an email, President and CEO of the California Resources Corporation Francisco Leon expressed disappointment in the ruling, writing: “This project is the result of years of work, including close consultation with surrounding communities where we received overwhelming support for our efforts. This order is a step in the wrong direction for addressing the impacts of climate change and reflects the weaponization of CEQA by a narrow group of special interests. We are still evaluating the order and will aggressively pursue all available options to protect and advance this important project.â

Some environmental groups have said TerraVault I will, in effect, extend the life of the Elk Hills Oil Field, the seventh most productive in the U.S. The California Resources Corporation has said it could also store carbon from a range of not-yet-built factories in the region, which could produce, among other things, cement and steel. These new industries, opponents say, would further pollute a low-income area already struggling with bad air quality.

In their CEQA lawsuit, the plaintiffs argued the environmental impact report, prepared by the California Resources Corporation and approved by Kern County, didn’t properly account for the eight possible industries TerraVault I could capture carbon for, even though the new factories were a “reasonably foreseeable consequence” of the project. Superior Court Judge Marcos Camacho agreed.

“The record evidence shows that all CO2 capture equipment, transportation pipelines, compression facilities, injection and monitoring wells, and underground pore space exist solely to receive and store CO2,” Camacho wrote in the ruling. “Thus, the source facilities and industries unquestionably change the scope and nature of the project… The Court finds that such omission indicates that the whole of the project was not considered, in violation of CEQA.”

The judge found plenty of other shortcomings in the environmental report, referred to in the ruling as the REIR.Â “The issue of atmospheric leakage of CO2,” for example, was not “fully addressed.” He also found the report “fails to adequately mitigate the project’s greenhouse gas impacts.”

“This is a lack of analysis in the REIR, not a disagreement among experts,” Camacho wrote.

The ruling means TerraVault must temporarily shut down. The California Resources Corporation will have to prepare a new environmental impact report, a long and costly process, before it can restart operations.

The fight over TerraVault exposes a deep and long-standing divide within the environmental movement. Some groups believe climate change is the biggest threat to life on earth, and to avoid the most dire consequences, we must employ any and all tactics to remove carbon from the atmosphere. One report by the Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change reads, âThe deployment of [carbon dioxide removal] to counterbalance hard-to-abate residual emissions is unavoidable if net zero CO2 or GHG emissions are to be achieved."

Other groups, including the plaintiffs suing to stop TerraVault, say the way to stop climate change is to cut emissions.

“California needs to invest in real solutions like clean wind and solar to solve our energy and climate emergencies,” said Michelle Ghafar, an attorney with Earthjustice that represented the plaintiffs, in a written statement. “We canât waste time on âHail Maryâ projects pushed by the fossil fuel industry that will only delay our progress and further entrench pollution in frontline communities.â

The constitutional amendment passed without opposition.

RIO DE JANEIRO (CN) â Brazil approved a constitutional amendment Tuesday that expands the federal governmentâs role in public security, directs oil revenue to policing and prisons and calls for tougher penalties against criminal organizations.

The Senate approved President Luiz InÃ¡cio Lula da Silvaâs proposal in two rounds of voting, with no opposing votes, after separating out amendments that would lower the age of criminal responsibility. The lower house approved the amendment March 4, clearing the way for Congress to formally enact it without presidential approval.

The vote marks a victory for Lula after a presidential campaign in which public security figured prominently. The amendment also clears the way for a Public Security Ministry, whose creation Lula had made contingent on its approval.

The government secured approval before the new Congress takes office in 2027, when the opposition will have greater strength in the Senate.

Lula welcomed the vote in a social media post, saying the new ministry would focus on intelligence, planning and cooperation with states and municipalities to confront criminal factions and militias.

âProtection for citizens. Prison for criminals,â Lula wrote. âThe Brazilian people have the right to work, return home and live in peace. Guaranteeing that right is a commitment of Brazilâs government.â

JoÃ£o Gabriel Madeira Pontes, an attorney who holds a doctorate in public law from Rio de Janeiro State University, welcomed greater federal involvement and cooperation among different levels of government.

âUnder the original framework of the 1988 Constitution, public security was almost exclusively the responsibility of the states,â Pontes said.

The amendment adds the Unified Public Security System, which already exists under federal law, to the Constitution. It provides for joint operations, information sharing and integration of federal, state and municipal agenciesâ systems.

It restricts the governmentâs ability to freeze money in federal public security and prison funds or use it for other purposes, while directing 10% of the surplus in the oil-funded Social Fund to those programs. The transfers will begin in 2027 and reach the full percentage in 2029.

The text requires legislation establishing tougher penalties for members of criminal organizations based on their rank within those groups. These include incarceration in maximum-security or other specialized facilities, limits or bans on moving to less restrictive prison regimes and confiscation of assets linked to criminal activities.

The amendment also expands the Federal Policeâs authority to investigate militias and criminal organizations operating across state or international borders. The Federal Highway Police will be able to patrol federal railways and waterways in addition to highways.

Municipalities will be able to establish civilian police forces for patrols and community policing, provided they meet requirements for training, funding and coordination with other forces. Public prosecutors will exercise external oversight.

Pontes said the main challenge will be integrating new federal and municipal responsibilities with existing state police structures. The amendment maintains the division between military police, responsible for patrols, and civil police, responsible for criminal investigations.

âHow will this fit together with an old institutional structure that has been criticized for many years â the statesâ public security structure?â Pontes said. âI think there will be considerable difficulty integrating these changes with the institutional framework that already existed at the state level.â

Pontes also questioned the effectiveness of relying on incarceration, which he described as âsomewhat the logic behind the amendment.â

âMass incarceration has always been a phenomenon in Brazil, and it grows every year. And we havenât achieved much through incarceration. I really donât know how this could improve public security, specifically the fight against organized crime,â Pontes said.

A dispute over the age of criminal responsibility, currently 18, had threatened to delay approval. The opposition proposed lowering it to 16 generally and 14 for certain crimes, while a Workersâ Party proposal would lower it to 16 only for crimes classified as heinous under Brazilian law. Senators voted 38-36 to consider those proposals separately, avoiding another vote on the amendment in the lower house.

Senator FlÃ¡vio Bolsonaro, whom Lula defeated in the presidential election, participated remotely from the United States and voted against considering the proposals separately. He left Brazil on Oct. 27, after a Supreme Court justice ordered him to surrender his passports as part of an investigation into suspected money laundering.

#7660. New York State Bar Association tells lawyers not to bill for time saved by AI

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use it. (Image from Shutterstock)

The New York State Bar Association is calling for restrictions on how much lawyers can bill clients for the amount of time saved using artificial intelligence tools or expended learning how to use it.

Law360 reported Monday that the state bar association’s Committee on Artificial Intelligence and Emerging Technologies issued a report classifying the cost of buying and maintaining such software as an overhead expense that can be passed along as a disbursement only when tied to a specific client matter and when the basis for the charge has been disclosed.

According to Law360, the report added that lawyers generally don’t have to tell clients about AI use for administrative tasks—such as word processing, spelling and grammar checks, calendaring or timekeeping—provided that the use doesn’t affect fees.

“Generative AI is indelibly changing the practice of law. As part of our mission to be the leading voice for the legal profession, we are providing clear guidelines on the use of AI tools as a resource, so attorneys can use AI responsibly and ethically in their practices,” said Taa Grays, the president of the New York State Bar Association, in a statement. “The guidelines can help attorneys avoid possible perils of using AI, including inadvertently practicing law in a jurisdiction where they are not licensed or failing to notify clients or the courts of AI use.”

The committee also flagged familiar hazards, such as biased training data that may deepen existing inequities. Confidentiality is another concern: If an AI tool learns from one client’s information in a way that makes it available in another client’s matter, lawyers must turn to the New York Rules of Professional Conduct.

The report cautioned against building tools that deliver automated legal services in ways that could amount to unauthorized practice or using AI to pass as a human with prospective clients.

Supervising lawyers were reminded that they remain responsible for their subordinates’ compliance and should not assume that a law firm-approved tool or policy removes the need to review work on each matter.

According to Law360, the state bar association’s governing body adopted the report Saturday.

The fate of billable hours is in the hands of artificial intelligence

#7658. Oregon wildfire victims defend jury instruction in billion-dollar PacifiCorp suit

The fires over Labor Day weekend in 2020 displaced thousands of Oregon residents.

PORTLAND, Ore. (CN) â Victims of the destructive series of wildfires that ravaged Oregon over Labor Day weekend in 2020 implored the state Supreme Court on Tuesday to revive a jury verdict in their favor.

In one of the state’s largest disasters, fires blazed across Oregon during a historic windstorm in September 2020. PacifiCorp and Pacific Power had left their power lines energized, and those energy lines ignited the flames.

Thousands of survivors of four fires â the 242 Fire, the Echo Mountain Complex Fire, the South Obenchain Fire, and the Santiam Canyon Fire â sued the power companies, accusing them of failing to reasonably maintain the power lines, clear vegetation surrounding the lines and protect against fire. They also claimed the companies negligently failed to shut down power to the lines despite warnings.

The trial court certified a class of fire survivors harmed by the four fires and structured the trial so the jury would determine liability and causation for each fire. After an eight-week trial, the jury found PacifiCorp caused the fires and harmed class members. Nineteen damages-only trials then produced verdicts and judgments exceeding $1 billion.

However, PacifiCorp appealed, challenging an instruction that told the jury the class representatives brought evidence on behalf of absent class members and jurors could âassume that the evidence at trial applies to all class members.â

The Oregon Court of Appeals sided with PacifiCorp, holding that common evidence didnât prove causation and the jury may have assumed evidence of liability for one fire meant liability for the others.

Before the Supreme Court Tuesday, the fire survivors â a class of over 2,400 individuals â argued the appeals court made a mistake.

âAt the end of the day, what they really don’t like is the jury verdict in this case,â said Nicholas Rosinia, attorney representing the class of wildfire survivors said, referring to the power companies. âThey bet the company on a class action wildfire trial, and they lost.â

âHere, the jury decided the case on a fire area by fire area basis," Rosinia continued. “That’s not to say the evidence was not common across the class as a whole, but it permitted, in this case, PacifiCorp to make fire-specific defenses to the extent it had fire-specific defenses.”

The fire survivors argue the jury simply needed to determine that PacifiCorpâs fires were a substantial factor in the resulting harm.

âThe PacifiCorp’s conflagration of fires was the common evidence that proved the ultimate harm, and that’s why all of the class members relied on that same body of evidence with respect to the conflagration to prove their case,â Rosinia said.

The wildfire survivors said there was no dispute that there was harm across the class area.

âThe only dispute was whether PacifiCorp’s conflagration of fires was a substantial factor, and the evidence that everybody relied on was common as to that question,â Rosinia said.

PacifiCorp disagreed, arguing the class action was unprecedented, that the class should not have been certified, and that the instruction invited the jury to assume the evidence presented at trial applied to every single class member.

âFor the jury, class actions are hard enough, but they’re told this is one big class. This wasn’t subclasses by fire areas â one big class, 17 class representatives, they widely differ among them, and the jury is told, âYou can consider all of the evidence as applying to all the class members,â" said Theodore Boutrous, attorney for PacifiCorp. âI’ve never seen anything like it.â

Oregon Supreme Court Justice Christopher Garrett questioned PacifiCorpâs theory.

âIt appears just from reading the briefs and the verdict form that the case was pretty clearly tried on a fire-by-fire basis and the verdict form reflects that,â Garrett remarked. âSo how real is the worry that the jury would have transposed causation from fire number one to fire number three?â

PacifiCorp argued the worry is quite real, given the sheer size of the class and varying circumstances.

âDo we really think the jury would think that a fire burning a hundred miles away proved a different fire?â questioned Oregon Supreme Court Justice Meagan Flynn.

PacifiCorp contended that yes, the jury very well could have thought so. It also argued the trial court should not have certified such a large class.

âThere hasn’t been a class action certified anywhere in the country with one wildfire. Here, we’ve got four fire areas, and there were dozens of fires within those fires,â Boutrous said. âIt was just a fundamental error to certify one big class with 17 representatives who themselves couldn’t have been in a class just alone because they were in completely different places.â

The Oregon Supreme Court did not indicate when it would rule.

#7657. The border wall dispute isn’t fit for the emergency docket

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

In its latest request to the Supreme Court over President Donald Trump’s approach to immigration, the Justice Department turned to the court’s emergency docket to ask for fast-track permission to construct a border barrier system along a 517-mile stretch in remote west Texas. Stymied by a federal district court’s preliminary injunction issued in October, the Justice Department argues that Supreme Court intervention is needed to prevent irreparable harm to the country. But details of the government’s legal argument reveal that the Trump administration hopes to use the emergency docket as a fast track to victory regardless of the actual urgency of the legal dispute.

Early this year, the Department of Homeland Security began taking important preliminary steps to build physical barriers through Big Bend National Park, Big Bend Ranch State Park, and nearby property along the U.S.-Mexico border. Part of the Border Patrol’s Big Bend Sector, covering approximately one-quarter of the entire border, no artificial barriers exist there. Despite its massive geographic reach, the region is sparsely populated and at immense distance from large urban centers. Unlike other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, few people or goods cross from one country to the other in the Big Bend Sector. Indeed, according to U.S. District Judge Kathleen Cardone, who issued a preliminary injunction blocking DHS from carrying out its plans to erect a border barrier in the area, this is the border region with “the lowest aggregate number of apprehensions [of migrants] and the lowest number of apprehensions per mile of border.”

In Mullin v. Friends of the Ruidosa Church, a group of individuals with personal or business ties to the region, along with two advocacy groups, argued that DHS had failed to comply with required environmental reviews. Pointing to a 1996 law signed by President Bill Clinton, the Justice Department responded that Secretary of Homeland Security Markwayne Mullin and his predecessor, Kristi Noem, waived application of those environmental laws. The government also argued that the district court lacked the power to decide the lawsuit in the first place.

Cardone disagreed with the government on both counts. Congress narrowed courts’ jurisdiction in border-barrier disputes, but left room for courts to consider constitutional challenges to DHS’s conduct, she concluded. The challenge to Mullin’s waiver of environmental laws raises a constitutional question, Cardone added.

Having concluded that she could consider the challengers’ lawsuit, Cardone then turned to the criteria that Congress imposed on the secretary of Homeland Security to waive environmental review. The 1996 law directs the immigration agency “to waive all legal requirements” that could slow or impede construction of border barriers and roads. But the same law also instructs DHS to build barriers and roads “in areas of high illegal entry into the United States.” Considering the government’s data about apprehensions of people and seizures of drugs in the Big Bend Sector, as compared to other parts of the U.S.-Mexico border, Cardone concluded that the region cannot be considered to have high levels of illegal entry. “[I]f the Big Bend Sector is an area of high illegal entry, so is every other sector,” Cardone announced.

Seven days after Cardone released her opinion, the U.S. solicitor general asked the Supreme Court to intervene. Much of the government’s argument turns on its disagreement with Cardone about what constitutes an area of “high illegal entry.” Mullin determined that the Big Bend Sector constitutes an area of high illegal entry because Customs and Border Protection, the DHS agency that enforces immigration laws at and near the border, apprehended 89,000 people and “seized enormous amounts” of illicit drugs from fiscal years 2021 to 2025, the government explains. In addition, failure to build a border barrier in this region “would act as a dangerous magnet” for additional illegal entries, the solicitor general claims. Despite Mullin’s assessment that the facts on the ground met the “high illegal entry” threshold required by Congress, “the district court nonetheless issued an unprecedented injunction blocking those waivers and halting associated border-wall construction,” the solicitor general wrote to the court.

Unsurprisingly, the challengers disagree. Opposing the government’s request for relief from the justices, they describe Mullin and Noem’s waivers as “unprecedented” and claim they “carry undisputed and extraordinary political and economic significance.”

The solicitor general’s claim is fundamentally a dispute about the proper interpretation of the text of the 1996 law. The government argues that courts cannot second-guess Mullin’s decision to waive environmental laws, and that Mullin’s view of what constitutes “high illegal entry” is all that matters. Cardone disagrees and contends that courts have a role to play here.

By turning to the emergency docket, the Justice Department has dispensed with the ordinary appellate process in favor of a fast-track path to, it hopes, final victory. Wanting an answer sooner rather than later is understandable, but a party’s interest in “line-jumping,” as Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson has described the emergency docket, isn’t reason enough to circumvent the slower course of the ordinary appellate process. Jackson would prefer to limit the emergency docket to situations in which an actual emergency exists. It’s hard to see what exigency exists in west Texas, however. The solicitor general argues that drugs and people will continue to enter through the Big Bend Sector. That is undoubtedly true, but, as that stretch of land has been unfortified since it became a border on March 18, 1848, nothing is likely to occur in the near future that is markedly different from past decades.

The government’s request for fast-track intervention by the Supreme Court also does not meet the standards set by Jackson’s ideological opposites. Explaining his view of the court’s emergency docket in Trump v. CASA, the court’s fast-track decision announcing that district courts are not authorized to issue universal injunctions, Justice Brett Kavanaugh wrote that its alternative pathway is appropriate when “Congress passes a major new statute, or the Executive Branch issues a major new rule or executive order.” Neither applies to the border-wall dispute. Congress enacted the contested statute 30 years ago and the waivers issued by Mullin and Noem are neither an agency rule nor an executive order.

Nor is the border-wall legal battle the type of dispute that only the Supreme Court can resolve. In a 2021 speech, Justice Samuel Alito compared the court’s emergency docket to a hospital’s emergency room, suggesting that, in his view at least, the fast-track process is proper only when no suitable alternative exists. But an alternative does exist to decide if Cardone overstepped. The government could have appealed Cardone’s decision to the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 5th Circuit. Like other circuit courts, the 5th Circuit regularly reviews preliminary injunctions granted by district courts. As Kavanaugh explained in CASA, “The courts of appeals and this Court can (and regularly do) expeditiously review district court decisions awarding or denying preliminary injunctive relief.” Instead of asking the 5th Circuit to correct the mistake it claims Cardone committed, the solicitor general skipped the 5th Circuit and went directly to the Supreme Court.

The reason it did this is not difficult to figure out: The administration is hopeful that it will receive a friendly audience at the Supreme Court. But this is a fast-track procedure meant for exceptional circumstances. And there is nothing exceptional about the legal fight over the administration’s attempt to build new segments of border barrier in rural west Texas. If the court grants the government’s request to pause Cardone’s preliminary injunction, allowing construction to move forward where no barrier currently exists, it should, at the very least, explain how this case meets the criteria that the justices have previously provided and if the term “emergency docket” is a misnomer.

César Cuauhtémoc García Hernández is the author of three books about immigration law and policy.

Those claims were investigated by the FBI. Paxton called the investigation a “bogus witch hunt.” The Justice Department ultimately declined to prosecute. The Republican promised to advance President Donald Trumpâs agenda if elected, including “cutting taxes, securing the border and deporting illegal aliens, ending the weaponization of government, and draining the Swamp."

âI will commit that I will be praying for him, that he will do good for Texas and this nation,â Paxton said in his concession speech.

Republican Governor Greg Abbott also conceded Tuesday. He had about 46% of the vote as of 1 a.m. Central time, while Hinojosa had about 53% of the vote.

Abbott was elected governor of Texas in 2014 and has held the office since 2015. He spent at least $281 million to defend his office during this campaign, while Hinojosa had a campaign spend in the neighborhood of $37 million, according to reporting from The Texas Tribune.

This election cycle, Abbott focused on, among other issues, lowering property taxes for homeowners. He promised to give voters the opportunity to abolish school district property taxes on homeowners’ residences, which go to help fund schools, so that aim might be achieved.

In her victory speech in Austin Tuesday evening, Hinojosa described how she became motivated to enter politics because of her children. When her sonâs elementary school almost closed due to state budget cuts, she ran for Austinâs school board and became its president in 2015. With an aim to help other schools in the state, she ran for the Texas House, which sheâs served in since 2017.

âIt never bothered me that they doubted me. It bothered me that they doubted us. Hundreds of millions on attack ads,â Hinojosa said during her victory speech. âBut Texas, my faith in you never wavered.â

#7655. Fox Doesn’t Want To Talk About Roku, But It’s Got Lots To Say About Tubi And Politics

Any investor hoping to ask about Fox’s pending Roku acquisition during its fiscal Q1 2027 earnings call on Monday was out of luck.

Fox’s IR rep made that clear up front and pointed analysts to Fox’s SEC filings instead.

However, CEO Lachlan Murdoch did share a mini update, including that shareholder and foreign regulatory approvals are in, although Fox is still working with the DOJ on antitrust clearance.

“[We] expect to close the transaction as soon as we can,” Murdoch told investors, noting that Fox’s “conviction in the opportunity has only grown.” Pairing Roku’s platform with Fox’s sports, news and entertainment content is a good recipe for building “our position in the fastest-growing segments of the media landscape,” he said.

Fox’s revenue rose 22% to $4.6 billion in the quarter, including a 47% jump in advertising revenue (60% in its TV segment) driven by the World Cup, early midterm spending and Tubi, its free ad-supported streaming service.

Tubi grew revenue 35% year over year, alongside a 23% uptick in total view time.

Fox attributed that engagement to a combo of Tubi’s content library, 10 new originals and a World Cup hub, which drew on Fox’s US English-language rights to the tournament.

Tubi also got a boost from viral content from more than 600 creators. Its Tubi for Creators program launched in 2025 with six creators and has since wooed big YouTube names like MrBeast and Jomboy Media.

And profits are growing, too, despite higher content costs, according to CFO Steve Tomsic, who noted that Tubi is contributing more to the bottom line than it was in the year-ago quarter when it turned its first profit – a development Murdoch himself apparently didn’t see coming.

A Bank of America analyst on the call reminded Murdoch that a year or so ago he’d said that Tubi’s growth, then in the midteens, wouldn’t be sustainable.

“I don’t remember saying that, but I’m sure I did … Thank you for calling me out on that one,” Murdoch said, adding that Tubi’s profit margins should settle in the 20% range once it reaches “further maturity.”

Advertising is the main engine behind Tubi’s momentum, which Murdoch said is continuing into the current quarter. Tubi’s audience is young, diverse and mostly cord-free, he said, which is like catnip for advertisers.

“They’re a very hard market for advertisers to reach,” he said, which, in a midterm year, is a pretty good pitch to political campaigns.

Fox booked more than $350 million in political ads this cycle, and Tubi was responsible for roughly $50 million of that.

Most of the rest – $250 million-plus – went to Fox’s local stations, including many in battleground states, where demand is so high that some stations run out of ad inventory. The remaining $50-ish million went to political ads across national sports, news and entertainment.

But if you squint, and not that hard, Tubi also kind of counts as local advertising in Murdoch’s view. “It’s effectively local revenue because it’s targeted,” he said.

Politics aside, sports has been a tailwind, too.

The FIFA World Cup final was the most-watched soccer telecast in US history; the World Series, which aired on Fox, averaged 12 million viewers; and Fox’s NFL “America’s Game of the Week” is drawing an average of nearly 25 million viewers per game.

But Murdoch was also careful to temper expectations for Fox One, Fox’s streaming service for Fox content.

It’s not like there’s a World Cup every year – or a midterm election.

“It’s always a point in time,” Murdoch said. “Every couple years, you’ve got to be careful to understand the strength of the political cycle.”

And not everything at Fox was a win this past quarter, no matter how you spin it.

Fox News finished its fiscal Q1 as the most-watched cable news network, with 2.1 million primetime viewers and 1.3 million across all dayparts. But those figures were down 17% and 16% year over year, according to Nielsen, and Fox News was the only major cable news network to see declines. The slide has continued into October, when total-day ratings fell 27% ahead of the midterms.

Murdoch blamed tough comps against last year’s “tremendous news cycle,” which included the inauguration, Charlie Kirk’s assassination and DOGE-related drama. He compared this cycle to the 2006 midterms, when a second-term president was halfway through his term.

It’s not that viewers are defecting to CNN or MS Now, he said. They’re “just fatigued and watching slightly less television overall.” (Even so, Nielsen does show CNN and MS Now both up from last year.)

Meanwhile, cable advertising rose 8%, helped along by sports, but digital news ad revenue fell. Asked about that – we mourn you preemptively, open web – Murdoch pointed to Fox News Digital’s standing as the top news site in the US and called digital news a “hyper-competitive market.”

Disaffection and outright anger toward US sports institutions run deeper than logo-cluttered fields. Leagues and teams are sacrificing player safety and fan enjoyment for marketing dollars.

People Inc.’s referral traffic from Google search is down 70% over the past two years, and by 26% in Q3 alone. But its digital revenue is still growing, albeit slowly.

On Tuesday, Chord, a six-year-old commerce tech startup, acquired Zenlytic, an AI startup with an anthropomorphized data analyst agent named “Zoë,” for $5 million.

If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.”

It’s fall, and M&A is in the air. Two acquisitions happened this week: Stagwell bought Freestar, and DoorDash bought Instacart.

Starting in Q4, Reddit will test logged-in-only mode to protect its user engagement, improve ad targeting and keep AI from scraping its content.

#7654. Alaska judge finds Bonanza Channel gold mining proposal unlawful

Tribal villages successfully questioned official approval of corporate plans to dredge for gold in Safety Sound and the Bonanza Channel.

ANCHORAGE, Alaska (CN) â An estuary abundant with wildlife in northwestern Alaska will likely be spared from an industrial suction dredging operation, though a federal judge Tuesday refrained from making the final call for now.

U.S. District Judge Sharon L. Gleason, a Barack Obama appointee, ruled the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers unlawfully approved a Nevada companyâs gold mining project plan in Safety Sound and its Bonanza Channel, located east of Nome.

The five Alaska Native tribal groups who sued the Corps, including the Village of Solomon and the King Island Native Community, had asked Gleason to vacate the Corpsâ 2024 approval. Instead, the judge asked them and the agency to provide additional briefing within three weeks on what a court-imposed remedy should look like.

The Bonanza Channel is renowned for birdwatching, having received formal recognition as an area of importance by Audubon and the American Bird Conservatory. Itâs also home to fish and marine mammal species, all contributing to an ecosystem that has supported Alaska Native subsistence living for countless generations.

Plans by Las Vegas-registered IPOP LLC to mine the estuary date back to 2018, when the corporation said it would bundle a reality television show, âRivers of Gold,â with the mineral operation.

IPOP and its president, Beau Epstein, have since claimed to have dropped that concept, but the mining plan, which entails vacuuming the estuary bed, removing more than 4 million cubic yards of material over five years and significantly altering sections of terrain and vegetation, has hit legal roadblocks at multiple points. In 2022, the Corpsâ Alaska District rejected IPOPâs Clean Water Act permit request for the proposal after concluding that Safety Sound waters would face significant degradation threats.

In 2023, however, Corps official and current Army Major General Kirk Gibbs vacated that permit denial after IPOP appealed, accusing the Alaska District of being biased towards Alaska Native interests. The permit review was then assigned to the Honolulu-based Pacific Ocean Division â a larger agency that oversees the Alaska District plus work in Hawaii and East Asia â which approved the plan under Gibbsâ leadership as division commander.

The Pacific Ocean Division opted not to make an Environmental Impact Statement for the proposal, as the Corps often does for large-scale resource development projects, writing instead that the IPOP projectâs impacts âare expected to be not significant and adverse.â

In her ruling, Gleason repeatedly drew from the Alaska Districtâs nearly 120-page explanation for denying the permit in 2022, rebuffing the Pacific Ocean Divisionâs approval as inconsistent with environmental law.

âThe Division did not explain why it disagreed with the Districtâs conclusion that impacts to birds and other wildlife would be major or why, in its view, the project constituted only a small part of the estuary system such that any impact would be minor and temporary,â Gleason wrote, finding the Corps’ approval in violation of the Clean Water Act and Administrative Procedure Act.

After submitting supplemental briefs to Gleason by Nov. 24, the Alaska Native plaintiffs and Corps will be given another two weeks to respond to each other.

âItâs frustrating that our communities have to continually defend our lands, our waters, and our way of life against decisions that fail to recognize just how much is at stake for our people,â said Deilah Johnson, tribal resources director for the Village of Solomon. âThese arenât just environmental concerns to us. This is our food security, our traditions, and the future of our children. We shouldnât have to fight this hard to be heard, and we certainly shouldnât have to wait until the damage is done for our concerns to matter. This ruling is an important victory, but our work isnât finished. We will continue to stand together and fight for the protection our communities deserve.â

IPOP LLC did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

#7653. Affle Acquires Perion For $420 Million, Because ‘Synergies’

If you ask the executive leadership of Affle and Perion why the two companies are merging, the answer you’ll get is “synergies.”

Tal Jacobson, Perion’s CEO, is well aware that the term has become a total cliche. “Every time I write an email and use ‘synergy,’ Google pops up and says people don’t like that word,” he joked on Monday, the day after Affle agreed to acquire Perion for $420 million in cash.

But even so, it’s the best shorthand for what each company is missing that the other can supply, he told AdExchanger.

Affle is an India-based holding company for mobile ad tech built around performance marketing, largely in emerging markets, while Perion focuses on CTV, digital out-of-home and retail media. Most of its clients are big brands and agencies in developed markets, mainly in North America.

For the past few years, Perion has been evangelizing the concept of outcome-based advertising with its clients. But there was a hole in its offering. “We never had good performance-driven technology for mobile,” Jacobson said. “Affle has pure technology just for that.”

For its part, Affle gets a foothold with the agencies, holding companies and brands that Perion already works with, said Sameer Sondhi, Affle’s CEO of North America and chief strategic investments officer.

Perion, which has roughly 500 employees, will operate as a wholly owned subsidiary under Affle and brings the combined company’s headcount to just over 1,000 people. Jacobson, who will stay on as CEO, said that everyone from Perion is staying aboard.

LUMA Partners advised Affle on the deal, which is expected to close in early 2027.

AdExchanger spoke with Jacobson and Sondhi about how the pieces fit, what happens now to Perion’s own string of recent acquisitions and why Jacobson would rather call this a merger than a sale.

AdExchanger: Why sell to Affle and why now?

TAL JACOBSON: We don’t think about selling. We think about merging – taking two successful companies and making them a bigger engine of growth. “Selling” has a negative connotation, like somebody gave up, and that’s not the case.

Neither of us has the growth potential separately that we have together. We’ve spent a few good months working side by side, and the teams are working very well together.

Why is $420 million the right price? Perion paid $100 million alone to acquire Hivestack in 2023, $65 million for Greenbids last year and $12 million for PRN, which does in-store retail media, just a few months ago.

TJ: It’s a tricky question. For a public company, the right price is what investors will pay, and I don’t believe Perion was valued correctly in recent years. So, if the public market doesn’t see our long-term potential, why not join forces with someone who does?

The price doesn’t reflect the full long-term value; it reflects a point in time, and Affle wouldn’t buy this if it didn’t think the potential was bigger than the price.

SS: Both of us are listed, so the number is always going to be debated. There are plenty of public reference points – DoubleVerify, Nielsen, LiveRamp, IAS – and the boards have to approve. In the end, a number is a mindset thing.

Affle has been pushing a cost-per-converted-user (CPCU) model, where advertisers only pay for conversions. Will Perion’s DOOH, CTV and retail media inventory be sold that way?

TJ: Not necessarily. It depends on the channel and the customer’s goal. You can’t sell out-of-home on a CPC model, because you can’t click on an ad. But you can say, “Pay us for performance.”

Some formats might be CPC, others CPA or CPL. Whatever helps an advertiser’s business, that’s what we want to focus on.

So not CPCU, exactly, but a CPCU mindset?

TJ: We’re outcome-driven. The KPI is whatever defines success for that advertiser.

SS: With the targeting you can do on DOOH screens and the signals we get from mobile, the goal is to help clients with whatever way they’re used to buying. We don’t want to confuse them. We want to educate them.

Perion’s open web spend fell by around 23% in Q2. Doesn’t seem like a good sign for the future of the open web.

TJ: We’ve been telling investors and clients that the open web is not the future. Forget channels; focus on outcomes. When a CFO approves a budget, they don’t care if it’s websites or out-of-home.

And yes, everybody’s hyped about CTV, but if it doesn’t help the business, it doesn’t matter.

How much of this deal is about agentic AI?

TJ: Both companies have invested a lot in AI over the past two years. Our Outmax agent trades media, mostly in walled gardens, and Affle’s AI is focused on the deeper funnel and conversions. I don’t think we’ll merge the algorithms into one, but it helps to have all those tools under one roof.

SS: The systems don’t need to unify; they just need to talk to each other better.

Perion has made several acquisitions of its own and now it’s being acquired itself. How do all the nesting dolls fit together?

TJ: Affle lets every company it acquires stay independent under its own name and with its own road map and team. We’re not combining everything. Greenbids, for example, gives us the walled gardens – YouTube, Meta, TikTok – which neither Perion nor Affle had. PRN is just another extension of out-of-home, but inside retail stores.

The point is to sit in front of a CMO and be able to say, “Whatever you need, we probably have it.” We’ve worked hard over the past three years to roll up other companies, and this is just another phase of that.

This industry does not need 150 ad tech companies. It needs to consolidate.

This interview has been lightly edited and condensed.

#7652. Will an ability to hold federal officers accountable survive this term?

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

At a time when there is a desire to hold ICE agents accountable for their constitutional violations, the Supreme Court might be poised to eliminate the only way to hold them civilly liable under federal law.

By way of background, if state or local officers violate the Constitution, they can be sued under a federal statute, 42 U.S.C. Section 1983. But no federal law authorizes suits against federal officers for constitutional violations. Rather, the ability to sue a federal government officer for money damages comes from a 1971 Supreme Court decision, Bivens v. Six Unknown Named Agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. There, the court said that it would allow a cause of action for money damages under the Fourth Amendment even without a federal statute authorizing it.

Nevertheless, for decades, the Supreme Court has refused to extend or even apply Bivens to other violations of constitutional rights by federal officers, and several conservative justices have called for it to be overruled. Now, in Nielsen v. Watanabe, to be argued on Nov. 9, the court will again confront whether to allow a Bivens suit – and perhaps whether to end such claims entirely.

The underlying issue is about separation of powers: should the court provide a remedy for constitutional violations or is that entirely the province of Congress? But it also is about accountability: without Bivens, how can those who violate constitutional rights, including ICE agents, be held responsible and how can those injured be compensated?

Webster Bivens alleged that he had been subjected to an illegal and humiliating search by agents of the Federal Bureau of Narcotics. Bivens sought money damages as compensation for the harms he suffered. The court held that a federal law cause of action for money damages could be inferred directly from the Fourth Amendment. The majority, in an opinion by Justice William Brennan, emphasized that individuals whose rights have been violated should not be relegated to state law remedies, which might be inadequate or hostile to the federal constitutional interest.

In an important and often-cited concurring opinion, Justice John Marshall Harlan explained that the federal courts long have devised remedies for violations of federal law. Harlan said that it is essential that federal courts be able to provide such relief because “it is apparent that some form of damages is the only possible remedy for someone in Bivens’ alleged position. … For people in Bivens’ shoes, it is damages or nothing.” Harlan rejected the claim that the court violates separation of powers when it creates such a cause of action and remedy. In his view, the court is responsible for upholding and enforcing the Bill of Rights, and, hence, the judiciary need not wait for the legislature in order to act.

Chief Justice Warren Burger and Justices Hugo Black and Harry Blackmun dissented. Each wrote an opinion arguing that separation of powers means that Congress, and not the court, should create a cause of action for damages against federal officers. Black explained that “[s]hould the time come when Congress desires such lawsuits, it has before it a model of valid legislation, 42 U.S.C. §1983, to create a damage remedy against federal officers.” Similarly, Blackmun argued that “it is the Congress, and not this Court, that should act.”

For a decade after Bivens, the court applied and extended it. In 1979’s Davis v. Passman, the court allowed a Bivens suit under the due process clause of the Fifth Amendment for an equal protection claim. Congressman Otto Passman fired his administrative assistant, Shirley Davis, because he wanted a male to fill the position. In allowing the suit against the congressman, the court emphasized the judiciary's role in ensuring effective protection of constitutional rights.

And only a year later, in Carlson v. Green, the court allowed a Bivens suit for violation of the Eighth Amendment. A mother sued federal prison officials on behalf of her deceased son, claiming that he was the victim of gross inadequacies of medical facilities and staff, which caused his death and constituted cruel and unusual punishment. A remedy was available under the Federal Tort Claims Act; thus, the issue before the court was whether a Bivens suit should be allowed in light of this alternative. The court concluded that Bivens suits were a “counterpart” to the Federal Tort Claims Act because the act creates liability for the federal government and a Bivens cause of action permits recovery from federal officers themselves. The court found no indication that Congress intended for the act to preclude Bivens suits.

Since 1980, however, the court has not ruled in favor of a Bivens claim. In its most recent decision about Bivens, 2022’s Egbert v. Boule, the court noted that it had “declined 11 times to imply a similar cause of action for other alleged constitutional violations” and that “in all but the most unusual circumstances, prescribing a cause of action is a job for Congress, not the courts.”

Specifically, the court has held that that such claims are not allowed if there is a statute that precludes suits (in 2010’s Hui v. Castaneda), or that provides an alternative remedy even if it is inadequate (in 1988’s Schweiker v. Chilicky). It has precluded Bivens claims for those injured while in the military, even for egregious violations of their rights (in 1987’s United States v. Stanley). It has ruled that Bivens suits should be allowed only if they are on balance desirable and consistently has found that they are not (in 2007’s Wilkie v. Robbins, 2017’s Ziglar v. Abbasi, 2020’s Hernandez v. Mesa, and Boule). And it has precluded Bivens suits against private prisons that contract with the federal government (in 2001’s Correctional Services Corp. v. Malesko) and the guards employed by them (in 2012’s Minecci v. Pollard).

Based on this line of cases, the court in Egbert v. Boule stressed that recognizing a Bivens cause of action “is ‘a disfavored judicial activity.’” The court stated that

The court then laid out the framework for Bivens claims going forward. According to the majority, this should be guided by a two-step inquiry:

This is a test that puts a very strong presumption against recognizing Bivens claims.

Like Carlson v. Green, Nielsen v. Watanabe involves an Eighth Amendment claim for cruel and unusual punishment.The case involves a prisoner, Kekai Watanabe, who alleges that he suffered a broken tailbone when attacked by other prisoners that caused him excruciating pain and that a staff nurse, Francis Nielsen, denied him medical care. The court granted review as to whether the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit “erred [here] in recognizing a Bivens cause of action.”

Watanabe argues to the court that this case is governed by Carlson v. Green and does not seek to extend Bivens in any way. His brief states: “Watanabe asserts the same kind of violation of the same constitutional right by the same type of defendant in the same institutional setting pursuant to the same substantive standards as the plaintiff in Carlson. This is precisely the kind of claim this Court has long understood Carlson to encompass.”

In response, Nielsen argues that Bivens suits are strongly disfavored and that there are “significant factual differences such as the immediacy and severity of the harm alleged” compared with Carlson. But that is not all: Nielsen also expressly argues that “Bivens should be overruled” and that “Congress, not the judiciary, creates causes of action.”

The court could affirm the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 9th Circuit and allow a Bivens suit, saying that this is governed by Carlson. Or the court could distinguish Carlson, accepting Nielsen’s argument that there are sufficient factual differences between the cases, essentially limiting Bivens claims only for cruel and unusual punishment claims involving deaths. Or the court could overrule Carlson but not overrule Bivens.

Or the court could overrule Bivens entirely, which several conservative justices have advocated in the past.

The fundamental disagreement, as it was in Bivens, is whether it is the judicial role to provide remedies for violations of constitutional rights or whether that is just for Congress. The practical reality is that without Bivens suits, those whose rights have been violated – even horribly – are left with no recourse. In Hernandez v. Mesa, for example, a boy in Mexico was killed by shot fired across the border by a federal agent in Texas. The court’s rejection of a Bivens suit left no remedy at all.

In that case, and in many other situations, the Federal Tort Claims Act does not allow suits against the United States. Often there are not state tort remedies available either. To paraphrase Justice Harlan, for people in the shoes of many injured by federal officers, it is Bivens suits or nothing.

I would like to think that the reports of egregious constitutional violations by ICE agents, including killings, would cause the court to realize the importance of Bivens suits and to not end such causes of action. That is what makes Nielsen v. Watanabe so important.

Erwin Chemerinsky is the Dean and Jesse H. Choper Distinguished Professor of Law, University of California, Berkeley School of Law.
