#7651. OpenAI May Not Be So Open For Long; Prediction Markets Bet On Endorsements

OpenAI has been following the classic walled garden platform playbook for its ChatGPT advertising business. But people often forget that the first few pages are about opening up ad inventory to third-party intermediaries – before the walls go back up, of course.

YouTube allowed third-party ad serving … for a time. Facebook bought and then quickly shuttered the Atlas ad server. Amazon Prime once had a DSP partner program with full third-party programmatic visibility – but then dataxu, one of its partners, was acquired by Roku (so, buh-bye). The Trade Desk, the only other vendor in that program, was quietly cut off a few months later.

OpenAI may now be at that same early point in the cycle. The Information reports that Magnite and PubMatic have signed deals to “fill unused ad space” for ChatGPT. And they’re just the latest additions to OpenAI’s growing roster of ad-tech partners, which already includes LiveRamp, Criteo, StackAdapt and even Amazon Ads.

But this partner push has a pointed subplot: OpenAI’s VP of partnerships, Samantha Jacobson, was until recently The Trade Desk’s chief strategy officer. Jacobson announced her departure in May amid TTD’s painful exodus of senior executives. Now she’s helping build partnerships at one of the most coveted new media platforms in the world.

At TTD, the reaction may very well have been: “Don’t be a stranger. Seriously.”

Prediction markets Kalshi, Polymarket and Novig want to be household names. So they’re trading on the reputations of their celebrity spokespeople.

The sheer number of celebrities signing on to promote these controversial companies proves that the concept of “selling out” is officially dead, writes Amanda Mull at Bloomberg.

Consider a star-studded ad campaign Polymarket launched in September, featuring sports megastars Lebron James, Derek Jeter and Eli Manning, actors John Leguizamo and Alexandra Daddario, director Spike Lee and supermodel Emily Ratajkowski, to name a few. Or Novig’s headline-grabbing campaign with actress Sydney Sweeney.

It makes sense for Polymarket and Novig to associate themselves with these names, Mull writes. A March poll by Ipsos found that just 20% of respondents were familiar with the platforms, despite extensive marketing.

But what makes less sense is why celebrities would promote these companies, Mull argues. The same Ipsos poll found that, among consumers familiar with prediction markets, 40% viewed them as bad for society, while 60% thought they were no different than gambling.

Celebrities used to avoid tying themselves to such brands. But in this era of intensely devoted fandoms, “celebrities and influencers announce new ad campaigns and brand sponsorships to excited, congratulatory fans as though they are awards,” Mull writes.

So, if every celebrity is selling out, there’s nothing to criticize, she adds. “Maybe that’s why so many people agreed to be in that Polymarket ad at the same time – safety in numbers.”

Ad buyers are scrutinizing their Google search budgets more than ever, Digiday reports. And for good reason, too. Now that AI Overviews are encouraging users to click through at lower rates, those ads aren’t performing as well as they once did despite higher CPC rates.

One marketing expert told Digiday that he’s seen some advertisers reallocating 10% to 30% of their Google search budget into other channels. Others claim that some of their clients have started moving money into Meta and ChatGPT or into other Google products, including AI Max, YouTube and Demand Gen.

That shift in advertiser spending seems to mirror similar trends happening at Google overall. Last week, Alphabet’s stock price dropped over 10% after the company’s latest earnings report revealed a slowdown in search advertising revenue growth, which SVP and Chief Business Officer Philipp Schindler attributed to lower monetization of its AI Mode.

Meanwhile, Google is sticking to its assertion that AI-powered advertising campaigns and a more “conversational” search experience will ultimately provide greater value to advertisers in the long run. Which assumes the company won’t run out of money by then – a pretty fair assumption, given that it earned $127.6 billion in Q3 this year alone.

#7649. This Ad Tech Company Wants To Ensure Brands Don’t Go Viral For The Wrong Reasons

Some marketers say, “All press is good press,” but they probably wouldn’t be thrilled if their brand was the next to go viral for a blatantly offensive ad.

Ad tech company Digital Culture Group’s goal is to stop those ads before they ever go live by preemptively determining what sort of creative and messaging will resonate with – or offend – an audience.

Its flagship product, the Audience Resonance Index (ARI), uses a range of first- and third-party data to determine what kinds of people will be most interested in a product and how to connect with them through current cultural trends.

In late September, Digital Culture Group launched a new module within ARI called Resonance Studio. The new module takes the product a step further and predicts how creative will perform – including specific critiques customers may have and how to fix them – before it goes live.

Alongside Resonance Studio, Digital Culture Group also launched the ARI 100 Ad Pledge, which offered 100 pro bono creative assessments to brands and agencies.

The launch of the module and the associated pledge came on the heels of the Converse controversy in September in which the sneaker brand received backlash for an ad featuring imagery that many viewers said clearly evoked the KKK and lynching.

Converse pulled the ad after two weeks, but the damage was done, with some longtime Converse fans throwing away – or even burning – their shoes and posting to social media.

It was “an extremely unfortunate thing for the Converse team to experience,” said Crystal Foote, CEO and founder of Digital Culture Group, but it was also horrible for “the communities that were impacted by that.”

Foote uploaded the ad to both ChatGPT and to ARI, asking each one to rate the ad and provide feedback. ChatGPT gave the ad a B minus and said that it “would not classify this creative as culturally insensitive or recommend suppressing it on cultural grounds alone.” Rather, its only critique was that the depiction of the sneakers “could be interpreted as gender non-conforming styling” (the horror), which could offend some viewers.

ARI, on the other hand, gave the ad an F, citing “hate symbols,” including robes and hoods that could evoke KKK imagery. It also noted that “the dangling shoes could be read as echoes of hanging or lynching imagery” and could offend Black Americans and descendants of lynching victims, said Foote, quoting the model outputs directly.

In terms of how to fix it, ARI suggested what seemed obvious to many: Avoid white robes, cone-shaped hoods and dangling feet. Instead, position the product in a shoebox or on a shelf.

ARI is trained on data from sources ranging from the American Community Survey (an annual demographic survey) to eMarketer’s predictive analytics to research from Nielsen’s cultural team, said Foote. The model is trained to recognize historically offensive or non-resonant imagery before a current customer ever lays eyes on it.

It also has a social listening feature, so it can tap into conversations happening on social platforms, including Reddit, X and Meta.

Since the Converse ad was already live, ARI was likely influenced by real people’s reactions to it. But ARI and Resonance Studio would ideally be able to predict – and prevent – an outcome like the one Converse faced even before the ad went public, due to its ability to denote the offensive imagery.

The predictive analysis was a big draw for humanitarian organization CARE, which began working with Digital Culture Group in September and participated in the ARI 100 Ad Pledge.

CARE submitted two pieces of creative to ARI for analysis: one in support of its National Women’s Day campaign and one encouraging people to contribute financially to the company’s care packages.

For the National Women’s Day campaign, CARE submitted an ad it had used in the past that emphasized the importance of providing opportunities for women globally and in various professions. Its focus was “leveling the playing field” for all women, “from the sports field to the farm field to the conference room,” said Mary Kate Wilson, CARE’s associate VP for creative and content marketing.

The ad’s call to action asked viewers to sign a pledge that would “level the playing field for women and girls everywhere,” said Wilson – but ARI determined that CARE’s audience needed more.

The ad needed to be more specific about where, exactly, the signatures were going, like whether they would be added to a petition or sent to a legislator. People want to know, “What difference do I make by lending my signature to this?” Wilson said.

The second ad focused on the history of the care package, which was created toward the end of World War II by an American cooperative (which later became CARE) that sent food packages to families in Europe.

ARI gave the ad a high score on cultural relevance and receptivity, since it emphasized multiculturalism and different types of care packages, depending on a community’s needs. But where it had room for improvement was making it “more time-bound to today,” Wilson said.

Again, people wanted to know where their dollars were going, what the resulting care package would look like and who it would serve.

Sensitive industries – particularly those that cater to people’s health – require more than just accurate targeting, said Joy Allen-Altimare, president of women’s health and sexual wellness brand Vella Bioscience.

For Vella (another brand participating in ARI’s pledge), “cultural understanding” is a key marketing focus, including who is represented in the ads and challenging outdated stereotypes and stigma around discussing topics like menopause.

One of the ads it submitted for review was for its Meltwater product, a vaginal moisturizer made with hyaluronic acid and aloe vera.

The ad was “really trying to be an ingredient story” and emphasize the ways that moisturization and restoration can apply to intimate areas, said Allen-Altimare. In many ways, Resonance Studio determined that the ad was effective. The predicted click-through-rate was 106% of Vella’s benchmark goal, and the psychographic alignment (or, how well the ad would resonate with its intended audience) was estimated to be around 85%.

However, Resonance Studio determined that there was room for improvement around model inclusivity, regarding age and race. Since the messaging was focused on ingredients, only one shot in the ad included a model. ARI suggested incorporating multiple images, or a video where several women interacted with each other, to diversify the ad and connect with a wider range of women.

When developing a “product storytelling moment,” Vella wants to ensure it’s representing consumers of various ages, sizes and races, said Allen-Altimare. Plus, she said, there’s an added barrier of having to use ambiguous wording around pleasure and intimacy, since most ad platforms are strict about the way they can portray sexual wellness products – particularly ones that target women.

ARI’s Resonance Studio “will help us understand if we’re talking to ourselves,” Allen-Altimare said, or if the ad is truly making sense and resonating with the women it’s trying to reach.

#7648. Chord Buys Its Rival Zenlytic To Build An Agentic Version Of A CDP

Two data infrastructure startups with agentic commerce ambitions are combining forces.

On Tuesday, Chord, a 6-year-old commerce tech startup, acquired Zenlytic, an AI startup with an anthropomorphized data analyst agent named “Zoë,” for $5 million.

Chord’s co-founder and CEO, Bryan Mahoney, told AdExchanger that the combined business has around 30 full-time employees and some 60 customers, with an annual run rate nearing $10 million.

Chord launched as a “headless commerce” software company, Mahoney said.

At the time, the headless approach was catching on with Shopify merchants and social-native sellers. The idea was to decouple the front-end website from back-end fulfillment, making for a more agile business and faster-loading pages at a time when Google’s SEO prioritized speed. Shopify has since addressed the problem by taking steps to make its own storefronts faster.

Since the rise of LLMs, Chord and Zenlytic have both pivoted to become explicitly AI-based data infrastructure services. For instance, Mahoney said, Chord is now paid on a usage basis rather than traditional subscription pricing. And because pricing is usage-based, Chord closely tracks how often users prompt its AI agent for an answer – a rate that has accelerated to about once every 20 seconds, he said.

Although the more people use agents, the more ways they find to abuse them.

Mahoney pointed to a recent story in which someone figured out they could use McDonald’s online customer support and ordering agent to answer demanding math and computer science questions – a workaround to having to pay for one’s own AI tokens. (McDonald’s has since fixed this, by the way.)

Chord guards against this kind of misuse. It’s trained its AI agent with the necessary context so that off-base prompts return a response that this isn’t the right agent for the task. That includes requests to use its agent “like a therapist,” say, or for something like “make these results look better to a CFO,” Mahoney said.

Those guardrails matter more as Chord’s business shifts.

The business model is now more like an agentic version of a CDP, Mahoney said. For example, Sonos, a Chord client, can use it to track customers and enrich first-party data, such as understanding when customers are moving to a new home – an opportune time to send emails or SMS notifications about new products.

The data analyst agent “largely replaces” Chord’s own analyst agent, Mahoney said.

Guess human data analysts aren’t the only ones who need to be worried about being replaced by AI. Even agents can be put out of work.

But Chord also has other agents that work better alongside Zoë, Mahoney added. Chord has gone deeper into commerce infrastructure, for instance, with use cases geared toward Shopify-type businesses, and customers using the Snowflake data warehouse in particular. Zenlytic, by contrast, has tended to work with large enterprise brands of all kinds, not just in ecommerce, and supports many more cloud data warehouses.

The goal, Mahoney said, is for some of Zenlytic’s large customers, including Black & Decker, Verizon, J.Crew and Stanley, to adopt Chord’s data infrastructure and activation, including the ability to segment profiles or audiences for campaign targeting and measurement.

But winning over large brands requires confidence in the technology, and right now there’s an odd mix of growing trust and distrust of AI agent outputs.

Mahoney noted that the outright “hallucinations” of earlier LLMs have become relatively rare. “Now it might be more like a lucid dream,” he said. The outputs are believable and often can feel correct.

And so marketers need to be aware that a confident-sounding AI agent can still lead them badly astray. It’s a concern Mahoney shares.

“We constantly [need to] evaluate the answers that we’re getting back to make sure that the way we’re using AI is increasing confidence on a daily basis, not getting eroded,” he said. “These are some of the things that keep me up at night.”

#7646. With Search Traffic Down 70%, People Inc. Bets On Revenue Beyond Site Visits

People Inc. isn’t mincing words about the current state of digital publishing: It’s bad.

The company has seen a “critical loss of sessions,” Barry Diller, People Inc.’s chairman and senior executive, told investors during the company’s Q3 earnings call Tuesday morning.

People Inc.’s referral traffic from Google search is down 70% over the past two years, dropping 22% in Q3 after a 40%% drop in Q2.

AI Overview summaries now appear at the top of 90% of Google searches associated with People Inc.’s content, said CEO Neil Vogel.

Traffic declines aren’t just limited to Google search, though. People Inc.’s core sessions were down 26% in Q3, the biggest single-quarter decline the company has seen yet.

That traffic is gone, and it isn’t coming back, Vogel conceded to investors. The loss contributed to People Inc. laying off 195 employees, about 6% of its staff, last week.

However, People Inc. believes that it has weathered the worst of Google’s AI search overhaul and that the biggest referral traffic drops are behind it.

Vogel emphasized that, despite its traffic challenges, People Inc.’s digital revenue is still growing, albeit slowly.

Digital revenue rose 2% year over year in Q3, to $289 million, marking People Inc.’s twelfth consecutive quarter of digital growth, even as total Q3 revenue for its overall media business was down 5% to $409.9 million.

Despite revenue declines, Vogel credits People Inc.’s ongoing digital growth to the fact it was able to predict changes to the digital publishing model.

People Inc. coined the term “Google Zero” after all, he noted. Anticipating that most search traffic will disappear, People Inc. has spent the past three years transforming its business to focus more on non-session revenue and advertising products like its D/Cipher contextual targeting tech, he said.

The time is right for these investments to start paying off, and the company should see the first major returns in 2027, according to CFO Tim Quinn.

That better be the case. Diller said he would be “very disappointed” if People Inc. didn’t return to double-digit growth next year.

Looking ahead, People Inc. plans to focus on growing non-session revenue, meaning everything that isn’t tied to website visits. Non-session revenue already accounts for 43% of its digital revenue and grew 15% YOY in Q3.

By comparison, session-based revenue – which accounts for the remaining 57% – was down 6% last quarter.

People Inc.’s non-session growth priorities include live events and activations and content licensing deals with news aggregators, including Apple News and Yahoo, and AI companies, such as OpenAI, Meta and Microsoft.

Licensing revenue grew 49% in Q3, led by content deals with aggregator platforms and AI vendors. But this growth will slow a bit in Q4 as People Inc. laps the licensing deal it announced with Meta last year, Quinn said. That deal boosted last year’s Q4 numbers, which makes for a tougher comparison.

People Inc. has been exploring licensing its publishing brands for product and retail opportunities, but there’s been little sign of a return so far. For example, it’s been talking about releasing a Southern Living-branded sweet tea line for the better part of a year, but the product has yet to launch.

Also in the non-session revenue mix is D/Cipher, which People Inc. extended last year to include contextual targeting on third-party sites in addition to its own properties. D/Cipher’s targeting capabilities extend to CTV, which People Inc. sees as an untapped growth opportunity, Vogel said.

People Inc. is also expanding its non-session footprint on the digital media side, chiefly by launching more video series on social platforms.

One example is “The Intern,” a short-form video series featuring the InStyle editorial staff, which People Inc. is monetizing by allowing brands to sponsor a full season comprising seven three-minute episodes. “We weave that sponsor into the plot line in a wink, wink way that users enjoy,” Vogel said. “They then have the opportunity to layer on events at InStyle, events at People, media across YouTube and Instagram and across all these other places.”

While a show like “The Intern” is “very lucrative and very high margin” on its own, Vogel added, the opportunity to package other digital inventory and live activations into the sponsorship feels “very modern and very exciting for advertisers.”

People Inc. is also packaging more marketing opportunities across its highest-profile brands.

For example, Vogel pointed to People’s revamped “Sexiest Man Alive” offering, which this year features Noah Wyle, star of “The Pitt.”

“What started as a magazine cover, then a web feature, has become a robust franchise that lives across Instagram, TikTok, YouTube, Apple News, our People app and VIP subscription, podcasts and our distribution partners,” Vogel said. “We grew revenue associated with SMA this year 50%.”

The picture is less rosy elsewhere, though. Vogel did what he could to sugarcoat the 6% Q3 decline in session-based revenue by noting it could have been worse. After all, web sessions were down 26%.

But People Inc. offset the traffic decline with higher premium ad rates for both programmatic and direct-sold inventory, Quinn said.

Still, People Inc.’s advertising revenue was down 8% YOY in Q3. Its plan to get back to growth is to keep demonstrating strong performance for advertisers to compensate for traffic declines, Quinn said.

That being said, People Inc.’s performance marketing revenue growth slowed from 13% in Q2 to 2% in Q3. This slowdown was largely due to Amazon Prime Day falling in Q2, which shifted roughly 4% of growth to the earlier quarter, Quinn said.

But People Inc. remains bullish on the opportunity to reach readers directly through its owned-and-operated apps, including MyRecipes and the People VIP paid subscription tier. It’s exploring ways to monetize these apps further, Vogel said.

However, People Inc. has abandoned its plans to parlay its stake in MGM Resorts into a bid to take the company private, Diller said, though it still owns 26% of MGM’s stock and expects to buy more.

Diller also rejected a proposal by MGM to acquire People Inc., he said, adding that he doesn’t see any other proposals meeting his expectations for a sale. Meanwhile, pulling back from the MGM deal should free up some capital for People Inc. to reinvest in the company and buy back its own stock.

People Inc. is open to making its own acquisitions and plans to aggressively pursue M&A opportunities, Diller said, though he noted that any acquisitions would likely be small and “bolt-ons to the publishing business.”

In other news, Quinn said that People Inc. is still holding out hope for a nine-figure damages payout in its ad tech antitrust lawsuit against Google. He noted that USA Today’s Google lawsuit is moving forward and that People Inc.’s is next in line.

If it comes, a court-mandated payout may just be the last big check People Inc. gets from Google for the foreseeable future.

Correction 11/3/26: This article was updated to clarify the difference between People Inc.’s decline in Google search traffic and overall declines in its core sessions. We’ve also updated People Inc.’s overall revenue numbers to focus solely on the company’s media business, rather than revenue for the entire parent company.

#7645. Court seems poised to side with Catholic preschools in religious discrimination dispute

Type to search articles, cases, and authors.

The Supreme Court on Tuesday appeared ready to hold that the exclusion of Catholic preschools in Colorado from the state’s universal preschool program violates the First Amendment. After just over two hours of oral argument in St. Mary Catholic Parish v. Roy, a majority seemed to agree with the challengers that Colorado’s refusal to provide them with an exemption from rules that would require the preschools to admit all students – including LGBTQ children and children with LGBTQ parents – should be subject to a more stringent constitutional test than that applied by the lower court. The court could decide to apply that standard itself or send the case back to the lower courts for them to do so.

Colorado launched the universal preschool program, which provides families in the state with up to 15 hours of free preschool per week at participating schools, in 2023. To participate in the program, preschools must meet a variety of state standards and sign a nondiscrimination agreement, in which they consent to “provide eligible children an equal opportunity to enroll and receive preschool services regardless of race, ethnicity, religious affiliation, sexual orientation, gender identity, lack of housing, income level, or disability.” The preschools cannot decline to serve LGBTQ families, because Colorado believes such refusals would violate the nondiscrimination agreement.

The plaintiffs – the Archdiocese of Denver, two Catholic parishes with preschools (one of which has since closed), and two parents of preschool-aged children – went to federal court to challenge the state’s policy. They contended that requiring Catholic preschools to agree to the nondiscrimination agreement to participate in the universal preschool program constitutes unlawful religious discrimination and that the First Amendment requires Colorado to carve out a religious exemption that allows them to take part in the program.

After both the district court and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the 10th Circuit rejected the challengers’ claim, they came to the Supreme Court last year, asking the justices to take up the case – which the court agreed in April 2026 to do.

Representing the challengers, Nicholas Reaves told the justices that the schools in the Archdiocese of Denver “exist to pass on the faith to the next generation.” “[T]his is not a zero-sum game,” he said, because “letting Catholic schools” participate in the universal preschool program “will create more seats for everyone.”

Representing the state, Colorado Deputy Solicitor General Helen Norton countered that “Colorado welcomes religious preschools to” the program and allows them to teach their religious beliefs. It simply asks them, she emphasized, to comply with the same rules as everyone else.

One of the major points of contention at Tuesday’s argument was the significance of the Supreme Court’s 2022 decision in Carson v. Makin, in which the court struck down a Maine law that allowed public funding to be used for private schools, but not for schools that provide religious instruction. The case was the third in a trilogy of decisions on the availability of public funding for religious institutions. In Carson, the majority applied strict scrutiny – the toughest constitutional test – after it concluded that the Maine law barred some private schools from receiving public funds “solely because they are religious.”

In response to a question from Justice Clarence Thomas about whether a ruling for the challengers would require the court to extend its ruling in Carson, Reaves responded that it would not. In Carson, he insisted, the court’s “focus … was to look at … what is happening to the religious believer?” The court in Carson, he said, “didn’t focus on the text of the law in Maine. It focused on whether schools are being excluded on account of their religious exercise.”

Chief Justice John Roberts pressed Reaves on that point, observing that the law at issue in Carson specifically discriminated against religious schools – which, Roberts suggested, is not the case with the Colorado program.

Reaves pushed back. He noted that the laws in other cases involving public benefits had been neutral, rather than discriminating against religious people or organizations – for example, the court’s 1963 decision in Sherbert v. Verner, reversing a ruling by the South Carolina Supreme Court that had rejected a constitutional challenge to the denial of employment benefits from a Seventh-day Adventist whose religion barred her from working on Saturday.

Roberts later questioned Norton on a related point, asking her to differentiate the Colorado program from the law at issue in Carson and telling her that the effect of the Maine law was “pretty much the same as the effect of the law here.” He also told Norton that the state was trying to “bury Sherbert” even though “nothing in our precedent has backed away from” it.

Two of the court’s Democratic appointees, however, echoed Roberts’ initial skepticism that Carson dictated the outcome of the challengers’ case. Justice Elena Kagan told Reaves that the trilogy of cases culminating in Carson involved laws that had excluded religious institutions and schools because of their religion. “[I]t was a nondiscrimination principle,” she emphasized, but “you’re asking us to” issue a decision that would go “far beyond” its earlier cases. In particular, she suggested, the challengers were seeking a ruling that religious people “need a special accommodation” because of their faith.

Reaves responded that an interpretation of the court’s decision in Carson that focused on whether the law at issue expressly discriminated against religion would be “very easy to circumvent.”

Kagan responded that this isn’t “a good case to raise the kind of specter of circumvention.” “[T]his is a case,” she continued, “of a state trying to enforce its own nondiscrimination principles.”

Justice Ketanji Brown Jackson appeared to agree. She characterized Carson as a case that prohibited governments from treating religious schools worse than it treated secular schools. That doctrine, she posited, was “pretty narrow” and made “perfect sense.” But, she told Reaves, “your schools want to discriminate by exclusion” when no other school participating in the universal preschool program does so.

Some of the court’s Republican appointees were more persuaded by the challengers’ argument – also advanced by Sarah Harris, the principal deputy solicitor general who argued on behalf of the Trump administration in support of the challengers – that Carson should apply even if the Colorado law does not specifically target religion.

Justice Neil Gorsuch, for example, asked “what would be left” of cases like Sherbert “if everything turned on express discrimination” against religion, while Justice Samuel Alito appeared dubious that the legislators who enacted the Colorado universal preschool law “would not understand what the effect of” the law’s requirements “would be.”

Similarly, Justice Amy Coney Barrett asked Norton why, if Colorado cannot expressly exclude religious schools from its program, it can “impose a condition” – the nondiscrimination requirement – that it knows “schools will be unable to agree to?” Barrett pointed to a New York Times op-ed written in the wake of Carson by law professor Aaron Tang, who she stated suggested that states counteract some of the effects of Carson by enacting nondiscrimination requirements.

Norton resisted any effort to link Colorado’s nondiscrimination requirement to an intent to target religious schools, stressing that there was no evidence of the legislature’s motives and (in response to a question from Jackson) that the requirement predated the inclusion of religious schools in the program.

The justices and advocates also debated, although less extensively than the significance of Carson, whether Colorado’s conditions were neutral and generally applied to every preschool, regardless of religion – the kind of government actions, the Supreme Court held in 1990 in Employment Division v. Smith, that are subject to a less stringent constitutional test, known as rational-basis review.

Reaves told the justices that the Colorado nondiscrimination requirement was not the kind of “across-the-board” prohibition that the court envisioned in Smith because the Colorado law contains a series of preferences to facilitate the matching of families to preschools, including a “catch-all” preference that allows preschools to request (and the state to grant) a preference not listed in the regulation. Moreover, he added, the law also creates exceptions to accommodate children with disabilities and children from low-income families.

For her part, Norton characterized the preferences as very different from the kind of exclusion that the challengers seek. Even if a school receives a preference, she stressed, it is still subject to the nondiscrimination requirement.

Justice Brett Kavanaugh appeared to approach the case from what he regarded as a practical angle, asking Norton why the state wouldn’t “seek the win/win?” With over 2,000 preschools participating in the Colorado program, he said, there should be “plenty of opportunities to respect the rights of the religious believers” and, at the same time, “the ability of LGBT parents” to find a school that is a good fit for their families. “Why,” he asked, “has this been provoked?”

Justice Sonia Sotomayor took a different tack, suggesting that a ruling for the challengers could have broader implications. A Catholic preschool, she told Reaves, could reject a child “merely” because his or her parents are LGBTQ. Would this, she queried, also allow a religious preschool to turn down Black children?

Reaves said that it would not. He pointed to a 1983 case in which the Supreme Court, applying strict scrutiny, upheld the Internal Revenue Service’s decision to revoke the tax-exempt status of a private university and private school with racially discriminatory admissions policies. The government in that case, he emphasized, indicated that its interest in prohibiting such policies was not merely “compelling” (the first factor under strict scrutiny) but “overriding.”

He told the justices that strict scrutiny should similarly apply to this case. “And then the government can come forward and say we have a really good reason for” excluding Catholic preschools from the program. But, he concluded, “we just don’t think they’ve done that in this case.”

By the end of the argument, Sotomayor seemed to leave little doubt about where she stood. “No matter what line of cases we follow,” she said, “there will be tremendous problems and a great cost to someone.”

A decision is expected sometime next year.

Amy Howe is the co-founder of SCOTUSblog and its primary reporter.

#7644. Google Plays Hardball With Schoolchildren; Reddit Upvotes Search Ads

Schools looking to ban AI for students are realizing just how much weight Google has to throw around. It’s a story publishers and ad tech companies know well.

As more K-12 schools ban AI, Google is playing ball by turning off the AI features in its products (unless school admins actively opt in to using them). But, because Google has so thoroughly baked AI into its search experience, Google has determined that turning off AI for schools also means turning off search, The New York Times reports.

Call it malicious compliance on Google’s part. After all, Google is kind of known as the search platform (as in, monopolistically). But, if you don’t want its AI, you don’t get its search platform either.

Taking away access to Google search makes the new policy feel like a way “to force AI on us all,” Morgan Polikoff, an education professor at the University of Southern California, tells the Times.

Polikoff may be onto something. After all, Big Tech has untold billions invested in the idea that the next generation must use AI.

By giving schools an ultimatum between permitting AI use or losing access to the largest search engine in the world, says former FTC chair Lina Khan, “Google is making clear it will punish those who don’t fall in line.”

Less than a week after announcing its shift to login-only viewing, Reddit is now beginning to test ad placements in its own search pages, the company shared in a blog post on Tuesday.

Reddit’s search ad algorithm will prioritize contextual relevance. For example, “A search for ‘espresso station’ could surface ads for espresso machines, coffee beans, or mugs,” the blog post reads.

Reddit has long planned to build up its own search platform, since its relationship with Google Search is on the outs.

As Reddit admitted during its Q3 earnings call last week, its search traffic dropped precipitously in October because Google has been sending less users there (or anywhere, really, thanks to the growing prominence of AI Overviews). That’s despite Google relying on Reddit’s content for AI scraping and training purposes.

Meanwhile, Reddit’s ad revenue has grown exponentially, with the company topping a $3 billion run rate for the first time this year. And now that logins will soon be required, users might be more inclined to use Reddit’s internal search engine rather than going to Google and typing, say, “espresso station reddit.”

Maybe there’s a silver lining for Reddit’s notoriously anti-ad user base, though. If marketers can simply buy more kinds of ad inventory on Reddit search, maybe they won’t spend so much time trying to astroturf and spam the actual content of subreddits.

Versant Media Group – the portfolio of networks that Comcast spun off in January – announced its third-quarter earnings on Tuesday. And the results are a mixed bag.

Versant saw a 4% year-over-year drop in revenue to $1.59 billion last quarter, which the company chalks up to general declines in the pay TV industry.

On a better note, platform revenue – which represents revenue from nonlinear sources, such as direct-to-consumer and streaming offerings – was up 10% YOY last quarter.

And it wouldn’t be a TV network earnings report without mention of the live sports biz. Versant closed its acquisition of Full Swing last quarter, building on its existing golf programming portfolio from Comcast, including Golf Channel and GolfNow. As TV publishers compete to grow their live sports offerings, Versant wants to claim golf as its differentiator.

Netflix is launching a new interface called AI Discover to provide more targeted content recommendations to users. [THR]

Disney plans to eliminate thousands of jobs, giving managers a goal of 20% reductions. It’s Disney’s fourth round of layoffs this year. [Bloomberg]

#7643. DoorDash’s Instacart Deal: What A Successful Integration Will Mean For Retailers

Running a local business is already a full-time job. Becoming an expert in every advertising platform shouldn’t become a second one.

So will DoorDash’s $17 billion acquisition of Instacart make local retailers’ jobs any easier?

It can, if the combined company makes its tools practical for businesses that can’t hire a highly specialized marketing team.

Streamlining operations for retail media advertisers is one of the biggest untapped opportunities in ad tech. Which is why consolidation is coming to local commerce.

Recently, DoorDash has added value by partnering and buying rather than building everything itself.

Its 2025 acquisition of Symbiosys, valued at $175 million, extended its advertising capabilities into search, social and display. Instacart would bring deeper grocery expertise, relationships with more than 2,200 retail banners and technology built for the complexity of running a grocery business. Many grocers already use that technology to run their own sites and retail media networks.

For merchants, the question is what they can realistically manage.

Commerce media asks two different things of grocers. Every retailer needs to advertise its own business, reaching shoppers on search, social and delivery apps. Some also run media networks for CPG advertisers, which means selling ad inventory, extending it off-site and demonstrating incrementality to brands that expect closed-loop measurement.

Not every local or midsize grocer needs to launch a network. But whichever role a retailer takes on, it has to do it all on slim grocery margins.

Either way, a retailer should be able to reach more customers without having to become an expert in every advertising platform. That’s the promise for local businesses in the DoorDash/Instacart deal: access to more sophisticated marketing and commerce capabilities without having to assemble and manage every piece. The companies say more grocers could use Instacart’s technology to run their own websites and retail media networks, alongside both companies’ advertising and AI tools.

DoorDash’s moves on the consumer side – particularly its app-bundling strategy – also impact its network’s reach and its usefulness for local grocers and advertisers.

The person ordering dinner and the person buying groceries are often the same person, working with the same household budget. A bundle has to earn its place in that budget.

DoorDash has partnered its way into being more useful to consumers. Since late 2024, US DashPass members who link a Lyft account get 5% off on-demand rides and 10% off up to four scheduled airport rides a month. DoorDash didn’t have to build a rideshare business to offer it.

The Instacart deal applies the same idea to groceries. After closing, households that pay for both DashPass and Instacart+ would pay a single membership fee, which the companies estimate would save members $100 million a year combined.

A membership that covers dinner, groceries and the ride home is easier to justify keeping.

Two adoption questions are converging. For consumers: What makes the service worth trying and the membership worth keeping? For local businesses: What makes these tools practical to use?

Meanwhile, DoorDash paid a lot less for Instacart today – $17 billion – than the rumored $40 billion it was considering back in 2021.

But Instacart isn’t a failed business. It’s growing. On the day the deal was announced, Instacart reported third-quarter orders up 10% and advertising and other revenue up 23% year over year. A company can be doing well and still benefit from a broader path to its next customer.

A broader ecosystem helps in a few ways. DoorDash would give Instacart’s grocery capabilities more occasions for use, from the dinner order to the convenience run. And the companies say Instacart customers would gain access to more than 50,000 additional stores. It could also put Instacart’s tools within reach of more retailers, including stores that couldn’t justify building them on their own.

The companies expect the deal to close in late 2027 or the first half of 2028, which leaves time to show retailers what they’ll get.

DoorDash has committed that local grocers can work with any delivery platform they choose after the deal closes. I’d also want to see measurement that holds up across both apps and a retailer’s own site, as well as ad tools designed for the smallest merchants rather than scaled down from enterprise tools built for the largest.

Whether the deal proves successful depends on whether retailers gain profitable incremental sales while spending less time managing the tools.

#7641. Sports Leagues Can’t Stop Putting Ad Revenue Ahead Of Fan And Player Interests

I recently rewatched the famous Mets vs. Red Sox 1986 World Series game 6 broadcast to celebrate its 40th anniversary.

If you’re not familiar, perhaps you recall the “Curb Your Enthusiasm” episode that plays on former Red Sox first baseman Bill Buckner’s inability to field a ball.

As a Mets fan who wasn’t alive in 1986 and has never seen a World Series victory, this particular game is part of the lore I grew up with. But until this rewatch, I had never been so keenly struck by how much the fan experience of sports has changed.

The 1986 World Series broadcast obviously had no digitally superimposed brand banners behind home plate and along the field walls; nor was the pitcher’s mound virtually branded with a sponsor logo. The broadcast also runs for tens of seconds at a time with just fan noise filling the air.

Today, the silence would be occupied by announcers doing sponsor integrations, picture-in-picture-style ads overlaid on the live broadcast, pop-up marketing along the lower bar of the TV, maybe even an entire commercial break inserted into the action.

There is a powerful undercurrent of disaffection and outright anger from the American populace toward US sporting institutions right now. Often, that manifests as frustration over how complicated and expensive it is to find and watch a game, or private equity ownership of kids’ sports leagues and equipment that drives up the cost to play.

Against this backdrop, griping about advertising taking over sports almost feels quaint, like a throwback to a less-commercialized era.

But this isn’t just about logos cluttering the playing field. Sports leagues and teams are making decisions that sacrifice player safety and the enjoyment of their own fans in various bids for marketing revenue.

The biggest example of sporting greed in recent memory has to be the World Cup “hydration breaks” introduced this year.

Let’s call these what they were: 3-minute-long commercial breaks inserted into the first and second halves of each game.

FIFA proposed World Cup hydration breaks ostensibly on player welfare grounds, since high temperatures were forecasted for some of the games. Never mind that players and coaches blasted the breaks for messing with the usual flow of a soccer game.

During the World Cup, FIFA denied that it was profiting from the breaks. But post-tournament, FIFA has been unabashedly bragging about the breaks’ successful sponsorship haul. FIFA will now require them as part of future World Cup broadcast deals, regardless of whether the host nation’s weather calls for water breaks.

The shameless cash grab of hydration breaks is just one example of how pro soccer leagues prioritize sponsor interests. And the ploy of calling it player welfare is an affront, considering there are real player safety issues that clash with sponsor interests. And the leagues always defer to ad revenue.

Consider those waist-high walls of advertisements – sometimes made of brick or concrete but increasingly composed of LED screens – which are now omni-present around pro soccer fields.

Having just played DIII NCAA soccer, I am shocked by how closely hedged pro soccer fields are by these walls of ads. Players run full-tilt just feet away from these things. And they’re wearing metal-tipped cleats, so any jump over or atop the wall is fraught with accidental danger.

“Players must get hurt all the time,” I’ve often thought. Turns out, they do.

British midfielder Jordan Henderson was forced out of the World Cup with a broken wrist that needed surgery after toppling over a sideline ad board. The Paraguayan men’s team coach called for a reassessment of the practice when his striker was hurt crashing into an ad screen during a game with Australia. Togo international player Samuel Asamoah had his neck broken in a collision with an ad board a year ago. (He’s alive but partially paralyzed.) That incident came not long after Billy Vigar, a young British player coming up with the Chichester City club, died in a similar headfirst tumble.

For years now, players and lower-level leagues without major broadcast sponsor demands have called for reviews of what’s dubbed “pitch perimeter safety.”

The fix is simple. Just move the boards back a little bit. There’s often a huge expanse of space available between the ads and the stadium seats.

But the rationale for having ads hug the perimeter of the field is because that’s how you create viewable inventory for TV. Sponsors are paying for constant on-screen presence, and that’s not feasible if the screens are backed up to a safe distance.

And the problem goes well beyond international fútbol.

The US Open tennis tournament this year made the marketing decision to give many social media creator-influencer types free tickets. Which sparked backlash from players and fans.

The stadiums were full of influencers doing their livestreams and vlogs, not bothering to watch the tennis. And the niceties of tennis etiquette (as in, quieting down during play) were largely lost on the creator crowd. At least one player even stopped midmatch to complain about the smell of weed wafting from the audience (lol).

Whether it’s social media tweenagers muddying the experience of the US Open or a pointless stoppage of World Cup play brought to you by Powerade, it can feel like the wearisome beat of progress or modernity that’s changing these games.

But, actually, the only thing that’s inevitable is sports leagues putting advertisers’ interests above that of fans and players.

Look at the NFL, which is already the most lucrative and heavily saturated sport when it comes to advertising, since it’s a game with plenty of natural stoppages and downtime. But even the NFL can’t resist the temptation to cram in more ads any more than FIFA.

The NFL RedZone channel, created in 2009, for years had the tagline “seven hours of commercial-free football.” But commercials arrived in 2024, and now the show has some 16 ad breaks per Sunday. Relatedly, ESPN acquired the NFL Network and distribution rights to RedZone last year.

And none of the above even approaches the most insidious aspect of modern sports marketing: partnerships with sportsbook apps and prediction markets.

All of the big five US sports leagues – the NFL, NBA, MLB, NHL and MLS (sure, we’ll go ahead and count MLS) – have partnerships with gambling companies and feature them prominently during TV broadcasts. Top players endorse the gambling apps, and the leagues provide live, in-broadcast marketing integrations for betting lines, prop bets and insights from DraftKings, Fanatics, FanDuel, et al.

And yet, these five leagues recently formed a new lobbying coalition to advocate for state laws cracking down on sportsbook app users who threaten or harass players. Call it a stopgap against the inevitability that some fans are going to lose their shirts betting on the games and blame the players.

No wonder sports gambling marketing integrations are mostly loathed by players (presumably aside from those who are paid endorsers). Athletes have to weigh the chance to be the next generation’s childhood hero against being constantly lambasted by young or middle-aged men who’ve lost their paychecks to an app.

The leagues would prefer to offload the issue to state legislatures. But what if the problem is coming from inside their own house?

It is the leagues and their broadcast partners that time and again have failed to uphold standards of quality and, frankly, decency when marketing revenue is in play.

Some of the biggest Super Bowl advertisers of the past few years have been the sportsbooks themselves. DraftKings and Fanatics advertised during this year’s Big Game, while FanDuel ramped up its marketing in the lead-up to the event.

But before the sportsbook apps, there were back-to-back years when the Super Bowl was taken over by Temu – which, not to put too fine a point on it, is a malicious Chinese government infosec data-capture vehicle that also sells shoddy merchandise.  The NFL and CBS let that company buy six Super Bowl ads in 2024.

Before Temu, multiple crypto exchanges, including the now-infamous pyramid scheme FTX, were big NFL and Super Bowl sponsors.

That list seriously calls into question the judgement of the NFL and its Super Bowl broadcasters (primarily NBC or Fox, depending on the year).

Is there seriously no interest in live sports from quality advertisers? Or are more reputable sponsors just being outbid by brands like FTX, Temu and DraftKings?

More worryingly still, do the NFL, CBS, Fox, NBC and the rest no longer know the difference between good and bad brand associations?

The answer can be “Yes all around,” by the way.

But while the leagues might be missing the picture, some of their brand partners aren’t.

Despite the smashing ad monetization success of this year’s World Cup from FIFA’s perspective, its biggest brand sponsors were nonplussed. McDonald’s is pulling its 32-year World Cup sponsorship, which “underperformed our expectations,” CFO Ian Borden told investors during a quarterly earnings report last week.

And other publicly traded brands like Adidas, Visa, Hershey and Coca-Cola are all hard-pressed to justify their sports marketing investments right now.

As those well-known global consumer brands reconsider their sports budgets, they send sports leagues into the open arms of sportsbooks, GLP-1s, crypto exchanges and other forms of cynical advertising.

As always, the losers are the fans and the players.

#7640. Intent Data Is A Gift, With Edible Brands

Edible Arrangements sells 350 SKUs on its website year-round. But for Valentine’s Day and on Mother’s Day, only around 10% of them are available to buy.

That might sound like a counterintuitive move for a retailer on its busiest days of the year. But Edible shrinks its catalog on purpose, says Erica Randerson, chief digital officer at Edible Brands, which owns Edible Arrangements, on this week’s episode of AdExchanger Talks.

The logic is based on shopper behavior. Most gift shoppers, as it turns out, became terrible procrastinators during the pandemic.

Pre-pandemic, many Edible orders arrived a week or even 10 days ahead of a holiday, Randerson says. Now, most come in during the final 48 hours – and those shoppers know what they want, because they’re in a time crunch.

At peak times, on-site conversion rates can hit between 10% and 15% compared with the 3% or 4% that’s typical for ecommerce, a difference Randerson attributes to the high intent that gift buyers bring.

So Edible gets out of their way. Fewer choices means a faster path to checkout and a more manageable load for the franchisees who make and deliver every order. The stakes are high, though. Valentine’s Day and Mother’s Day together drive roughly 40% of Edible’s annual orders.

But gifting data also has a quirk that most ecommerce data doesn’t. Every order has two customers, the buyer and the recipient – and knowing both is a major advantage, Randerson says.

Edible won’t market to a recipient, however, until it gets explicit permission.

“A customer actually cannot even opt their recipient into communications,” Randerson says. “That mechanism doesn’t exist.”

Recipients can opt in themselves, though. Every Edible gift package comes with a hang tag that has a QR code, and if the recipient scans it, they land on a page offering a free gift in exchange for their email address.

That’s a rather traditional albeit effective approach for gathering first-party data. But there’s also a newer source of intent arriving from a very different place: AI search.

Although chatbots currently send less than 10% of traffic to the Edible Arrangements site, those visitors tend to convert better and spend an average of $10 more per order – which “is not insignificant,” Randerson says.

“It’s clear that these channels are helping convert our customers before they get to us,” she says.

Also in this episode: how Edible Brands decides what tech to build in-house versus what to buy off the shelf, how it’s planning for the chaos of Valentine’s Day – which lands on Super Bowl Sunday this year! – and the origin of Edibles.com, its marketplace for hemp-derived THC products. Plus: Randerson’s former life as a competitive clogger.
